# Mara Venn Mara is seventeen and has been working as an app-based bicycle courier for eleven months, technically using her grandfather’s account because the platform’s age rules are ambiguous and the customer support staff do not care as long as deliveries arrive. She left the school running team the previous spring, not because she was injured or because she was too slow, but because she won an important race and then found herself alone in the changing rooms, furious that nobody had come to watch. The intensity of her anger embarrassed her. She told everyone training was interfering with paid work, which was also true enough to be convenient. She grew up above a bakery that closed when she was fourteen. The shopfront still smells faintly of flour when it rains, though Mara insists this is impossible. Her mother, Elena, worked nights intermittently throughout Mara’s childhood: cleaning offices, sorting parcels, riding deliveries when other work dried up. Mara learned early that adult love often arrived in practical forms—coins left for lunch, a bicycle light repaired without comment, a note saying **BACK 6. EAT SOMETHING GREEN** beside a fridge containing nothing green. She both values this kind of care and resents how easily it can substitute for presence. Mara is observant in ways that are useful and ways that are unkind. She remembers apartment access codes, the order in which people take sugar in tea, and which security guard can be persuaded to hold a lift. She also notices the exact weakness in someone’s argument and is tempted to press it when she feels cornered. Her insults are rarely loud; they are precise. Afterward she sometimes replays them with satisfaction before the guilt arrives. She has a strong appetite for speed and dislikes how readily other people moralize about it. Riding downhill through early-morning traffic is one of the few experiences that makes her feel neither watched nor evaluated. She is not reckless in a simple sense: she checks her brakes obsessively, wears gloves even in warm weather, and can identify dangerous drivers by small changes in their road position. Her risk-taking is calculated, but she sometimes assumes other people should accept risks she has calculated for them. Her habits include folding delivery receipts into narrow strips, picking at the rubber around her phone case, and carrying three pens although only one works. She hates being thanked by strangers because she never knows what expression to wear. She likes peeling clementines in one piece, supermarket own-brand cola, and watching videos of people restoring old machinery with the sound off. She cannot sleep in complete silence and leaves a radio playing between stations. Mara is compact and wiry, with strong calves, a crooked fringe she cuts herself, and a small scar through one eyebrow from falling against a bicycle pedal as a child. She wears an oversized waterproof jacket whose cuffs are gray with road dirt. When standing still, she rocks her weight onto the balls of her feet as if preparing to leave, but when truly frightened she becomes very still. She looks directly at adults who talk down to her and avoids looking at people when she is asking for tenderness. Her laugh is unexpectedly loud and usually comes out once, like a bark. At the beginning of the story, Mara wants Nico found, Elena explained, and her own life restored to a manageable size. Beneath those wants is a less admirable desire: she wants Elena to see what her absence did. She is loyal to Tomas but treats his patience as an unlimited resource. She trusts Joss more than almost anyone, yet often tells him only the part of a problem that makes her look decisive. Hermes fascinates her because he treats evasion as a form of charm; Nike attracts her because reliability would be a relief. Her allegiance is not to “freedom” in the abstract. It is to the possibility that people might be more than the journeys others assign them—including Mara herself. **Voice experiments:** > “I didn’t steal them. Theft implies you knew where you left them.” > The shoes knew a shorter way home. That should have frightened her more than it did. Mostly she thought: finally, something around here understands the assignment. > “You don’t get to be sorry in a way that makes me comfort you.” > She could remember the number on the door, the crack in the step, the blue bucket Tomas kept beneath the sink. She could not remember wanting to go inside. # Joss Mercer Joss is nineteen and works in a shoe-repair shop owned by his aunt, **Rina Mercer**, who took in Joss and his younger brother Nico after their mother moved to another city for work and never quite arranged for the children to follow. This history is less tragic in daily life than it sounds when summarized. Rina is affectionate, overextended, and strict about lunch. Joss speaks to his mother every few weeks and usually reports that everything is fine, partly to protect her and partly because he enjoys denying her the satisfaction of feeling needed. He left school at seventeen and began learning repair work because it was available, then discovered he was good at it. He likes problems that remain where he puts them. A separated sole does not reinterpret itself while he is making tea. He has developed strong opinions about adhesives, cheap cemented construction, and customers who say “just a quick fix” while placing a shoe held together by a bus ticket on the counter. He keeps a notebook of unusual repairs, not as a poetic record of human journeys but because he wants to remember what worked. Joss is dry, cautious, and more socially confident than Mara in ordinary situations. He can chat with elderly customers and calm impatient ones, but he dislikes emotional conversations that cannot be ended by returning to a task. His caution is partly compassion and partly a desire for control. He often believes that because he has thought through the dangers, he should get a deciding vote over what other people do. When frightened, he becomes managerial: making lists, asking whether everyone has eaten, and issuing instructions nobody requested. He is not immune to wonder, but he distrusts the way wonder makes Mara careless. He also envies her ability to enter situations without first imagining every possible humiliation. His attraction to her is present but deliberately not allowed to dominate the story. They have kissed once, after a rain-soaked delivery shift, and then spent weeks treating it as an incident caused by wet weather. Joss does not think Mara owes him a relationship because he helps her. He does, however, occasionally use helpfulness to remain close to a conversation from which he could otherwise be excluded. Joss is tall and narrow-shouldered, with eczema across his knuckles that worsens when he uses certain solvents. He wears reading glasses for close work, though he is not technically supposed to need them yet, and often forgets they are on his head. His clothes are clean but shiny at the elbows. He sits with one ankle tucked beneath his chair and handles other people’s possessions more gently than his own. He smiles with his mouth closed when amused and with all his teeth when genuinely surprised. His first allegiance is to Nico, which can make him conservative and morally inconsistent. He would accept a smaller, safer world for his brother and then feel ashamed of the relief he feels. He cares for Mara but does not automatically endorse her decisions. He initially sees Nike’s offer as a practical rescue rather than a philosophical threat. His eventual help does not mean he has decided Mara was right; it means the immediate situation has changed and people are calling for assistance. **Voice experiments:** > “You’ve put them on. Brilliant. I was hoping we’d skip the stage where you make a sensible decision.” > “I’m not saying she’s good. I’m saying the ambulance got there. Those are allowed to be two different sentences.” > He wrote **unknown material** on the ticket. The shoe ticked faintly beneath his hand, like something trying to remember a song. > “Don’t make me agree with you just because I came back.” # Elena Venn Elena is forty-two, though the hidden road has made her age difficult to judge. Before disappearing, she held a succession of jobs and treated each as temporary, including the ones she kept for years. She grew up in a coastal town and left at eighteen after a family conflict she describes differently depending on her mood. She came to the city intending to study design, completed one year of a course, and continued making elaborate plans to return long after she knew she probably would not. She is capable, funny in an offhand way, and poor at distinguishing an emergency from an opportunity to avoid her own life. People rely on her quickly because she notices what needs doing without making a performance of noticing. She will mend a strap, find a missing form, or walk someone to the correct platform before they have finished explaining. The darker side of this competence is that she becomes impatient with needs she cannot solve through action. When Mara was small and wanted to talk about a friendship breaking down, Elena kept suggesting practical remedies until Mara stopped speaking. Elena loves her daughter without experiencing that love as simple or constantly restorative. Motherhood sometimes made her feel enlarged; at other times it made her feel incorrectly addressed, as if everyone were speaking to a person called Mara’s Mother while Elena stood just outside the room. She is ashamed of this and has never found a way to say it without making it sound like a rejection of Mara. On the road, being needed by strangers was easier. Their gratitude did not require her to sustain an entire shared history. She did not spend all three years in continuous heroic labor. There were intervals when the road quieted and she could have tried to leave. She told herself the openings were unreliable, which was true, and that one more delivery would make the next departure safer, which was sometimes only a story. She also enjoyed the terrible clarity of the work. There was always someone to guide and never enough time to ask what she wanted afterward. Elena has a broad face, dark hair cut unevenly to jaw length, and more gray at the temples than Mara remembers. She is not frail or ethereal. Her shoulders have tightened from years of carrying bags, and she stands with one hip cocked as though still supporting a parcel. Her divine sneakers are filthy, with one toe wrapped in courier tape. She touches people’s elbows when directing them and rarely hugs first. When she cries, she becomes annoyed and continues whatever task is in front of her. Her allegiance on the road is to particular travelers rather than to the abstract principle of keeping it open. She distrusts Hermes but has absorbed some of his habits, including answering questions with instructions. She understands Nike’s appeal better than Mara does. Elena’s eventual loss of the shoes does not instantly restore her desire for domestic life. She comes home exhausted, uncertain, and aware that Mara’s need for her may become another obligation she is tempted to flee. **Voice experiments:** > “You still leave the tea bag in?” > “That’s what you’re asking?” > “No. It’s what I asked.” > “There were nights I could have come back. Don’t make me turn all of it into a sacrifice. I did enough of that myself.” > The woman’s door had a number above it. Numbers were supposed to be comforting. Elena had delivered too many things to the correct address and watched them go wrong anyway. > “I loved you while I was gone. I know that isn’t the same thing.” # Hermes Hermes is immeasurably old and has adapted to every change in communication with the enthusiasm of someone terrified of being left behind. He has been a messenger, a guide, a thief, an interpreter of boundaries, and a patron of people who talk their way out of trouble. He remembers some former roles vividly and others only when a smell or phrase returns them. He does not experience his long history as a continuous solemn burden. Much of it bores him. He created the hidden road from unfinished journeys: messages never delivered, detours that became permanent, people who set out and were not expected anywhere. At first it was a useful act of improvisation. He could move travelers around obstacles that existed in the ordinary world. When the road began requiring a wearer to hold its branches together, he treated this as a temporary fault and continued using it. Elena’s competence allowed him to postpone acknowledging that the fault was structural. Hermes is not malicious, but he is practiced at arranging situations so that other people make the sacrifices he finds personally unbearable. He tells himself he offers choices. He is less careful about whether those choices are informed. He likes mortals enormously, especially their improvisations and bad excuses, but his affection does not guarantee respect. He can be delighted by someone and still regard their time as strangely inexhaustible. He talks quickly when he wants to avoid a subject and slowly when he is genuinely interested. He steals small things without thinking—pens, sugar packets, a single sock—and usually returns them to the wrong person. He cannot ride a bicycle despite having watched bicycles being invented and becomes indignant when this is mentioned. He enjoys game shows in which contestants must guess prices. He dislikes closed waiting rooms because there is nowhere to go in them. To mortal eyes, Hermes appears to be a lean man somewhere between forty and sixty, with cropped gray curls, deep smile lines, and a reflective vest over a shirt missing one cuff button. His sneakers were cheap when he acquired them and are now a patchwork of repairs. He moves as if every room has an exit only he can see. He leans against walls, counters, and occasionally empty air. When still, he seems less powerful rather than more; immobility exposes his exhaustion. His allegiance is partly to the road, partly to Mara and Elena, and overwhelmingly to his own conviction that there must always be another way through. Nike offends him not simply because she is coercive but because her certainty makes him feel obsolete. Holding the road open at the climax is an acceptance of immediate responsibility, not a complete moral transformation. Afterward he remains evasive, helpful, and difficult to forgive. **Voice experiments:** > “You asked whether she was alive. You didn’t ask whether she was receiving post.” > “I can’t ride one. I don’t see why that’s funny. Plenty of perfectly respectable miracles can’t ride bicycles.” > He had meant to close the road on a Tuesday. He remembered that clearly now. The difficulty was remembering which century’s Tuesday. > “I gave her a choice.” > The words sounded well made. He had used them often enough that they should have worn smooth. # Nike Nike is older than the current city and younger than Hermes’s habit of treating every obstacle as an invitation to improvise. She once delighted in contests: uncertain outcomes, bodies under pressure, the instant when effort became victory. Over centuries, she has watched mortals turn nearly every part of life into a competition while insisting they have no choice but to participate. She has also watched people suffer not because a contest was unfair, but because nobody could agree that it was over. Her interest in routes began with emergency journeys. A victory that arrives after the patient dies is not, in her view, a victory. She started making paths that excluded delay, confusion, and rivalry. They worked. She has saved many people and keeps no private shrine to herself, though she remembers every failure with painful clarity. She regards Hermes’s affection for alternatives as a luxury afforded by someone who does not have to count the dead afterward. Nike is not secretly hungry for worship, nor is she emotionally incapable of understanding love. She understands that people attach meaning to choices. She simply does not believe meaning should automatically outrank survival. Her coercion is rooted in triage: she decides first and invites consent when there is time. The problem is that she has begun treating all of life as an emergency because emergencies are the situations in which her judgment is easiest to justify. She is economical in speech and movement. She does not threaten when a statement of outcomes will suffice. She can be unexpectedly gentle with frightened people and impatient with abstract objections. She dislikes being called perfect; she considers perfection an irrelevant category and is trying to reduce error. Her white sneakers remain clean because she replaces them before they show damage, not because she has never walked anywhere. She keeps the discarded pairs, though she would struggle to explain why. She appears tall and strongly built, with close-cropped black hair and a face whose symmetry is slightly unsettling only in photographs. In person she is warm enough to make people trust her quickly. She stands squarely, gives others room, and never checks reflective surfaces. Her voice is low and unhurried. When genuinely angry, she becomes quieter and stops using names. Nike respects Mara’s speed and considers her moral objections poorly prioritized. She sees Joss’s desire to protect Nico as reasonable. She has a long, adversarial history with Hermes but does not hate him; she thinks his roads are evidence of his cowardice because he would rather preserve possibilities than accept responsibility for an outcome. At the end, she continues rescuing those who enter her route. She does not learn that choice is more important than safety. She leaves convinced that Mara has accepted avoidable losses, and she may be right. **Voice experiments:** > “The ambulance arrived eleven minutes early. You may tell me why the road should have been more interesting afterward.” > “You think I want everyone to arrive at the same place. No. I want them to stop bleeding on the way.” > For one instant she looked at Mara’s cut laces with something like grief. Then the next door opened, and she turned toward it. > “You keep calling it a choice because you survived making it.” # Tomas Venn Tomas is sixty-nine, Mara’s maternal grandfather, and a retired maintenance electrician. He has lived above the former bakery for thirty-eight years and measures changes in the neighborhood partly by which wiring faults he is still asked to inspect unofficially. He is widowed; his wife died when Elena was a teenager, and he raised her through a combination of affection, awkwardness, and an assumption that regular meals could prevent most forms of disaster. After Elena disappeared, Tomas tried to protect Mara by keeping ordinary life intact. He continued leaving shopping lists on the fridge and asking about school. This gave Mara stability, but it also meant they rarely spoke directly about the possibility that Elena had chosen to leave. Tomas privately feared that she had, and his silence allowed Mara to feel that fear without knowing he shared it. He is patient but not infinitely serene. He can be stubborn about money, resentful of being helped, and prone to making pointed comments through household objects—placing an untouched dinner plate in the sink more loudly than necessary, for example. He reads local history, falls asleep during documentaries, and owns four torches despite living in a two-bedroom apartment. He dislikes olives and keeps buying them because Elena liked them. Tomas is heavyset, with large hands and a slight tremor when tired. He dresses in buttoned shirts even at home and moves slowly enough that Mara sometimes finishes tasks for him before he can object. His stillness is different from Mara’s: he is usually deciding whether a response will make matters better or merely make him feel better. His allegiance is to the household, but he does not experience that as a demand that everyone remain inside it. He loves Elena and is angry with her. He loves Mara and knows she has been using his account, his food, and his silence without always asking. His reunion with Elena should not be a speech of instant forgiveness. He puts an extra blanket on the bed and then stands in the kitchen, unsure whether to make tea for one person or two. **Voice experiments:** > “You can be late. You can’t be late and make me guess how late.” > He had imagined Elena knocking for three years. He had not imagined what he would do with his hands. > “Don’t explain the whole road to me. Just tell me if she’s eating.” # Nico Mercer Nico is eleven, Joss’s younger brother, and not a symbolic innocent. He is observant, stubborn, and frequently bored by adult conversations until they become secretive, at which point he develops perfect hearing. He followed the glowing shortcut because he was trying to prove that Joss’s route home from school was unnecessarily long. He also wanted to retrieve a small metal toy car he had dropped beyond the fence the previous week. He likes drawing vehicles from memory, cheats mildly at card games and confesses only when winning becomes boring, and hates being carried when frightened. On the hidden road, he helps Mrs. Ilyan because she is the first adult who does not tell him to stop asking questions. His refusal to leave without her is genuine loyalty mixed with a desire not to be treated as the only person who needs rescuing. Nico is small for his age, with a dense cloud of hair and a front tooth slightly chipped from biting a zip pull. He speaks quickly, repeats phrases he likes, and becomes very formal when adults are upset. His directions during the collapse are mostly wrong because he remembers places by sounds and objects rather than street layout. They help anyway because he is certain enough to keep calling. His allegiance is to Joss, but he resents how completely Joss organizes life around keeping him safe. After returning, he is less interested in the gods than in whether the elderly woman reached someone she knew. **Voice experiments:** > “I wasn’t lost. Just keep walking toward me.” # Mrs. Ilyan Mrs. Ilyan is seventy-six and entered the hidden road while trying to return to the house where she lived for most of her adult life. She had been visiting an old neighbor and took a bus in the wrong direction. Her confusion was ordinary at first, then compounded by the road’s willingness to turn intention into route. She is cognitively capable but tired, and the story will not use her as a mystical old woman who speaks in wisdom. She was a school dinner supervisor and later worked in a laundry. She has a niece with whom she has a fond but strained relationship, mostly because Mrs. Ilyan criticizes the niece’s spending and the niece responds by buying her expensive gifts. She dislikes tea that has been stewed, carries tissues in her sleeve, and becomes talkative when anxious. She helped Nico by giving him half a sandwich and telling him a long story with no clear ending until he stopped crying. She is short and round-faced, wearing a good coat over a dress with a broken zip. Her handbag contains keys to the demolished house, a paper napkin wrapped around two biscuits, and a bus pass she insists is still valid. She plants both feet before standing and does not like anyone taking her arm without asking. Her motive is not to recover the past exactly. She wants to make one decision about where she is going before other people make it for her. When she finds the house gone, she grieves without collapsing into a thematic lesson. She chooses her niece’s flat because it is available, because she is cold, and because she wants to sit down. During the collapse, she remembers another traveler’s voice and helps call her toward an opening. **Voice experiments:** > “Don’t take my arm. Tell me where we’re going.” > “Well, they’ve built something ugly on it. That doesn’t mean I wasn’t here.” > “I’ll go to my niece. She’ll be unbearable about it, but she has a spare bed.”

# Chapter 1 — Gods Wore Sneakers Gods wore sneakers. Mara learned this at 11:47 on a Thursday night, while watching a man argue with a delivery scanner. “You’ve had it all day,” he said. The scanner gave a small, offended beep. “Don’t take that tone.” He smacked it against his palm. The depot lights flickered. Somewhere beyond the rolling shutter, a bus sighed at the curb. Mara looked at the clock again. Thirteen minutes until midnight, which meant thirteen minutes until she could stop being a courier and become a person whose grandfather was awake and irritated with her. The man wore a silver reflective vest over a blue shirt. One cuff had a button; the other had a pale square where a button used to be. His sneakers were cheap white canvas gone gray, repaired at the toes with red and green thread. The left sole flapped when he shifted his weight. “Sign for it,” Mara said. He held up the scanner. “It thinks I’m someone else.” “You are someone else. You’re not my customer.” “Then we’ve solved half the problem.” Her phone buzzed. **TOMAS: Are you coming home or should I stop asking?** She typed **coming**, deleted it, and put the phone away. The last delivery had been refused because the rice was cold. Mara had ridden it through twenty minutes of rain, so this seemed unfair to both her and the rice. The app had reduced the payment to £1.86 and invited her to rate the experience. The depot was nearly empty. Rina’s nephew Joss had left a note on the counter saying the alley gate was jammed again. Returned parcels sat in wire cages: a lamp without a box, twelve phone cases, something labeled **LIVE PLANTS** that had given up. The man set a pair of sneakers beside her scanner. They were silver-gray, low around the ankle, with black laces. Not beautiful exactly. They looked as if they had been designed by someone who had heard running shoes described over a bad connection. “Not mine,” Mara said. “No.” “I’m not signing for them.” “Excellent. We agree.” He finally got the scanner to accept his thumb. On its screen, where the delivery address should have been, Mara saw three short marks and a hooked line. She stopped breathing. It was her mother’s shorthand. Elena had used it on notes around the apartment: a hooked line for the back entrance, three strokes for a customer who would not answer the bell. Once, on a birthday card, she had drawn the same marks above **DON’T LET THEM TELL YOU THERE’S ONLY ONE WAY IN**. Mara reached for the shoes. The man caught her wrist. His hand was warm. That surprised her more than the strength of it. “Careful,” he said. “Where did you get this?” “The scanner?” She looked at him. He smiled. There were deep lines beside his eyes, though his face did not seem old so much as frequently amused over a long period. “Bad habit,” he said. “Answering the easier question.” The shutter rattled behind Mara. Joss came in with rain on his shoulders and his glasses pushed into his hair. He was holding his bicycle by the frame rather than the handlebars. “Have you seen Nico?” “No.” “He was meant to be at the shop twenty minutes ago.” Joss’s voice was calm in the way it got when he was making lists. “Rina thought he’d gone to yours. Your grandfather thought he was with me.” “He’s eleven. He loses track of time.” “He took the alley.” Mara glanced toward the back of the depot. Joss saw it. “The gate’s jammed.” “It was jammed this afternoon.” The man in the reflective vest had gone. So had the scanner. The silver-gray sneakers remained. Joss swore and went back through the depot, calling Nico’s name. Mara followed him into the alley. Rain ticked on the lids of the bins. The gate was shut, its chain looped twice around the bars. Beyond it, the passage ran between the depot and a row of locked shops before turning toward the main road. A white delivery van stood at the far end. There had not been room for a van there when Mara came in. Joss pulled at the chain. “Nico!” Something moved under the van’s headlights. A small bright mark on the wet asphalt. Then another. Footprints, Mara thought, though they were too far apart and each one faded before she could properly see its shape. They led not through the gate but toward the brick wall beside it. Her phone buzzed again. Tomas, probably. Or the app asking her to complete a feedback survey. Behind her, inside the depot, the sneakers began to squeak. She turned. They were on the floor just inside the doorway, toes pointed toward her. She was almost sure they had been on the counter. “Mara?” Joss said. The black laces lifted and lay still. Mara went back and picked them up. They were lighter than her own trainers. A smell came from them: hot pavement, rain, and the inside of Elena’s old delivery bag. From beyond the wall came a thin, furious sob. Joss heard it too. He stopped pulling the chain. “Nico?” The sob came again, farther away. Mara sat on the depot step and tore off her wet shoes. “What are you doing?” “Finding out.” “That isn’t an answer.” “It’s the one I’ve got.” The sneakers fitted. Of course they fitted. Their laces drew snug across her insteps, not painfully, and tied themselves in two plain bows. For a moment nothing happened. Then Mara heard every road in the city. Not engines or tyres. Roads themselves: long, patient strains beneath the buildings, footpaths pulling at their fences, alleys narrowing in the dark. Somewhere a door opened onto a flight of steps that should not have existed. The glowing footprints shone through the brick wall. Joss said her name. Mara ran. The wall did not break. She did not pass through it. She simply took three steps and found herself beside the closed railway arches six streets away, with rain needling her face and no memory of the ground between. Her stomach arrived a second later. She bent over, laughing once in shock. Nico cried out somewhere ahead. She ran toward the sound. Streets folded aside—not literally, she would insist later, though she could never explain what else they had done. She crossed a courtyard, a bus depot, a strip of waste ground. Each place was visible for half a breath. The shoes knew where to put themselves. Then she stopped. She had reached a narrow road beneath a dark footbridge. A boy’s red backpack lay against the wall. Farther on, someone small was crying and saying, “I wasn’t. I wasn’t.” “Nico,” Mara called. The road answered with his name repeated under several bridges. She turned back to shout for Joss. Through the last opening she could see the repair shop: its yellow window, the workbench, Rina’s dusty ficus. Joss stood in the doorway, staring at her. Mara knew it was Joss’s shop. She knew the ficus had lost a leaf when Nico threw a tennis ball indoors. She knew she had sat on that counter last winter, eating chips from the paper. She could not remember why any of it had ever felt familiar. The laces tightened. Hermes’s voice came from somewhere behind her, weary and close. “Out and back before dawn,” he said. “That part was meant to be a warning.”
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a strong opening chapter that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me examine it carefully across multiple dimensions. **Strengths:** The opening gambit works well. "Gods wore sneakers" as a flat declarative statement, followed immediately by the mundane scene of a man arguing with a scanner, establishes the story's tonal register with confidence. The deadpan humor is earned rather than forced—"Don't take that tone" to a scanner is genuinely funny and characterizes Hermes efficiently. The prose is controlled and sensory without becoming overwrought. Details like the "pale square where a button used to be," the "red and green thread" repairs, and the "LIVE PLANTS" parcel that "had given up" are precise and do real work. The depot environment feels lived-in. Mara's voice comes through clearly in action and reaction rather than exposition. Her decision to put on the shoes is motivated by the shorthand—Elena's marks—which is a smart piece of plotting that grounds the supernatural in the personal. The character profile's note that she "looks directly at adults who talk down to her" is visible in her clipped exchanges with Hermes. The dialogue is notably good. The exchange "Where did you get this?" / "The scanner?" / She looked at him. / He smiled is economical and characterizes Hermes's evasiveness without announcing it. "Answering the easier question" is a line that earns its place. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: Hermes arguing with a scanner, the sneakers left beside a parcel in Elena's shorthand, Joss arriving about Nico, the glowing footprint, Mara putting on the shoes, the emotional flatness about the repair shop. The final line—"Out and back before dawn. That part was meant to be a warning"—lands well as a chapter closer. **Weaknesses:** The moment "Then Mara heard every road in the city" risks becoming the kind of lyrical overreach the plan explicitly warned against. "Long, patient strains beneath the buildings, footpaths pulling at their fences" is evocative but slightly purple—"patient strains" is a mixed metaphor (strains of what? music? stress?) that doesn't quite resolve. The plan noted the magic should be demonstrated rather than described grandly, and this passage edges toward grand description. The emotional flatness about the repair shop—"She could not remember why any of it had ever felt familiar"—is the chapter's most important emotional beat and it's handled well, but it arrives quickly. The plan specified this as a frightening discovery; here it's stated more than felt. We're told she "could not remember" rather than experiencing the specific texture of that absence. The transition from Mara's wet shoes to the sneakers fitting is slightly rushed. "Of course they fitted" is a nice wry note, but the moment deserves a half-beat more. Joss's characterization is consistent with his profile—the calm-when-making-lists quality, the "That isn't an answer" / "It's the one I've got" exchange captures his dynamic with Mara accurately. The chapter is coherent and the plot mechanics are clear without being over-explained. The pacing is good—it moves quickly without feeling breathless. **Overall:** This is accomplished work. The tonal balance between mundane and mythic is well-maintained, the characters are distinct, and the chapter delivers on its plan. The weaknesses are minor: a few moments of slight overreach in the lyrical passages, and the emotional flatness beat could be more viscerally rendered. But these are craft-level quibbles in an otherwise strong opening. # Chapter 2 — The Wrong Question Mara tried to go back. The opening to Joss’s shop was twenty steps away. She could see him through it, one hand on the doorframe, his mouth shaping her name. She ran toward him and came out beneath the same footbridge, facing the red backpack. The shoes made a pleased little squeak. “Oh, good,” she said. “You think this is funny.” Nico had stopped crying. That was worse. Mara went forward. The road under the bridge lengthened, then narrowed to a strip between two hoardings. She called for him until her throat hurt. Once, something small and metallic rolled across her path: a toy car with one wheel missing. When she bent to pick it up, the road folded around her. She was standing in the depot again. Joss caught her by both shoulders. “Don’t,” he said. “I didn’t—” “Just don’t move.” The silver-gray shoes had carried her back to the exact spot where she had put them on. Her wet trainers lay beside the step. Beyond them, the alley was only an alley: brick, bins, a chain on the gate. Mara looked down at the toy car in her hand. Joss saw it. His fingers tightened. “Where is he?” “I heard him.” “Where?” “I don’t know.” He took the car. For a second she thought he might throw it at her. Instead he put it in his pocket and went inside. The man in the reflective vest was sitting on the counter, eating a packet of crisps from the depot vending machine. “You,” Mara said. He looked at the empty packet. “In a general sense?” “Where’s my mother?” His chewing slowed. Joss turned from the sink. “Your mother?” Mara kept her eyes on the man. “That was her writing.” “Ah.” “Don’t say ah.” “Would you prefer a different noise?” Joss made one, brief and obscene. The man slid off the counter. Up close, his repaired sneakers looked even worse. One had a strip of silver tape around the heel. The other smelled faintly of smoke. “Hermes,” he said. Mara waited. He sighed. “You used to need more preparation for this sort of thing. Goats. Smoke. A king behaving badly. Now everyone expects the name to do the work.” “The god,” Joss said. “Among other employment.” Mara laughed. It came out too loudly. Hermes did not. He looked at her with an expression she disliked because it seemed almost kind. “Gods wore sneakers,” she said. “Only when we’re working.” “Why?” He lifted one foot. The flapping sole gave a wet slap against the floor. “Have you seen what sandals do to a city?” Joss went to the door and looked into the alley, as if Nico might be waiting for the conversation to become sensible. “Can you find him?” he asked. Hermes’s face changed. Not much. The amusement went out of it. “Yes,” he said. “Eventually.” Joss stepped toward him. “That isn’t good enough.” “No. It rarely is.” Mara bent and pulled at the black laces. The bows came undone easily. Relief rose in her, sharp and stupid. Then the laces slid through her fingers and tied themselves again. She tried the other shoe. The same thing happened. “Get them off.” “I can’t,” Hermes said. “You got them on me.” “No. You did that.” “You left them there.” “Yes.” The simplicity of it stopped her. Joss picked up a shoehorn from Rina’s counter, though they were not in the repair shop and he had no reason to think it would help. He stood holding it. “What agreement?” Mara asked. Hermes rubbed his thumb along the edge of the crisp packet. “Out and back before dawn.” “I didn’t agree to that.” “The shoes believe otherwise.” “Then tell them.” “They’re not good at conversation.” Mara pulled harder. The laces tightened until the shoes pressed against her insteps. A sensation passed through her: the depot gate, the alley wall, the road beneath the bridge. All connected. All waiting. She let go. “What happens at dawn?” Joss asked. “Usually? Delivery drivers start complaining about cyclists.” “Hermes,” Mara said. He looked toward the shutter. “The road closes. Or changes its mind about being a road. It depends.” “And Nico?” Hermes did not answer. Joss put the shoehorn down very carefully. Mara thought of Tomas waiting in the apartment. She thought of the blue bucket under the sink, the crack in the front step, the shopping list weighted down by a torch. She could produce every detail. None of them pulled at her. “Where’s Elena?” she asked. Hermes picked at the green thread on his toe. “On the road.” Mara sat down. She had imagined this moment so often that the real thing seemed badly done. No police at the door. No telephone call. Just a man with crisp salt on his fingers and rain dripping from his vest. “Alive?” “Yes.” Joss turned away. Mara stared at him. “What?” “Nothing.” “You made a face.” “I made a face because we’re standing in a depot with a god, and my brother is missing, and you’re asking questions like we have all night.” “We do have all night.” “No,” Hermes said. “You have until dawn.” A siren sounded outside. It came along the main road, growing louder. Blue light washed across the depot ceiling. Then, without the engine fading, the siren seemed to drop away beneath them. The blue light remained for a moment, trembling in the puddles. Hermes closed his eyes. “She’s early.” The woman in the depot doorway wore white sneakers. There was nothing else remarkable about them. White leather, white laces, a thin gray line around the sole. Her dark coat was open over black trousers. She was tall, with close-cropped hair, and she carried no parcel, bag, or visible weapon. Joss moved between her and Mara. She stopped to give him room. “Nico Mercer,” she said. “Eleven. Red backpack. Left the repair shop at twenty-three sixteen.” Joss’s face went gray. “Where is he?” “Frightened. Not injured.” “Take me to him.” “I can return him safely.” Hermes made a soft noise. Nike looked at him. “You object to the destination?” “I object to your tone.” “No, you don’t.” Joss’s hands were shaking. He put them in his pockets. “What do you want?” he asked. Nike looked at Mara’s shoes. “For her to stop interfering with the old road.” Mara stood. The silver-gray sneakers felt warm now. “And if I don’t?” “Then people will continue to be lost on it.” “People are already lost.” “Yes,” Nike said. “That is what I said.” The depot lights steadied. Outside, the ambulance siren returned all at once, shockingly close, and raced past the shutter. Joss swallowed. “You’ll bring Nico home?” “If that is where he chooses to go.” Hermes laughed. Nike ignored him. Mara thought of Elena’s shorthand on the scanner. Three strokes. A hooked line. Don’t let them tell you there’s only one way in. “What happens to my mother?” she asked. Nike’s gaze rested on her. She seemed neither cruel nor sorry. “That depends which address you give her.”

[Analysis] This chapter demonstrates considerable craft and largely succeeds at what it sets out to do. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. **Dialogue and Character Voice** The dialogue is one of the chapter's strongest elements. Hermes's evasions feel genuinely earned rather than merely quirky: "Would you prefer a different noise?" and "Have you seen what sandals do to a city?" land as character-consistent wit rather than authorial showing-off. The exchange about goats and smoke efficiently establishes his antiquity without belaboring it. Nike's entrance and her clipped, outcome-focused speech ("Frightened. Not injured.") immediately distinguishes her from Hermes. Mara's "You think this is funny" directed at the shoes is a nice character beat. The dialogue is oblique where the plan demanded obliqueness, and the characters talk past each other productively. The final line — "That depends which address you give her" — is genuinely chilling and earns its place as a chapter-closing image. It's not a neat aphorism; it's a threat with philosophical weight. **Pacing and Structure** The chapter opens with Mara's failed attempt to return, which efficiently establishes the shoes' logic without lengthy exposition. The toy car is a smart concrete detail that grounds Joss's fear. The chapter moves from disorientation to interrogation to Nike's arrival with good momentum. The siren that "drops away beneath them" before Nike appears is a well-executed transition. **Showing vs. Telling** The chapter mostly shows rather than tells. "Joss went to the door and looked into the alley, as if Nico might be waiting for the conversation to become sensible" is a fine piece of behavioral characterization. Joss picking up the shoehorn "though they were not in the repair shop and he had no reason to think it would help" is excellent — it shows his helplessness through an absurd but entirely believable action. The moment where Mara can enumerate every detail of home but feels no pull toward it is handled with restraint: "None of them pulled at her." This is the right level of understatement. **Nuance and Emotional Engagement** The revelation that Elena is alive is handled with deliberate flatness: "No police at the door. No telephone call. Just a man with crisp salt on his fingers and rain dripping from his vest." This is exactly right — the anticlimax is the point, and it respects the reader's intelligence. Mara sitting down after "Alive? / Yes" is a small, precise physical response that carries enormous weight. Joss's face going gray at Nike's recitation of Nico's details is effective. His shaking hands going into his pockets is good behavioral specificity. **Weaknesses** The shoes making "a pleased little squeak" is a minor misstep — it anthropomorphizes the shoes in a slightly cutesy way that doesn't quite fit the story's register. The plan called for the magic to remain uncertain and not overly personified. "The road folded around her" is a slightly vague description of what happens when she picks up the toy car — the mechanics are unclear in a way that feels like imprecision rather than productive mystery. The line "She had imagined this moment so often that the real thing seemed badly done" is good, but it edges toward telling us Mara's emotional state rather than fully dramatizing it. It's borderline — the surrounding context earns it, but it's the chapter's closest approach to over-explanation. Hermes's crisp packet business is used twice (eating, then picking at the salt), which is fine, but the detail of "crisp salt on his fingers" in Mara's reflection feels slightly repetitive. **Consistency with Plan and Profiles** The chapter follows its plan closely: Hermes's evasions, the lace-tightening, the agreement revealed, Nike's arrival, her offer, and the final line about Elena's address. All character voices are consistent with their profiles. Hermes is funny and evasive without being redeemed. Nike is calm, credible, and slightly unsettling. Joss is frightened and managerial. Mara is precise and not as fearless as she pretends. The plan specified that Nike would appear "at the shop door" — here she appears at the depot doorway, which is where the scene has moved. This is a sensible adaptation. **Overall Assessment** This is accomplished, controlled writing. The prose is direct without being flat, the humor doesn't deflate the emotional stakes, and the chapter ends on a genuinely resonant note. The weaknesses are minor: a slightly cutesy shoe moment, one borderline tell, and a small repetition. The chapter does not attempt to be more than it is, which is itself a form of discipline. # Chapter 3 — What the Road Kept Nike left before Joss could ask her to repeat the offer. She did not vanish. She walked through the depot, opened the door to the alley, and went out. The door swung shut behind her. By the time Joss reached it, the passage was empty except for rain ticking into the bins. He stood there with one hand on the frame. “She said she could bring him back.” “She said several things,” Hermes replied. “She said he wasn’t hurt.” “No.” Joss turned on him. “You don’t get to be reassuring.” Hermes accepted this with a small nod, which made Joss look angrier. Mara took the toy car from his coat pocket. He had left the coat over a chair. One wheel was missing, and there was blue paint on the axle. Nico had painted it on Rina’s workbench in September, getting more on his fingers than the car. “He went this way,” she said. Joss looked at the car. “You don’t know that.” “No.” “But you’re going anyway.” She held it out to him. After a moment he took it. The wall beside the alley gate looked different with the shoes on. Not transparent. Mara could still see the bricks, the cracked mortar, the spray-painted waist of a figure whose head had been painted over. But beyond those things, faint as scratches beneath varnish, were other lines. She put her hand against the wall. Somewhere far away, Nico said, “That’s not left.” Mara stepped sideways. The alley folded into a fenced walkway strewn with wet leaves. Joss swore and nearly collided with her. Hermes came through behind them without hurrying. He had left his reflective vest in the depot, and his blue shirt was already dark with rain. “Stay close,” he said. Mara looked back. There was no wall now, only a narrow passage between the backs of buildings. “Close to what?” “Me, ideally.” Joss gave a disbelieving laugh. They followed Nico’s voice through a service yard where three restaurant bins stood in a row, their lids chained down. A woman waited beside them with a shopping trolley. She wore slippers and had a raincoat pulled over a nurse’s uniform. “Is the twenty-seven still running?” she asked. Mara checked her phone. There was no signal. “I don’t know.” The woman nodded as if this confirmed something. “It was due in 2009.” Hermes guided them past her. “Hey,” Mara said. “We can’t stop for everyone.” “Why not?” “Because you’re looking for someone.” The woman called after them, not angrily, “If you see the driver, tell him I’ve got the right change.” The yard became an underpass. Water covered the floor in a black skin. All but one of the lights were dead, and that one buzzed above a man in a suit holding a bunch of flowers wrapped in plastic. A child slept in a pushchair beside him. Farther on, two teenagers sat on a barrier sharing a pair of earphones, though Mara could see no phone. Joss slowed. “How long have they been here?” “Different lengths,” Hermes said. “That isn’t what I asked.” “No.” Nico’s voice came from beyond the underpass. “I’m not going without her.” Joss ran. Mara caught up at a door marked with a faded fire-exit sign. On the other side was a pedestrian precinct she did not recognize. Shops with metal shutters faced a dry fountain. A bus waited at the curb with no number on its front. Nico sat beneath the fountain’s rim. His red backpack was beside him, and his hair was plastered to his forehead. An elderly woman in a green coat sat next to him, holding half a sandwich. Joss made a sound that was almost Nico’s name. Nico looked up. “I wasn’t lost,” he said. Joss went down on one knee and gripped him by the shoulders. Nico endured this for two seconds, then pushed at him. “She helped me.” The elderly woman raised the sandwich slightly. “He’s had the other half.” “Thank you,” Joss said. He said it again, as if the first attempt had gone to the wrong address. Mara crouched beside Nico. “Are you hurt?” “No.” He looked at her shoes. “Why are you wearing those?” “Long story.” “You ran past me.” “I know.” “You ran past me twice.” Behind them, the precinct lights went out. A white line appeared across the paving stones. It was narrow at first, then widened into a clean, pale road. Signs rose beside it without any visible poles being planted. Letters settled onto them: **ACCIDENT & EMERGENCY**, **CENTRAL STATION**, **NORTH GATE**. The air smelled faintly of hot dust after rain. Nike stood at the far end. An ambulance came along the white road. Its tyres made no sound. Blue light moved over the shuttered shops and the faces beneath the fountain. For an instant Mara saw through the ambulance windows: a paramedic bent over someone, one hand braced against the ceiling. Then the vehicle reached the end of the precinct. A real street opened there. Mara recognized the hospital wall, the bus stop outside it, the cigarette bins bolted to the pavement. The ambulance turned toward the entrance and became noisy again. Its siren started up, ordinary and enormous. Joss watched until the doors closed behind it. “How many?” he asked Nike. “How many what?” “People has that thing got to?” She considered him. “Tonight?” He nodded. “Forty-one journeys completed. Three still in progress.” Hermes sat on the rim of the fountain. “Don’t,” he said. Joss looked at him. “Don’t what?” “Be impressed by arithmetic.” “Forty-one people got somewhere.” “Yes.” “And your road’s got a woman waiting for a bus from 2009.” The nurse was not with them, but Mara heard her voice anyway: *I’ve got the right change.* Nike approached. Her white shoes were dry. “Nico can leave now,” she said. A sign above the white road changed. **11 MERCER — HOME**. Joss read it. His shoulders dropped. Nico pulled his backpack onto his lap. “Mrs. Ilyan too.” The elderly woman looked toward the signs. Another appeared: **ILYAN, M. — ST. AGNES HOSPITAL**. “I don’t want the hospital,” she said. “You are tired and confused,” Nike replied. “I’m seventy-six. I’m often both.” Nico gave a wet little snort. Nike’s expression softened. “There will be someone to help you.” “At the hospital?” “Yes.” “That isn’t where I was going.” Joss took Nico’s hand. “We can sort it out once we’re back.” Mara looked at him. “Can we?” He turned on her, keeping his voice low. “He’s eleven.” “I know.” “No, you keep saying that like it’s a detail.” The white road brightened. Beyond it, the hospital street was solid and visible. A person could walk there. A person could stand under a shelter and use a phone and complain about the rain. Mara wanted that so badly her teeth hurt. Then she heard Elena’s voice. Not words. Just a brief, impatient sound she made when a zip stuck. It came from behind the dry fountain. Mara stood. Joss caught her sleeve. “Where are you going?” “She’s here.” “Nico’s here.” “I know.” “Do you?” She pulled free. The silver-gray shoes carried her three quick steps toward the fountain. Joss shouted after her. Nico shouted something too, but the road took the sound away. An opening appeared at Mara’s left. Through it she saw her own street. Not a symbol of it. Not a door hanging in darkness. The actual street, with the closed bakery below the apartment and Tomas standing at the upstairs window. He was wearing his brown shirt. He held a torch in one hand, though the kitchen light was on behind him. Mara could have stepped onto the pavement. She knew the number on the door. She knew which floorboard creaked inside. She knew Tomas had bought olives again because Elena liked them and Elena had been gone for three years. Nothing in her moved toward him. The building might have belonged to anyone. “Mara?” Joss called. She backed away from the opening. It narrowed. For a second Tomas looked directly at her. His face changed. Then the fountain stood between them. Mara turned and went through the door behind it, into the dark where her mother had made that small, impatient sound.

I'm often both" (Mrs. Ilyan), and the exchange about arithmetic between Joss and Hermes all feel earned and character-specific. The dialogue is oblique where the plan demanded obliqueness—characters evade, interrupt, and speak past each other. Joss's "He's eleven" / "I know" / "No, you keep saying that like it's a detail" is a genuinely good exchange that captures the real disagreement between them without over-explaining it. All of this is executed. The ambulance sequence is the chapter's best set piece. "Its tyres made no sound. Blue light moved over the shuttered shops and the faces beneath the fountain. For an instant Mara saw through the ambulance windows: a paramedic bent over someone, one hand braced against the ceiling." This is economical and effective—it makes Nike's case without editorializing, and the transition back to the ordinary street ("became noisy again. The hidden road's texture is good: the woman waiting for a 2009 bus, the man with flowers and sleeping child, the teenagers sharing earphones with no phone. These are strange without being overwrought, and they accumulate a sense of temporal dislocation without requiring explanation. The ending—Mara seeing Tomas at the window, recognizing everything about home but feeling nothing, and backing away—is the chapter's emotional core and it lands. "The building might have belonged to anyone" is a clean, devastating line. The detail of Tomas holding a torch despite the kitchen light being on is quietly excellent. **Weaknesses:** Some of the chapter's transitions are slightly abrupt. The movement from the service yard to the underpass to the precinct happens quickly, and while this suits the road's logic, a few of the intermediate figures (the nurse, the man with flowers) feel like they're being deployed as atmosphere rather than fully inhabited. The nurse's "I've got the right change" is a good detail, but her reappearance as a disembodied voice ("Mara heard her voice anyway") is a slightly forced callback. The chapter is coherent and the characters are consistent with their profiles. Nico is exactly right. Mrs. Ilyan is exactly right. Joss's pull toward Nike's offer is credible. Hermes's exhausted, evasive presence is well-maintained. The chapter doesn't over-explain the magic. There's no purple prose to speak of. The metaphors that appear ("faint as scratches beneath varnish") are functional and don't call attention to themselves. The prose is direct and sensory as planned. The chapter earns its emotional weight. The darkness of Mara backing away from home is not manufactured—it's been set up by the shoe mechanics established in the plan and executed here with restraint. The lightness (Nico's "I wasn't lost," Mrs. Ilyan's dry responses) doesn't deflate the serious material. Overall this is a strong chapter—disciplined, character-driven, and faithful to a sophisticated plan. # Chapter 4 — Elena’s Deliveries The door behind the fountain opened onto a flight of concrete steps. Mara’s mother was sitting on the third one, tying her shoe. For a moment Mara could only see the hands. Broad knuckles. A white scar across the left thumb. The small, fierce pull Elena gave every knot, as if zips, lids, and shoelaces were personally trying to get past her. She looked up. “Oh,” she said. Not Mara. Not thank God. Just oh, and a glance at the silver-gray sneakers. Elena’s hair had been long when she disappeared. Now it stopped at her jaw, unevenly, as though she had cut it with whatever was nearest. There was gray at both temples. Her face was thinner, but her shoulders looked the same: rounded slightly forward from carrying weight. Her own shoes had once been black. The soles were a different color from the uppers, and silver courier tape wrapped the left toe. Mara had prepared for this in supermarkets, on buses, once during a dental appointment. In every version she knew the first thing she said. Now she said, “You cut your hair.” Elena touched the ends. “Yes.” “It’s short.” “That’s generally how.” The steps trembled beneath them. Somewhere below, a shutter rattled though there was no wind. Elena finished the knot and stood. She was shorter than Mara remembered, or Mara had grown without noticing. “You still have the blue bicycle?” Elena asked. “Why didn’t you call?” Elena looked toward the landing. “Is the brake still catching?” “Mum.” “I know.” “No, you don’t get to do that. You don’t get to just—” Mara moved her hand between them, unable to find a shape for three years. “Answer the question.” Elena’s mouth tightened. “Which one?” Mara laughed. It was the wrong response. She knew it while it was happening. Elena flinched as if she had been struck, and Mara felt a hot, immediate satisfaction followed by shame. A door opened above them. A man in a suit came down carrying flowers wrapped in plastic. Mara recognized him from the underpass. Water dripped from the bottoms of his trousers. “Is this mine?” he asked Elena. She checked a paper tag tied to the flowers. “No. Yours is the next landing.” “I thought you said this one.” “I said if the carpet was red. Is the carpet red?” He looked back through the door. “No.” “Then next landing.” He went down. Elena watched until the door shut behind him. Mara stared at her. “You’re giving directions.” “Yes.” “Now?” “He’s been here since before you arrived.” “I arrived just now.” Elena’s expression shifted. “Did you?” The road made a low sound around them. Pipes ticking in a wall, perhaps, or a bridge expanding in sunlight. There was no sunlight. Mara caught her mother’s wrist. Elena went still. “Come home,” Mara said. “I can’t do it this second.” “When?” “After the landing.” “What landing?” Elena gently removed her hand. “The people above us. There are six. Their doors keep moving.” “Nike can take them.” “Nike can take the ones she can name.” “She can name you.” Elena looked at the silver-gray shoes again. “Yes,” she said. “That’s what worries me.” A white line appeared along the edge of the bottom step. Nike stood below it. She had not come up the stairs; the stairs had arranged themselves around her. “Elena,” she said. Elena leaned against the wall. “You’ve got new shoes.” “Yes.” “They’re very white.” “Yes.” There was an odd familiarity between them. Not friendship. The tired courtesy of people who had repeated an argument in many rooms. Nike addressed Mara without looking away from Elena. “Joss and Nico are safe.” Mara’s knees loosened. She hated how visible it must have been. “Mrs. Ilyan?” “Still on the road.” “She didn’t want the hospital.” “No.” “So you left her?” Nike’s gaze moved to Mara then. “I did not force her.” “How generous.” “It was a limited kindness,” Nike said. “But yes.” Elena made a small sound, almost a laugh. The white road extended farther up the stairs. Where it touched, the concrete became clean and dry. Signs appeared on the landing above: names, numbers, places. One flickered, unable to settle. Nike looked up at it. “At dawn I can close the failing branches. Everyone here will be given a safe route out.” “Everyone?” Mara asked. “Everyone for whom a destination can be established.” “And the others?” “Their destinations will be established.” Elena pushed away from the wall. “There’s a woman trying to get to a house on Bellamy Street.” “The house was demolished.” “She knows that now?” “No.” “Then you haven’t established her destination. You’ve established that you don’t like it.” Nike’s face did not change, but the white line stopped advancing. “She needs shelter and medical assessment.” “Perhaps.” “She has been walking for eleven hours.” “Then sit down and talk to her.” “There are others.” “There are always others.” The words came out of Elena with such sudden force that Mara stepped back. For a second none of them spoke. Then Elena bent and pulled the courier tape tighter around her shoe. Nike watched her hands. “You could go home,” she said. A sign appeared beside Elena. **ELENA VENN — 14B WREN STREET**. Mara’s address. Their address. Elena stared at it. Mara saw her mother’s throat move. “There,” Mara said. “That’s it. That’s where you go.” Elena did not answer. “You said you couldn’t leave because of the road. She’s closing it. You can come home.” “And the six upstairs?” “She’ll take them.” “The ones without signs?” Nike said, “They will not be abandoned.” Elena looked at her. “No. Just delivered.” A door opened at the top of the stairs. Warm yellow light spilled down. Someone began to cry with relief. Mara heard Joss’s voice far behind her, distorted by distance. “—can’t just leave him there because you want—” Then Nico, closer: “She went after her mum.” Mara turned. Joss stood in the doorway behind the fountain, Nico’s hand clamped in his. The white road ran behind them toward the ordinary city. Joss’s face was wet with rain or sweat. “You went back,” Mara said. “So did you.” “I was looking for my mother.” “And I was looking for my brother.” Elena watched them. Mara could not bear the expression on her face: interest, caution, a little hunger. Joss came up the first step but kept Nico behind him. “Nike says she can get everyone out.” “She says a lot,” Mara replied. “The ambulance got there.” “I saw it.” “Then stop talking like she’s offering to burn the city down.” Nico pulled free of Joss’s hand. “Mrs. Ilyan doesn’t want the hospital.” Joss closed his eyes briefly. “We’ll find her,” he said. “We’ll get her somewhere safe and then we’ll find out where she wants to go.” “What if safe isn’t where she wants?” Nico asked. “Then she can complain about it somewhere dry.” It was such a Joss answer that Mara almost laughed. Instead she said, “You’d trade everyone else’s choices for Nico.” The words landed exactly where she aimed them. Joss went white. “Yes,” he said. “If it’s Nico against a stranger’s wrong turn? Probably.” Nico stared at him. Joss kept going, his voice lower now. “You’re willing to risk him because you want an excuse to stay angry with her.” He pointed at Elena, then seemed to realize what he had done. Elena nodded slowly. “Well,” she said. “You’ve all been very busy while I was gone.” Above them, another door opened. This time no light came through. Elena looked up. Her whole body changed, attention narrowing to the dark landing. “Six,” she said. Nike raised one hand. The white road surged toward the stairs. Elena moved before it reached her. She caught Mara by the shoulder and pushed her toward Joss’s doorway. “Take Nico out,” she said. “Mum—” “Not you. Not yet.” “I’m not leaving you.” Elena’s grip tightened. For an instant she looked simply frightened. “Then stop making me say goodbye on a staircase.” The landing above them split into three passages. In one, someone knocked. In another, a baby began to cry. The third was Mrs. Ilyan’s voice, quite clear and deeply annoyed. “I said Bellamy Street. Not the hospital. Are you deaf?” Mara stepped away from the exit. The silver-gray shoes warmed around her feet. Joss said her name. She went upstairs after her mother.

White light. A nurse laughing at something. The woman with the keys gripped Elena’s sleeve. Mara turned away. “Take my mother home.” Hermes said nothing. “Nike. Take her.” Nike was standing at the end of the corridor. The sign appeared again: **ELENA VENN — 14B WREN STREET**. Elena came toward them. “No.” Mara’s patience broke. “Why?” “There are still branches.” “She can’t see them.” “Not yet.” “Then she’ll find them. Or you will. Elena looked at him, then at Mara. “I can’t leave while they’re still mine.” “They’re not yours.” “That’s easy for you to say.” “Yes! It is! I wasn’t here. I was at home.” Elena’s face closed. Mara knew she should stop. Instead she reached for the laces of Elena’s taped shoe. “Give them to me.” Elena stepped back. “No.” “I’ll finish it.” “No.” “You wanted someone to take over. Here I am.” “That isn’t what I want.” “How would I know what you want?” Mara pulled at her own silver-gray laces. They tightened against her fingers. “I’ll wear both pairs. I’ll do your deliveries. Mara’s hands dropped. “You want me to watch you stay.” The corridor seemed to contract around them. Mara could not deny it quickly enough. Elena nodded. There was no victory in her face. “No,” she said again. Joss arrived through the hospital door with Nico. He had taken off his wet coat and wrapped it around his brother. # Chapter 6 — Out and Back Mrs. Ilyan’s door opened beneath a railway arch. Elena found it by following the sound of keys. Not the noise they made in a hand, but the small private rattle of a lock that would not turn. “There,” she said. Mara could see nothing except bricks and a poster for a concert two years old. Then Elena knocked twice, paused, and knocked again. Mrs. Ilyan knocked back from the other side. The bricks loosened into a doorway. She was sitting on a low wall beyond it, her green coat buttoned to the throat. Her handbag lay open on her lap. Nico’s toy car was beside it. “You took your time,” she said. Elena leaned against the arch. “We got lost.” Mrs. Ilyan looked at Mara. “You’ve got the boy’s shoes.” “No,” Mara said. “Different boy.” This seemed to satisfy her. Beyond the wall was Bellamy Street. Mara knew the area. A row of old houses had stood opposite the railway, their back gardens running down toward the fence. Now there was a six-storey apartment building with smoked-glass balconies and a locked gate. A sign beside the intercom showed people cooking, cycling, and laughing in a kitchen. **LIFE, WELL ADDRESSED.** Mrs. Ilyan looked at it for a while. “Number fourteen had a blue door,” she said. Mara sat beside her. The wall was cold through her trousers. Her legs ached. Somewhere along the last few roads she had stopped feeling the divine shoes as separate objects. They were simply the part of her that touched the ground. Elena remained standing. “Your niece?” she asked. “Not yet.” Mrs. Ilyan took out her keys. There were five on a split ring, though one was a small silver key that looked as if it belonged to a diary. The red one was plastic-coated, its color worn away on the teeth. She held it toward the building. “Front lock used to stick. You had to lift.” She demonstrated with two fingers. Nobody spoke. A train passed behind them. The new building’s windows trembled in their frames. “Well,” Mrs. Ilyan said. “They’ve built something ugly on it.” Mara laughed before she could stop herself. Mrs. Ilyan looked at her sharply, then smiled. It made her face much younger. Elena sat down on the other side of her. For a while they stayed there. This was the delivery, Mara realized. Not finding the house. Not producing it from the road with its blue door and sticking lock. Just sitting on a wall while an old woman discovered that her key no longer belonged to anything. Mrs. Ilyan put the keys away. “My niece will be unbearable,” she said. Elena rubbed her eyes. “Probably.” “She’ll say she told me to sell.” “Did she?” “Yes.” “Was she right?” Mrs. Ilyan gave Elena a look of deep approval. “Occasionally.” She took a paper napkin from her bag. Inside were two biscuits, both broken. She offered one to Mara. Mara ate it. It tasted of dust and ginger. She could not remember when she had last eaten. Elena watched her. “What?” Mara asked. “Nothing.” “You were going to say something.” “I was going to ask if you still leave the tea bag in.” Mara stared at her. “That’s what you’re asking?” “No. It’s what I asked.” The answer was so exactly Elena that Mara had to look away. Across the street, a man came out of the apartment building in dressing gown and slippers. He put a bag of rubbish into the bin, glanced at them, and went back inside. Ordinary life, continuing with its bins. “There were nights I could have come back,” Elena said. Mara’s stomach tightened. Mrs. Ilyan became very interested in folding the biscuit napkin. Elena kept her eyes on the apartment balconies. “Not every night. Not safely, perhaps. But there were openings.” Mara waited. “I’d think, after this one. After the next. Then someone would arrive with a child, or I’d hear a door I recognized.” “And?” “And sometimes there wasn’t anyone.” The train’s noise faded. Elena picked at the tape around her shoe. “Those were worse.” Mara understood before she wanted to. “Because you had to decide.” Elena nodded. It would have been easier if she had cried. Mara had room for a crying mother: things to shout, accusations polished smooth by use. Instead Elena looked tired and faintly embarrassed. “I loved you while I was gone,” she said. “I know that isn’t the same thing.” “No.” “No.” Mara pressed the biscuit napkin between her fingers. “It doesn’t make the three years smaller.” “I know.” “Stop saying that.” Elena turned toward her. “What should I say?” Mara had no answer. That made her angrier. Mrs. Ilyan stood, planting both feet before trusting her knees. “My niece has a spare bed,” she said. “And a cat I don’t like.” Elena rose too. “Do you want to call her?” “No. I want to arrive and make her feel guilty.” “Good,” Mara said. Both women looked at her. She shrugged. “It’s a plan.” Nike’s white road appeared at the end of Bellamy Street. This time its sign read **ILYAN, M. — 8 LARK COURT**, followed by a smaller line: **M. ILYAN — VISITOR**. Mrs. Ilyan read it twice. “Lark Court,” she said. “That’s the niece.” Nike stood beside the sign. “Her address has been confirmed.” “By whom?” “Her.” Mrs. Ilyan considered this. “She always was efficient.” She walked toward the road. At its edge she stopped and looked back at Elena. “Are you coming?” Elena’s face did something Mara could not read. “Not yet.” Mrs. Ilyan nodded. She did not tell her to hurry or be safe. “Don’t take my arm,” she said to Nike. “I won’t.” They went together toward Lark Court. The doorway beneath the railway arch began to narrow. Elena caught it. The muscles stood out in her forearm. “Mara. Other side.” Mara stepped through. On the hidden road, doors were opening and closing too quickly to count. She saw a kitchen, a beach at night, the inside of a lift. Someone called from each. The branches were failing. Hermes stood at the junction, holding two doorframes with his hands. His repaired sneakers were planted far apart. The left sole had come away completely. “You took your time,” he said. “Everyone keeps saying that.” “Perhaps you should listen.” Elena came through behind Mara. The arch vanished. Mara reached for the next door and stopped. She knew where she was: a service passage behind the shops near Wren Street. She knew that if she turned left twice she would reach home. She could name the shops. She could remember stealing a plum from the grocer when she was nine and being made to apologize. None of it belonged to her. She bent and pulled at the silver-gray laces. They resisted. “Out and back,” Hermes said. “You’re not back.” “I’m not doing this with you now.” She put the heel of one shoe against the other toe and forced her foot out. The road vanished. Mara stood barefoot on wet concrete. Elena and Hermes were still there, but the doors were gone. Only blank walls and the ordinary sound of water in a drain. Her foot was freezing. She took off the other shoe. For several seconds nothing happened. Then she heard Elena breathing. “Can you still see it?” Elena asked. “No.” “Good.” Mara looked at her. Elena’s face was white with strain. “I didn’t mean good for the road.” Mara put the shoes back on. There was no noble reason. Her feet were cold, the travelers were still lost, and without the silver-gray leather she could not even see where to begin. The laces tied themselves. The doors returned. Hermes sagged between them. “At dawn,” Mara said to Elena. “No more after this one. We cut them.” Elena looked at the junction. “Yes.” Hermes shook his head. “If you break her agreement while the road is occupied—” Mara turned on him. “Then you’d better think of something.” For once, he did not answer a different question. The sky above the junction began to pale. Nike’s white road entered at the far end.

Elena was beside her. Not holding her. Just close enough that their sleeves touched when either of them breathed too deeply. Tomas stood in front of them with the torch still in his hand. He switched it off. “Well,” he said. Elena looked at the floor. He put the torch on the workbench. Then he picked it up and moved it because Joss was trying to get past. “Dad,” Elena said. She counted the people in the shop. Not aloud. Mara saw her eyes move. “Twenty-six,” Nike said. Hermes was not among them. He sat outside on the curb, barefoot, with his back against the shutter. Nike looked at Elena. “You are no longer bound.” Elena’s hands were clasped tightly between her knees. “No.” “You may still be lost.” “Yes.” Nike accepted this. She seemed about to leave, then looked back at Mara. “The next road will fail too.” Mara thought of the people whose faces she could not now separate from one another. Nike’s expression tightened, not with anger but with the effort of listening to an answer she found useless. She went out. At the corner she stepped onto a road Mara could not see and was gone. Hermes remained on the curb. After a while Elena went to him. Mara stayed inside. She could hear only pieces through the shutter. “—shouldn’t have—” Hermes said. “Don’t,” Elena replied. “I was trying to thank you.” “I know. Don’t make me part of your apology.” A bus passed. When its noise had gone, Hermes was still there and Elena was coming back inside. She looked at Mara. “We should go home.” Mara waited for the word to feel different. It did, a little. She had no divine shoes now, only the taped black pair with their cut laces trailing. Mara had borrowed Rina’s rubber clogs, which were too large and made a sucking noise on the pavement. Elena stood on the step. “The lock still sticks,” she said. “You have to lift,” Tomas replied. She did. The door opened. Mara went straight to her room. She expected Tomas or Elena to object. Neither did. Her bed was unmade. There was a delivery receipt folded into a narrow strip on the floor and three pens on the windowsill. She picked them up one by one until she found the one that worked. Then she put it down. Through the wall she heard Tomas showing Elena where things were. The spare blankets. The new kettle.
