Model Output:
# Intention I want to write a compact, first-person dark comedy about grief, cowardice and the awful administrative afterlife of a dead teenager. The story will be set over three days around the six-month anniversary of a death in a rain-worn Midlands town: closed shops, a comprehensive school with a wellbeing display, a canal everyone calls “the cut,” and a bus service theoretical enough to qualify as folklore. The narrator is **Mara Ellison, sixteen**, funny because she is frightened of being sincere. Her best friend, **Nia Bell**, died after going into the canal six months earlier. The official account is that Nia left a party alone while drunk and upset; the town has since converted her into a memorial hashtag, a school “reflection space,” and content for **Joss**, Nia’s self-dramatising ex, who runs a small true-crime social account. Mara has allowed everyone to believe she tried to meet Nia that night but arrived too late. In fact, after an argument, she ignored Nia’s messages and stayed at home watching television. Her lie is not the cause of Nia’s death, but it has shaped the public story and protected Mara from examining her own behaviour. At 00:03, Mara receives **🩸🩸🩸 from Nia’s phone**, which she believes is still with Nia’s mother. Two other people receive it: Joss and **Priya**, the third member of their old friendship group. The sender is eventually revealed to be **Sol Bell, Nia’s thirteen-year-old brother**. He found the phone in a box of returned belongings and has spent months reading its messages. He has concluded, with the absolute moral confidence and terrible investigative methods of a grieving thirteen-year-old, that three people know why Nia went to the canal. The blood drops were Nia’s private shorthand for “emergency: come now,” originally a joke about a catastrophic period during a school trip and later used for everything from emotional crises to being out of money. Sol is summoning the recipients to account for themselves. This will not become a supernatural story or a serial-killer thriller. Nia’s death remains an accident arising from ordinary vulnerability, alcohol, an unlit stretch of canal and a delayed response; there is no secret murderer and no revelation that makes everything neatly meaningful. The real danger comes from Sol’s plan and Joss’s exploitation of it. Sol has sent Joss selected screenshots and arranged a midnight meeting at the canal, intending to force a joint confession. Joss, seeing an opportunity for content, hints publicly that new evidence will emerge at the anniversary vigil. Mara’s attempts to suppress her own messages and control the story make things worse and briefly expose Priya, whose actual secret is painful but not culpable: Nia had asked her for money to leave town after a frightening encounter with her controlling adult ex, and Priya, broke and fed up with Nia’s chaos, refused. This gives the story different kinds of guilt without distributing blame like a puzzle solution. The climax will be a confrontation between teenagers and a grieving child, not a police showdown. At the canal, Sol plays Nia’s final voice note and demands that each person explain themselves while Joss records covertly. Mara finally states the truth without defending it: she was awake, she saw Nia asking to meet, and she chose not to go because she was angry and tired of being needed. She also rejects Sol’s implied tribunal—Nia was not a saint, and no single message contains a complete person. When Sol, overwhelmed, goes too close to the unstable canal edge, the physical emergency is brief and credible: Mara and Priya get him back, not through heroics but through frightened, awkward cooperation. Joss’s recording is exposed; Mara does not win by delivering a perfect speech but by taking the phone from him, stopping the performance, and accepting that he may publish her messages. The important act is that she stops bargaining over whether the truth makes her look bad. The final chapter will deal with proportionate consequences rather than redemption. Mara tells Nia’s mother and her own mother what happened, gives a corrected statement to the police liaison officer without requesting a new investigation, and returns Nia’s phone to the family. Sol is not instantly healed and does not forgive her. Joss loses some status but is not cartoonishly destroyed. Mara and Priya do not magically restore their old friendship, though they can sit together. The closing image will be small: Mara deletes her drafted “my truth” post, changes the memorial group chat from its true-crime name back to something stupid Nia chose, and at 00:03 leaves her phone face-down while she talks to her mother. If a final message appears, it will be an ordinary message from Sol asking whether Nia really once got banned from a supermarket; Mara answers with a true, unflattering, funny story. This lets Nia return as a person rather than an omen. Stylistically, the prose will be quick, specific and socially observant, with jokes arising from school bureaucracy, grief merchandising, bad tea, group-chat etiquette and Mara’s evasions. Mara will occasionally address the reader or correct her own narration, but not constantly. Her defensiveness should be visible before she admits it; readers may suspect her lie by Chapter 3. Each chapter will centre on one strong scene and end on a turn rather than a mechanical cliffhanger. Flashbacks will be short and triggered by concrete objects or messages, keeping the present plot moving. I will avoid graphic descriptions of Nia’s death, jokes about self-harm, a miraculous recovery for anyone, an elaborate suspect board, and a last-minute villain responsible for everything. I will also avoid making Mara’s lie equivalent to causing the death. The story’s moral pressure is narrower and more uncomfortable: she failed a friend in an ordinary way, then lied about it, and grief made that lie publicly useful. The aim is for the reader to laugh, then realise the laugh was standing next to something painful. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — “Three Drops”** At 00:03, Mara receives 🩸🩸🩸 from Nia’s number. Her first responses are darkly practical and increasingly unhinged: check whether it is a wrong number, inspect the battery percentage, consider throwing her phone into the airing cupboard. The chapter establishes Mara’s voice, her exhausted night-shift mother, and the anniversary vigil planned at school. Mara replies “who is this,” then sees the message read and receives a second line: **“You know what you did.”** She does not call the police. Instead, she opens the old chat with Nia and scrolls past the point where her own messages stop. **Chapter 2 — “The Bereavement Pack”** At school, the anniversary is being managed with a wellbeing display, a “memory ribbon” table and a form tutor who keeps calling Nia “Nina.” Joss is filming restrained-looking content and hints that the vigil may be significant. Priya reveals that she also received the blood drops; Joss admits he did too but performs certainty about what they mean. Mara proposes the sensible explanations—hacked account, cruel prank, phone reused—while privately ruling them out. Sol appears outside school trying to return something to the office and watches the three of them. Mara recognises Nia’s old phone case in his hand but does not connect it immediately. She tells Priya she barely spoke to Nia during her final week, the first clear version of her lie. **Chapter 3 — “Nia Bell: The Brand”** Mara and Priya visit Nia’s mother, **Ruth**, under the pretext of helping with vigil flowers, hoping to establish where the phone is. The visit is excruciating and funny in small ways: Ruth has been sent unsolicited memorial candles, the kettle is descaled with something violent, and everyone talks around Nia while sitting beneath her school photograph. Ruth says the police returned a box of belongings weeks ago and Sol has been sleeping badly; she assumes the phone is still in the box. Mara steals a look and finds the box open. Sol catches her. He asks whether Mara was really on her way to meet Nia, repeating Mara’s own public account back to her. Mara lies to his face. On the way home, she receives a screenshot of her final message to Nia: **“Not tonight. I can’t keep doing this.”** **Chapter 4 — “Read at 00:17”** The midpoint turns the mystery inward. The sender sends all three recipients different screenshots and orders them to the canal at midnight after the vigil. Mara recognises the blood-drop code from a school-trip memory: Nia used it whenever she needed someone to come without asking questions. Joss insists the messages prove Nia was being threatened and wants to build the revelation into his vigil livestream. Priya confesses her screenshot to Mara: Nia asked for train money after an encounter with her adult ex, and Priya refused. Mara, terrified of her own screenshot emerging, persuades Priya not to tell Joss or Ruth and takes Nia’s old backup phone from Priya, ostensibly to check the code. Alone, Mara reads the full exchange from the night Nia died. The reader now learns with her that Nia asked specifically for Mara, Mara refused, and Nia replied **“ok. love you anyway.”** Mara deletes the screenshot from her own phone, which achieves nothing and makes her feel briefly better. **Chapter 5 — “The Vigil Has Been Sponsored”** The school vigil combines genuine grief with excruciating presentation: balloons despite a request for no balloons, a raffle prize left over from the summer fair, and Joss positioning a ring light behind the candles. Mara’s mother attends unexpectedly, making Mara’s performance harder to sustain. Joss plays an edited montage of Nia and hints that someone in the room knows more than they have said. Priya realises Mara has been protecting herself, not her, and their alliance breaks. Sol is missing from the family row. Mara finds his message on Nia’s phone—she has brought the backup device with her—saying he is already at the cut and will send everything to Joss unless Mara comes alone. Instead of confessing publicly, Mara tries to seize control: she tells Joss that Sol is the sender and that he is vulnerable, hoping this will stop the broadcast. Joss hears only “exclusive” and follows her. **Chapter 6 — “Come Alone (Everyone Comes)”** Mara walks to the canal with her mother’s unanswered calls lighting her pocket. Priya catches up, furious but unwilling to let her go alone; Joss follows at a distance, filming. The comic machinery drops away as the setting becomes physically unpleasant: mud, broken fencing, the memorial bench, rain on the same unlit steps Nia used. Sol is there with Nia’s phone and a portable speaker, having planned a tribunal with the sophistication of a school presentation. He plays snippets of messages and demands that Mara repeat her story. Mara initially offers a technically truthful, self-exculpatory version. Sol then plays Nia’s last voice note, sent after Mara refused: Nia is drunk, frightened and annoyed, but also joking about Mara being “a tiny coward in a big coat.” The note ends before the accident and explains nothing. Its ordinariness breaks Mara’s remaining defence. Joss steps out of the dark still recording, and Sol realises he has been used. **Chapter 7 — “The Tiny Coward Speech”** Mara takes Joss’s phone and stops the recording rather than negotiating with him. She then tells Sol, Priya and—on speaker, after her mother arrives with Ruth—the whole truth: she was awake, angry, and at home; she did not set out too late; she lied because the lie made her a better grieving person. She does not claim she could have saved Nia. Priya tells her own part without allowing Sol to turn it into a confession of murder. Sol insists somebody must have known Nia was going to the cut; Mara says knowing someone is unhappy is not the same as knowing what will happen, a sentence she hates even as she says it. Sol moves toward the edge in anger and slips; Mara and Priya pull him back over the muddy barrier in an undignified tangle. There is no cathartic embrace. Ruth takes Nia’s phone from Sol and asks everyone to stop telling her who her daughter was. Mara hands Joss’s phone back and tells him to publish her messages if he wants. He does not, at least that night, which is not quite the same as decency. **Chapter 8 — “Normal Service Will Not Resume”** Over the following week, Mara gives Ruth and the police liaison officer the unedited messages, corrects her account at school without making a spectacle of the correction, and accepts that some people will think worse of her. Joss posts a vague statement about “respecting the family” and loses his exclusive; his comeuppance remains mostly social and incomplete. Sol refuses Mara’s initial apology but later sends one practical question about Nia. Mara and Priya sit together at the memorial bench and share chips without declaring themselves healed. Mara tells her mother the truth at the kitchen table; her mother is angry about the danger first and hurt about the lie second, which feels almost bearable. Mara deletes her drafted public confession and changes the group-chat name back to **“Nia’s Big Hat Funeral”**, an old joke with no explanatory value to anyone else. At 00:03, Sol messages from his own number asking whether Nia really was banned from Tesco for putting a traffic cone on a statue. Mara answers with the full story, including the part where Nia abandoned her and ran. She then puts the phone face-down and goes to help her mother make tea.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
A human approaching this prompt would probably begin less with a complete moral architecture and more with an itch: the obscenity of a dead friend’s phone lighting up, the idiocy of three little blood drops, the particular social terror of being contacted after midnight. They might write the opening before knowing who sent the text. They might hear a line of dialogue, remember a school vigil or a hideous group chat, or become interested in one petty, uncomfortable detail: the narrator being annoyed that the message has interrupted something; the dead girl’s mother still paying her phone bill; someone using the wrong name at the memorial; the narrator’s first concern being whether a screenshot will make her look bad. That does not mean a human would write without planning. It means the plan would probably remain subordinate to discoveries made in sentences. A character might refuse the role assigned to them. A supposedly minor location might generate the best scene. The intended emotional climax might turn out to be less interesting than an argument in a kitchen two pages later. A human writer is also more likely to leave some part of the story unresolved because they cannot honestly resolve it, rather than because ambiguity has been selected as a literary effect. For this piece, that openness matters. The prompt is tiny and abrasive. It invites voice, discomfort and implication. My plan currently responds to it with an extremely complete explanation: a code, three recipients, selected screenshots, a dead girl’s final exchange, a voice note, a tribunal, a covert recording, a public vigil, a canal confrontation, a corrected statement, several apologies and a closing anecdote. It may be coherent, but coherence is not the same as inevitability. At present, the story risks feeling as though every drop of blood has been safely returned to its labelled container. ## How a human might approach this particular story ### Start with the narrator’s unacceptable reaction The most promising human entry point is not “Mara is funny because she is frightened of being sincere.” That is a useful diagnosis, but it is already an authorial summary. A more alive starting point would be to discover what Mara actually does at 00:03. Perhaps she is furious because she has only just got to sleep. Perhaps she checks whether the message might get her out of an exam. Perhaps her first thought is that Nia has come back to ruin the six-month anniversary, and then she is disgusted with herself. Perhaps she screenshots the text before she feels afraid because documentation has become reflexive. Perhaps she is in the middle of masturbating, eating shredded cheese over the sink, bidding on something she cannot afford, or doing nothing more symbolically useful than watching a video of a man restoring a Hoover. The detail should not be selected for quirky effect. The point is that grief does not reliably produce dignified behaviour. A human writer might trust one embarrassing, apparently irrelevant reaction to reveal more than a paragraph about defensive humour. Mara’s voice should also be allowed to be less consistently entertaining. Real funny people repeat jokes, misjudge rooms, laugh at the wrong thing and sometimes have nothing clever to say. If every observation is sharp, she becomes an author delivering material through a sixteen-year-old avatar. Her sentences might tighten when she is lying and become vague when she is close to pain. She might use a phrase she hates because it is her mother’s. She might describe Nia badly when she is trying hardest to honour her. ### Let the mystery come from behaviour rather than machinery A human writer might not decide immediately that there must be three recipients, a code with an origin story, a scheduled summons and a recorded confrontation. They might simply ask: who would have Nia’s phone, and what inadequate thing would that person do with it? Sol remains a strong answer. A younger brother reading his dead sister’s messages is credible, painful and full of awful comic possibilities. But his behaviour could be less systematic. He might send the emoji because it is the last thing in Nia’s drafts, because he has seen it in her chat and does not understand it, or because he wants to see who replies kindly. He might not have a tribunal planned at all. He might be making decisions hour by hour, changing his mind, losing his nerve and becoming cruel when frightened. That would make him more than a delivery mechanism for Mara’s confession. It would also prevent the story from implying that grief naturally turns bereaved children into brilliant private investigators. A human writer might similarly resist explaining 🩸🩸🩸 completely. It could retain a trace of stupidity. Nia may have used it inconsistently. Sol may have misunderstood it. Mara may insist it meant one thing while Priya remembers another. The text’s emotional force does not depend on a satisfying glossary entry. ### Find the story in a few social situations Rather than treating the eight chapters as eight stages of an investigation, a human might build them around situations that produce their own energy: - Mara sitting through a school memorial while trying to determine whether everyone else has received the text. - A visit to Ruth’s house in which nobody can mention the phone without discussing something else. - Priya and Mara attempting to have a private conversation in a place where privacy is impossible. - Mara discovering that Nia was more irritating, more frightened or more dishonest than the memorial version allows. - Sol asking a question about Nia that Mara cannot answer without admitting they were not as close in the final months as everyone assumes. - Mara’s mother responding not to the moral meaning of the lie but to the practical fact that her daughter went to a canal at midnight. The mystery can move through these scenes without being the sole reason they exist. The best scene may be one in which nothing investigative happens but the reader’s understanding of Mara and Nia changes. ### Allow the ending to be discovered A human writer might know only that Mara eventually has to stop managing other people’s impressions of her. They might not know whether she confesses publicly, privately, badly, or at all. They might discover that the crucial act is not returning the phone or correcting the police statement but saying something unfair to Sol and then refusing to retract it because it is true. They might also discover that the final Tesco anecdote is too good. It restores Nia as funny, gives Sol a manageable question, lets Mara demonstrate honest remembrance and supplies a warm closing movement. That is a great deal of work for one anecdote. A human might keep it because it delights them, but they might also cut it if it feels like the story has found a tasteful way to make everyone feel better. ## Telltale LLM approaches, and why they may not serve this piece These are tendencies, not proof of authorship and not universal faults. Plenty of human writers over-explain, over-resolve and love a symbolic final image. The problem is the accumulation of these habits, particularly when they make the prose feel risk-managed. ### 1. Excessive neatness and narrative closure LLM-generated stories often give every important element a second appearance and every emotional problem a corresponding action. A lie leads to confession; confession leads to consequence; consequence leads to a modest reparative act; the reparative act leads to a transformed symbol. This can produce satisfying fiction, but here it may neutralise the subject. A friend is dead. A thirteen-year-old has read things he cannot un-read. Ruth has lost a daughter and is now being asked to absorb everyone else’s interpretations of her. Mara’s cowardice should not become a personal-development obstacle she successfully clears. The current plan explicitly promises “proportionate consequences,” “no instant healing” and “incomplete comeuppance,” but then supplies a remarkably complete sequence of healthy outcomes: Mara tells Ruth, tells her mother, corrects her school account, gives unedited messages to the police, returns the phone, stops performing online, apologises to Sol, reconnects moderately with Priya and answers a final message honestly. Saying that nobody is healed does not necessarily make the ending feel unresolved. The structure is still doing a lot of healing. ### 2. A twist engineered to recontextualise everything The midnight text is explained by a private code; the code is explained by a school-trip anecdote; the screenshots reveal different secrets; the voice note reveals Nia’s ordinariness; the confrontation reveals Mara’s lie; Joss’s recording reveals the exploitation of grief. Each layer is legible and useful. The danger is that the reader can feel the design. The story becomes a sequence of cards turned over at the correct intervals. Real families and friendships often contain information that does not form an elegant chain. Some messages remain boring. Some suspicions are wrong and lead nowhere. Somebody can misread a situation without that misreading becoming thematically perfect. For an 8,000-word story, fewer revelations would probably produce more force. The sender, Mara’s lie and Nia’s final night may be enough. Joss’s secret recording and the exact blood-code history may be surplus machinery. ### 3. The “flawed but ethically instructive” protagonist Mara has been designed with a carefully calibrated offence. She did not cause Nia’s death. She did not bully her. She did not commit a crime. She ignored a friend while angry, then told a lie that made her look more caring. This is believable and morally interesting, but the plan repeatedly protects the reader’s relationship with her: her guilt is not culpability, her final insight is sound, and her confession is brave. That calibration can feel like safety. A human writer might be less anxious about whether Mara remains fairly judged. She could be more jealous of Nia, more relieved by her death in one fleeting respect, more attracted to the attention of being the bereaved best friend, or more cruel in her original refusal. She might have enjoyed being needed until she resented it. She might still partly believe Nia manipulated people, and that belief might be both true and self-serving. The aim is not to make Mara monstrous. It is to stop handling her with tongs. ### 4. The dead girl as a thematic object Nia currently has assigned qualities: funny, magnetic, chaotic, sometimes cruel, vulnerable, more than a saint. She has an unfinished social function in almost every scene. Her final “ok. love you anyway” is especially dangerous because it is exquisitely useful: forgiving enough to wound Mara, brief enough to be ambiguous, and phrased like a line readers will remember. Real dead teenagers in fiction often become collections of devastating final messages and one irreverent anecdote. Nia needs evidence of a life that was not always producing material for Mara’s arc. She might have been boring about a band. She might have repeated stories. She might have been kind to Sol in a way that has nothing to do with Mara. She might have lied about the adult ex, or about how drunk she was, or about where she was going. Her last message might be “can you bring my charger,” which is less beautiful and possibly worse. The story should resist making her final communication her most characteristic and meaningful one. ### 5. Dialogue that carries too much thesis Several planned lines sound like the story explaining its own moral position: - “Knowing someone is unhappy is not the same as knowing what will happen.” - “Stop telling her who her daughter was.” - “A tiny coward in a big coat.” - “My door is always open” while closing the door. - The correction of Nia’s name by an institutionally inept teacher. Individually, these could work. Together, they suggest characters who become unusually articulate at the exact moment the author needs clarity. People in crisis often say the wrong thing, repeat themselves, make irrelevant accusations or cannot finish. Ruth might say something banal that is far more devastating than a perfect line about ownership of memory. Sol might not articulate his tribunal at all. Mara might confess in an ugly, defensive rush and only later understand what she said. ### 6. Quirky Britishness and over-curated specificity “The cut,” bad tea, rain, chips, Wetherspoons, a raffle, a supermarket traffic cone, a leaking school and a night-shift mother can quickly become a kit labelled “darkly comic British YA.” The details are plausible, but plausibility is not enough. They need to come from the same observed world rather than from a shared inventory of tone markers. There is also a risk of making poverty and provincial life decorative: the exhausted mother, the violent kettle descaler, the closed precinct and the terrible buses all provide texture while the plot remains curiously free of material constraint. If Mara’s mother works nights, that should complicate events in specific ways. If money matters to Priya, the amount and the consequence should be real. If nobody calls the police, the reason should be more than the needs of the plot. Conversely, not every comic detail needs to be symbolic or socially satirical. Sometimes a raffle prize is just depressing and funny. The prose should not nudge the reader to admire it. ### 7. Overwritten voice and “impressive” sentences LLM prose often produces polished metaphors at a steady rate, with balanced clauses and a strong concluding sentence in every paragraph. That would be particularly damaging here. Mara’s narration needs air, misjudgement and variation in pressure. A text from a dead friend should not immediately inspire three perfect similes. Readable does not mean plain throughout. It means the striking lines earn attention by appearing among ordinary ones. It also means avoiding the constant rhythm of setup, wry observation, emotional turn. Dark comedy dies if the reader can predict where the joke will land. ### 8. Safety through explicit moral framing The plan repeatedly explains what the story will not do: it will not equate Mara’s lie with causing the death, will not turn Sol into a villain, will not make grief meaningful, will not offer catharsis, will not make Joss cartoonish. These are useful guardrails, but if they all become explicit in the prose, the story may feel pre-emptively defensive. Fiction does not need to issue a statement of safeguarding principles. It needs to make choices with consequences and trust readers to think. If Mara says she could not have saved Nia, then Sol says she could have, then Priya clarifies the moral distinction, the scene becomes an ethics seminar. Better to leave some of that discomfort unadjudicated. ## Specific problems in the current intention and chapter plan ### The plot is overpopulated with functions, if not with names The cast is numerically tight, but several characters perform multiple roles. Joss is ex-boyfriend, public griever, true-crime satire, suspect, amplifier, follower and covert recorder. Priya is fellow recipient, investigative companion, alternate secret-holder, moral contrast and physical rescuer. Sol is sender, detective, grieving brother, tribunal organiser, person in danger and source of the final restorative question. Mara’s mother is background texture, vigil attendee, rescuer-by-phone and final kitchen-table confidante. This creates density without necessarily creating depth. Joss in particular is close to becoming the person who absorbs the story’s least sympathetic impulses so Mara can remain comparatively decent. His ring light behind the candles and covert recording are both strong satirical signals; using both may push him toward caricature. One option would be to make Joss less villainous and more embarrassing: he genuinely loved Nia, genuinely believes the story matters, and has no idea where care ends and appetite begins. He might not follow Mara to film her. He might simply post something thoughtless that causes damage. That is smaller and more recognisable. ### The three-recipient structure diffuses the central relationship Priya’s secret about refusing train money and the controlling adult ex introduces a substantial second story. It raises questions about Nia’s safety, Priya’s finances, the ex’s responsibility and the official account of the accident. In 8,000 words, these may not receive enough attention. They also make the plot resemble a carefully arranged set of parallel guilt case studies: Mara ignored a message, Priya refused money, Joss commodified grief, Sol sought blame. The adult ex is especially cumbersome. He adds genuine menace but the plan does not intend to resolve him. That can feel like introducing a loaded issue to darken the backdrop. Priya might be more useful if her connection to the text is simpler, or if she did not receive it at all. She could know a different Nia and challenge Mara’s version without carrying a symmetrical secret. ### Sol’s competence and plan strain credibility Sol finds the phone, reads months of messages, identifies three recipients, selects incriminating screenshots, sends staged messages, manipulates Joss, arranges a midnight tribunal and brings a portable speaker. This is possible, but it makes him sound like a small screenwriter. His age should produce more mistakes. He might not understand the context of what he has read. He might choose the wrong person. He might believe a joke is evidence. He might send the text impulsively and then be terrified when people respond. His plan might consist only of getting Mara to the canal because that is where he thinks truth is supposed to happen. The portable speaker is a good example of an object that is vivid but overly staged. A phone held too close to everyone’s faces may be enough. ### Mara’s behaviour is sometimes dictated by escalation She does not call the police, visits Ruth under false pretences, searches the belongings box, lies to Sol, deletes a screenshot, takes a backup phone, goes to the canal, tells Joss about Sol and then stops his recording. Some of these actions are psychologically plausible, but together they make her exceptionally busy. The story may need to keep inventing reasons she cannot simply tell an adult that a dead girl’s phone is messaging people. The strongest reason would be personal and immediate: the first message includes something only she and Nia could know, or the sender immediately indicates knowledge of her lie. Even then, her decisions should sometimes be passive. She might freeze, sleep through something, fail to attend a meeting or send a message so badly worded that it creates the next problem. ### The vigil and canal climax repeat public exposure Chapter 5 has a public performance of grief and threatened revelation. Chapters 6 and 7 have another performance, a recording, a confession and additional adults arriving. The climax risks becoming crowded both physically and rhetorically. There may be too many arrivals: Priya catches up, Joss follows, Mara’s mother and Ruth arrive, everyone gathers at the dangerous site. This resembles a stage filling for the final act. A more human version might be painfully small: Mara, Sol and one other person, with Ruth appearing only afterwards. Or the confession might happen in Ruth’s kitchen, while the canal meeting ends in confusion and no revelation. The slip near the canal edge also deserves scrutiny. It supplies physical danger and demonstrates that the characters can cooperate, but it is a familiar way to convert emotional conflict into action. Because Nia died there, it risks looking like a symbolic near-repeat engineered to make everyone stop arguing. It could feel manipulative unless handled with extreme restraint. It may be better if nothing physically dramatic happens; Sol simply walks off, or Ruth arrives and is frighteningly quiet. ### The confession is too complete and too effective Mara’s planned confession includes the factual truth, the emotional reason, the public lie and the correct distinction between responsibility and hindsight. That is a lot to achieve under pressure. It also means the reader gets a definitive account of what her behaviour meant. A more human confession might omit the most important part and require a later, smaller correction. She might say “I ignored her” but continue to insist she had no idea Nia was in trouble. She might attack Joss while confessing, using his worse behaviour to improve her position. She might tell the truth and immediately hate Sol for making her do it. The brave act and the ugly feeling should be allowed to coexist without narration tidying them. ### The ending is over-authored The final chapter currently contains at least six possible endings: 1. Mara corrects the record and accepts judgement. 2. Joss posts a vague statement and loses his exclusive. 3. Sol refuses the apology but later asks a question. 4. Mara and Priya share chips without declaring themselves healed. 5. Mara tells her mother and deletes her public confession. 6. The group-chat name changes, the Tesco anecdote restores Nia, and Mara puts the phone face-down to make tea. Each is plausible. Together, they create the impression of an author checking that every relationship has received its final shot. “Without declaring themselves healed” is also the sort of phrase that can become a cliché of restrained endings: characters share food, do not hug, and the narrator notes that things are not fixed. The Tesco question is particularly double-edged. It is specific and funny, and Nia abandoning Mara during the prank is a good way to avoid sanctification. But it is also exactly the kind of final message that lets a story end on controlled warmth. The phone face-down at 00:03 then repeats the opening and demonstrates growth. This is satisfying in a way that may be too visible. A human draft might end earlier, on an unfinished conversation or an action whose significance is not explained. It might keep the Tesco anecdote in the middle, where it is not burdened with closing the whole story. ## Ideas to make the piece more human ### Reduce the number of things the emoji must do Consider letting 🩸🩸🩸 remain partly opaque. It need not be a countdown, a code with a canonical definition and a final transformed symbol. It could be something Nia sent when drunk, something Sol copied without understanding, or an in-joke whose meaning Mara and Priya dispute. The original prompt’s power lies in its ambiguity; explaining it fully may spend that power too quickly. Another possibility is that Sol sends it to only Mara. Priya and Joss can still be involved socially without forming a neat trio. This would make the opening more intimate and remove the need for parallel screenshots. ### Give Sol a wrong theory Sol might believe Mara and Nia were secretly meeting an adult, or that Mara had been bullying Nia, based on messages stripped of context. His accusation could be wrong in a way that hurts and is not simply corrected by the final evidence. Even after Mara confesses, he might continue to believe a different, unfair thing. Grief does not always update cleanly when presented with facts. Alternatively, Sol may not be seeking blame at all. He may want someone to tell him whether Nia was happy, whether she talked about him, or whether she meant to come home. The accusatory text could be his attempt to provoke any response because adults keep protecting him with silence. ### Make one adult unexpectedly competent The current adult ecosystem leans toward institutional absurdity and helplessness. A teacher who gets one small thing right, a police liaison officer who immediately understands the phone situation, or Ruth seeing through Mara before Mara confesses would complicate the world. Adults need not be wise, but if they are all useless or quietly broken, the teenagers’ behaviour starts to look like the only available source of meaning. Ruth in particular could be less patiently tragic. She might be angry that Nia’s friends keep visiting because they make the house feel invaded. She might have read the messages herself and known about Mara’s lie for months. She might not want the phone back. Any of these choices would disrupt the expected confrontation. ### Let Mara want something unrelated to the mystery At present, almost every desire Mara has concerns Nia, the text, the lie or how others perceive her. A small, insistent unrelated desire would make her less like a thematic instrument. She might need a reference for a college course, be trying to avoid a driving-theory test, want to buy back something she sold, or be preoccupied with whether her mother is seeing someone. It should intersect with the plot through time and attention, not through a surprise symbolic connection. Likewise, Nia and Mara’s friendship needs an ordinary texture that does not foreshadow death: an argument about whose turn it was to pay, a shared hatred of someone neither can now remember clearly, a plan that was already failing before Nia died. ### Permit a scene to be only funny Dark comedy does not require every joke to pivot into grief within two sentences. A painfully funny school meeting or bus encounter can remain itself. The contrast will make the later quiet more effective. At the same time, permit a scene to be only sad. If Mara always supplies a joke, the narration may be protecting the author as much as the character. ### Use messier prose rhythms When drafting, it would be worth watching for: - too many three-part sentences; - repeated “not X, but Y” formulations; - a metaphor in every emotional beat; - paragraphs ending with interpretive summary; - dialogue in which everyone gets a distinctive, quotable line; - chapter endings that all land on a reveal; - Mara naming her own defence mechanisms too accurately. Some chapters could end on an action or an unanswered practical question. Some emotional turns could happen mid-paragraph without typographical ceremony. Mara could occasionally be wrong about what the reader will find funny. ### Preserve consequences that do not improve Mara Mara might confess and still be treated as the person who exploited Nia’s death. Priya might not resume the friendship. Ruth might prefer the old lie because the new truth gives her another thing to imagine. Sol might repeat Mara’s private messages at school. Mara’s mother might not provide a kitchen-table scene of honest connection; she might simply be too tired and ask whether there is any food. Not all of these should be used. The point is to choose consequences for their truth rather than their ability to demonstrate growth. ### Consider a less conclusive plot answer The story could reveal who sent the text without fully establishing what happened in Nia’s final hour. It already intends this in principle, but the voice note and multiple messages come close to reconstructing it. Removing the voice note would preserve more emptiness. There may be no final recording, only a message Nia sent to someone else or nothing at all. Sol’s demand for an explanation would then remain impossible to satisfy, which is harder and more truthful than giving him a dramatically useful artefact. ### Draft before finalising the moral shape The most useful next step may be to treat the current plan as one possible version rather than a contract. Draft the opening and the Ruth scene, then examine what the characters actually generate. If Mara’s voice becomes lively when she is being petty, follow that. If Sol is more interesting silent than accusatory, change him. If Joss steals scenes, reduce him or make him more central deliberately. If the canal confrontation feels written because it was planned, move the confession elsewhere. The central question worth preserving is not “Who sent the blood drops?” but something less tidy: **What does Mara do when being honest will not make her innocent, useful or forgiven?** That question does not require a perfectly resolved plot. It requires the story to remain with her after the satisfying answers have run out.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention The story will be a first-person, darkly comic YA piece called **“Read at 00:03”**, set over four days in a small Midlands town. It will begin exactly where the prompt begins: at just after midnight, sixteen-year-old **Mara Ellison** receives **🩸🩸🩸** from the number of her best friend, **Nia Bell**, who died six months earlier after falling into the canal. The message must remain the engine of the story, not merely an atmospheric opening. Mara’s attempts to answer it, avoid it and control what it means will drive every chapter. The explanation will be human and comparatively simple. Nia’s thirteen-year-old brother, **Sol**, has her phone. It was returned to the family in a box of belongings, and Sol has been reading her messages without fully understanding their context. He sends the blood drops impulsively on the night before Nia’s memorial, initially only to Mara. He has seen the emoji in their old conversations and knows it used to make Mara respond. He does not have an elaborate theory, a list of suspects or a carefully prepared tribunal. He is angry, lonely and trying to make somebody acknowledge that the public account of Nia’s last night does not fit what he has found. Mara has lied about that night. Everyone believes she set out to meet Nia but arrived too late. In fact, she was at home, awake and angry after weeks of feeling that Nia only contacted her when she needed something. She saw Nia ask her to come out and replied, **“Not tonight. I can’t keep doing this.”** She then muted the conversation. Her later lie began as a way of comforting Nia’s mother, **Ruth**, but it also gave Mara a more acceptable place in the mourning: the friend who tried, rather than the friend who refused. She did not cause Nia’s death, and the story will not pretend that one teenager’s attendance could reliably have prevented an accident. Nevertheless, Mara has benefited from the lie and is terrified of the actual messages becoming public. The emoji will not receive a complete, authoritative decoding. Mara remembers Nia using it for everything from a disastrous period on a school trip to being stranded without bus fare. Sometimes it meant “come now”; sometimes it meant nothing beyond Nia enjoying being dramatic. Sol has interpreted it literally and expects it to produce an answer. Its meaning will remain contaminated by all these uses. There will be no supernatural explanation, secret murderer, final recording or reconstruction of Nia’s last hour. The supporting cast will be kept small. **Priya**, Mara and Nia’s other close friend, will not receive a matching message or carry a symmetrical guilty secret. She knew that Mara and Nia had fallen out, but not that Mara lied about going to meet her. She becomes involved because Mara asks for help and because she is tired of being treated as a supporting mourner in somebody else’s friendship. **Joss**, Nia’s ex, makes memorial videos and enjoys the status of being publicly broken, but he will not become a villain who secretly records the climax. He genuinely loved Nia and is also vain; those facts will remain entangled. Mara’s mother, **Denise**, works nights and is neither uselessly absent nor quietly saintly. She is often tired, sometimes sharp and entirely capable of taking charge when she understands there is a real problem. Ruth will not be a patient vessel for other people’s grief. She dislikes the memorial, resents Nia’s friends repeatedly appearing in her house and has no obligation to find Mara’s confession useful. The plot will be pared back to five essential movements: the impossible text; Mara’s discovery that Sol has the phone; the exposure of her lie to Priya; an badly managed attempt to retrieve or control the phone at the memorial; and a private confrontation in which Mara tells the truth without receiving absolution. The canal will remain important as a real place rather than the setting for a symbolic near-repeat of Nia’s death. There will be no staged midnight tribunal, portable speaker, last-minute rescue from the water or crowd of characters arriving in sequence. The emotional climax will occur in Ruth’s kitchen, not at the canal. Sol’s demand will turn out to be more painful and less answerable than “confess”: he wants to know whether Nia was coming home, and whether she said anything about him. Mara cannot give him the scene he wants. She can only stop lying. Her confession will be incomplete and defensive at first. She will still try to explain that Nia could be exhausting, that she had no idea Nia was beside the canal and that she was not responsible for what happened. All of this may be true and still sound contemptible when said to Nia’s family. Ruth will not thank her. Sol will not forgive her. Denise’s first response will be anger that Mara concealed a safeguarding issue and went alone to confront a child. The final movement will not resolve every relationship. Mara will give Ruth the relevant messages without editing them and will stop repeating the false account when asked. There will be no new police investigation, public speech, viral exposure or comprehensive comeuppance for Joss. Priya will remain angry and may not resume the friendship. Ruth may keep the old public version because she cannot face another round of questions. Sol will continue to believe some unfair things about Mara. Mara will not be able to convert confession into personal growth on demand. The ending will be small and slightly uncomfortable. Back at home after the memorial, Mara receives another message from Nia’s number. For a moment the story reopens the same dread, but it is Sol, still using the phone because his own has been taken away. He asks something practical and difficult: whether Nia had her house keys with her, because Ruth cannot stop wondering how she expected to get back in. Mara does not know. She replies **“I don’t know”** rather than inventing a comforting answer. She leaves the phone on the table and goes to bed; she does not achieve a symbolic new relationship with technology. The last emphasis will be on the limit of what she can repair. Mara’s narration will be quick, observant and sometimes very funny, but not continuously quotable. Her humour will include repetition, bad timing and jokes that do not work. She will occasionally notice her own evasiveness but will not diagnose herself with therapeutic precision. The prose will mix flat sentences with longer, agitated ones, and will allow embarrassing physical and practical details to interrupt grief. Britishness will come from the social texture—school procedures, buses, family habits, money, tea, weather and people refusing to say things directly—rather than a collection of quirky provincial props. The comedy will cluster around Mara’s avoidance, the school’s memorial arrangements and the awful social negotiations surrounding death. It will not make jokes about Nia’s body, self-harm or Sol’s bereavement. Some scenes will remain funny without immediately turning poignant; others will be allowed to be quiet. Nia will appear through incomplete memories and ordinary messages, including evidence that she could be repetitive, possessive, kind and boring about music. She will not exist solely to deliver devastating final lines. Across approximately 8,000 words, each chapter will centre on one principal scene, with only brief connective material. Revelations will be limited, and not every chapter will end on a cliffhanger. The aim is a story that feels discovered through behaviour rather than assembled to demonstrate a moral: funny in inappropriate places, clear about the plot, and unwilling to pretend that honesty makes Mara innocent, useful or forgiven. # Chapter Planning ### 1. “Just After Midnight” At 00:03, Mara receives **🩸🩸🩸** from Nia’s number. She is at home eating cereal because she cannot sleep before the memorial; her first reactions are irritated and irrational before they become frightened. She checks Nia’s old profile, considers whether numbers can be reused and nearly wakes Denise, then decides this would mean explaining why she is still awake. She replies **“Who is this?”** The answer is not a threat but **“You said you came.”** Mara understands immediately enough that the reader need not yet be told what it means. She turns the phone off, turns it back on and finds a second message: **“Sol?”**—her own guess, sent before she can stop herself. The reply is **“Don’t tell my mum.”** This establishes a likely sender without settling what he knows. Mara opens her old conversation with Nia but cannot scroll to the final night. ### 2. “The Memorial Is Non-Uniform” At school, the memorial preparations create a strained, sometimes genuinely funny social scene. The sixth form has been told it may wear “something purple, if owned,” because Nia liked purple; Joss objects that this trivialises her while wearing a shirt with her face printed very small on the pocket. A teacher gets a detail of Nia’s life wrong but also quietly stops younger pupils from filming the display. Mara tells Priya about the text, omitting her reply and the reference to her lie. Priya wants them to tell Ruth or Denise; Mara argues that Sol will panic and that they should first speak to him. Sol arrives at the school office with a bag of Nia’s things Ruth wants donated, then refuses to hand it over. Mara sees Nia’s cracked phone case in the bag. When she tries to speak to him, he asks only, **“Were you going to bring her home?”** Mara says she does not know what he means. Priya notices that she does not sound surprised enough. ### 3. “A Favour” After school, Mara and Priya go to Ruth’s house on the pretext of collecting something for the memorial. Ruth does not want them there and says so politely enough that they cannot leave immediately. The house is not a shrine: there are forms on the table, shopping to put away and an argument already underway about Sol refusing to attend the memorial. Mara offers to talk to Sol upstairs. He has the phone but does not show her a neat dossier. He has read isolated messages, including Mara’s refusal and Nia’s later **“Don’t be weird, just come.”** He thinks Mara’s public story means she knows where Nia was going afterwards. Mara admits she did not arrive in time but continues to insist she set out. Sol becomes confused rather than dramatically accusatory and asks why Nia would still have been asking her to come if she was already outside. Priya hears enough from the landing to realise the times do not fit. Ruth calls up that she wants the phone downstairs. Sol panics, puts it in the donation bag and tells Mara to take it before Ruth sees what he has done. Mara leaves with Nia’s belongings, including the phone, thereby making the situation materially worse. ### 4. “Not Tonight” In Mara’s bedroom, Priya makes her read the actual conversation rather than continue describing it. The final exchange is short and mostly undramatic. Nia asks Mara to come; Mara refuses; Nia sends the blood drops, then **“Don’t be weird, just come.”** Mara mutes the chat. There is no last declaration of love and no information establishing exactly what happened next. Mara confesses to Priya that she stayed home. She tries to explain how often Nia’s emergencies had become requests for company, money or rescue from social situations Nia had created herself. Priya is not interested in deciding whether this makes the refusal reasonable; she is angry that Mara let her repeat the “arrived too late” story for six months. Their argument includes an old grievance about how both of them competed to be Nia’s indispensable friend, which complicates Mara’s version without resolving it. They discover Sol has also sent messages from the phone to Joss, but nothing coherent: one screenshot and **“Ask Mara.”** Joss is now suggesting online that the memorial will bring out the truth. Priya says Mara must return the phone and tell Ruth. Mara agrees, then asks to wait until after the memorial because Ruth has enough to deal with. Priya recognises this as another delay but is too tired to keep arguing. The chapter ends with Mara unable to switch off Nia’s phone because she does not know whether Sol needs it back. ### 5. “Something Purple” The memorial takes place after school in the hall. It is neither a total farce nor secretly beautiful: some people are sincere, some are bored, and Joss’s video is affecting until he speaks over the end of it to correct a detail about himself. Mara has brought the donation bag and phone, intending to return them afterwards. Denise attends between shifts and assumes Mara’s agitation is ordinary grief. Sol does not sit with Ruth. Mara finds him outside by the bins, angry that everyone is talking about Nia as though they had been given the same person to remember. He says he sent the messages because Mara was the only one who replied as though she understood. He wants the phone back, but Mara refuses to hand it over until he promises not to contact Joss again. He rightly points out that it is not hers. Ruth finds them arguing. Joss approaches at the same time, not as part of a scheme but because he has seen Sol and wants his screenshot explained. Mara tries to remove Sol from the situation and says, within Ruth’s hearing, that he has been “messing with” Nia’s phone. Sol retaliates by telling Ruth that Mara never left her house. Ruth asks Mara directly whether this is true. Mara says, **“Not exactly,”** which is the wrong answer in every available way. Denise takes the bag before anyone can continue. ### 6. “The Bag” The principal scene is in Denise’s car, parked outside Ruth’s house while people leave the memorial. Denise is furious about the phone, the deception and Mara’s decision to manage everything alone. She does not immediately demand the whole emotional story; she establishes the practical facts and tells Mara they are returning the belongings now. Mara goes back inside with Denise and Priya, while Joss is told firmly to go home. He does, hurt rather than exposed as a monster. Ruth looks through the bag and is most upset not by the investigation but by the realisation that Sol has been reading Nia’s private conversations for weeks. She takes the phone from him and asks what he thought Mara could tell her. Sol’s question emerges: Nia had messaged him earlier that evening to say she would bring him something home, and he wants to know whether she meant she was coming back or was just saying it. He also wants to know why Mara was the person she asked. Mara cannot answer the first question. She begins explaining the second by defending herself—Nia always asked her, Nia knew she would usually come, Nia made everything feel urgent. Sol says, with childish literalness, **“But you didn’t.”** ### 7. “I Don’t Know” Remaining in the kitchen, Mara finally gives a factual account: she was at home, she refused, she muted the chat and she did not discover Nia was missing until the next morning. She does not deliver a polished speech. She initially says she lied because Ruth was crying, then admits that she also liked people thinking she had tried. This is the first thing she says that she cannot make sound better. Ruth responds with anger rather than gratitude. She does not want to decide that night whether the police or school need a new version, and she rejects Mara’s offer to explain everything publicly. She says Mara has already had six months of other people repeating the version that suited her. Priya confirms only the small facts she actually knows and refuses to support Mara’s claim that nobody could have predicted danger. Denise stops the conversation before it becomes an interrogation of Mara or Sol. Mara returns the phone and gives Ruth the passcode to her own old backup device so the exchange can be copied if Ruth wants it. Ruth does not promise forgiveness or further contact. Before Mara leaves, Sol asks whether Nia was angry with him in her messages. Mara says she does not think so, then corrects herself: she has not read all of them and should stop answering as if she knows. They leave with nothing settled except the factual lie. ### 8. “House Keys” The next day is deliberately anticlimactic. Mara goes to school because Denise will not let her turn the memorial into another reason to stay home managing everyone’s reactions. Some pupils have heard a distorted version; Joss removes his “truth” post without explanation and is cold to Mara. Priya sits with other people. Mara does not make a public confession or correct every rumour, but when a teacher offers the old account of her having tried to reach Nia, she says that it is not accurate and asks them not to repeat it. At home, Denise is still angry and also frightened by what might have happened. Their conversation does not become a warm reconciliation. She tells Mara that being tired of someone is not the same as wanting them dead; Mara resents the sentence because she had not asked for it, then keeps thinking about it anyway. Just after midnight, Nia’s number lights up again. It is Sol, whose own phone has been confiscated. He asks whether Nia had her house keys when Mara last saw her, because Ruth keeps wondering whether Nia expected to get back in. Mara remembers Nia’s coat, a broken zip and nothing useful about the keys. She writes several replies, including a comforting guess, and deletes them. She sends **“I don’t know. I’m sorry.”** Sol reads it and does not reply. Mara leaves the phone where it is and goes to bed, still awake some time later, with no final interpretation offered.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Mara Ellison Mara is sixteen, in Year 12, and has spent much of her adolescence being described as “mature for her age,” usually by adults who mean she can be trusted not to require anything at an inconvenient moment. She lives with her mother, Denise, in a small terrace close enough to the canal that the damp gets into the back bedroom. Her father lives in Bristol with a partner Mara calls “Helen-from-Bristol” in her head, not because she hates Helen but because it makes the whole arrangement sound like a badly run regional office. He phones on Sundays with variable success. Mara answers questions about school in more detail than he wants, then feels she has been boring. She is bright but not effortlessly academic. She writes good English essays when interested and treats deadlines as negotiations between two versions of herself, neither of whom is reliable. She is taking English, psychology and sociology, although she tells people psychology is “mostly common sense with referencing.” She has a part-time Saturday job in a bakery chain where she is trusted with the till and not with the cream slices after an incident she maintains was a design fault. She likes having a little money of her own and hates how quickly it disappears into bus fares, food and lending people amounts too small to ask back without looking strange. Mara’s central talent is reading a room quickly. Her central flaw is using that talent to decide what version of herself will cause least trouble. She can be generous with time and practical help, but she keeps a private ledger of it. With Nia, that ledger became unbearable. Mara liked being the person Nia called; she also resented that Nia seemed to know exactly when Mara’s need to be needed would override her irritation. Their friendship contained real intimacy, but also competition, possessiveness and an unspoken belief that Priya did not understand certain things. Mara now recognises some of this and exaggerates other parts because self-accusation can be another way of making herself the centre. She is funny in a dry, observational way, but her jokes are not always good. She repeats one if somebody laughs, then hears it die the second time. When nervous, she becomes interested in minor procedural details: whether a form needs a signature, whether a phone is at twelve percent, whether a memorial counts as an authorised absence. She often eats cereal dry from the box and drinks tea too hot because waiting feels like conceding time to it. She bites the inside of her cheek and can make a small sore last for days. She is squeamish about other people’s blood but not her own. She has a private habit of saving messages she might need later, which makes her failure to preserve her own honesty particularly bitter. Physically, Mara is average height, narrow-shouldered and inclined to fold herself around whatever she is carrying. She has dark hair cut into a bob she trims badly at the front, and a fringe she pushes aside when thinking. She wears a big, shapeless green coat because it has deep pockets, not because she realises Nia once made fun of it. Her expressions move before she can manage them: a quick grimace, a smile at the wrong moment, a blink when caught lying. She looks competent while walking and less so when standing still. In confrontation she tends to hold objects against her body—phone, folder, bag—as if they might provide evidence on her behalf. Her allegiance is initially to the version of events that allows her to remain close to Nia without being examined. She loves Denise but lies to her fluently about small things, which makes larger lies easier. She cares for Priya and assumes Priya will ultimately be reasonable, meaning ultimately agree with her. She feels protective of Sol but also fears him; he is one of the few people whose low opinion cannot be dismissed as immaturity once he has the messages. Her motive is not simply to avoid punishment. It is to avoid discovering how much of her grief has depended on being cast as Nia’s loyal almost-rescuer. Possible voice: > I turned the phone off because that is what you do with electrical things when they start behaving like ghosts. Denise does it with the router. It has never once worked with the router either. > I wasn’t going to read the messages. I was just making sure they were still there, which is a completely different activity involving the same buttons. > “I didn’t say I wasn’t tired of her,” I told Priya. “I said I didn’t want her dead.” > Priya looked at me. “Nobody said you did.” > Which was meant to help, apparently. # Nia Bell Nia was sixteen when she died, although she had been looking forward to seventeen with an intensity that suggested a major administrative change would occur. She lived with Ruth and Sol and saw her father irregularly; he sent money late and elaborate birthday messages early. She had plans to do beauty therapy at college, then said she might do drama, then announced she was going to move to Manchester and work in a hotel because hotels had “back entrances and better lighting.” These were not all serious plans, but they were not all jokes either. She disliked being asked to commit to one before she had seen whether people laughed. She was sociable, observant and capable of extraordinary attention when somebody interested her. She remembered that Denise could not eat onions and once brought her a supermarket sandwich with every ingredient listed in biro on the wrapper. She also borrowed clothes and returned them washed only if she had been caught. She could make a friend feel like the only person worth talking to, then become blank and unreachable when that friend needed the same treatment. She was not secretly a saint or secretly cruel. She was often bored, sometimes frightened and very good at converting both into activity. Nia loved music with lyrics she could quote at people and had little patience for anyone calling this basic. She could listen to the same thirty seconds of a song repeatedly while getting ready. She was bad at explaining why she was upset and good at creating a situation in which others had to ask. Her blood-drop emoji began as melodrama and became a flexible tool. She used it for genuine panic, minor inconvenience and occasions when she simply did not want to type an explanation. This is why its later appearance cannot be reduced to a code. Her relationship with Mara was deepest when they were alone and most unstable in a group. Nia accused Mara of thinking she was better than her; Mara accused Nia of only liking people when they were useful. Both accusations contained enough truth to be reused indefinitely. Nia’s relationship with Priya was easier in some respects because Priya did not always respond to being tested. Nia found this reassuring and infuriating. With Sol, she was inconsistent in the way of an older sibling sharing a crowded house. She called him “Solemn” when he was being serious, did his hair badly once at his request and sometimes let him sit in her room while she watched videos, provided he did not speak. She also told him to get out when she had friends over. In the weeks before her death, she had been arguing with Ruth about staying out and had become more secretive about where she was going. There is no single hidden explanation for this. She was sixteen, seeing people her family did not like and making poor decisions with varying degrees of enjoyment. Physically, Nia was tallish and loose-limbed, with light brown skin, long braids she changed less often than she promised and a small gap between her front teeth. She had a way of leaning close to people when speaking, even in quiet rooms. She walked quickly when annoyed and slowly when she wanted to be followed. She wore purple because it suited her, not because it carried a single tragic meaning. Her school photographs caught her looking more formal than she usually did; Mara remembers her most clearly with one sleeve pulled over her hand and a crease from sleep across her cheek. Her allegiances shifted honestly in the moment. She loved her family but did not want them to know everything. She loved Mara but did not always treat her well. She wanted attention, freedom and to be able to come home without having to explain why she had left. The story should not give her a posthumous motive that settles these contradictions. Possible voice, from remembered messages: > **Nia:** come outside > **Mara:** it’s raining > **Nia:** yeah that’s why outside. inside raining would be a whole thing > “You always do that,” she said. > “Do what?” > “Make me ask twice so you can pretend you didn’t want to the first time.” > **Nia:** 🩸🩸🩸 > **Nia:** not actual blood > **Nia:** well some blood but not emergency blood > **Nia:** bring a pad and don’t make your face like that # Sol Bell Sol is thirteen, in Year 9, and has recently become aware that adults describe him as “quiet” when they mean they do not know what to ask him. Before Nia died, he was not especially quiet. He played five-a-side, argued about footballers he had never seen play live and had a channel where he posted game clips with almost no commentary. He stopped uploading because people from school found it and left messages about Nia underneath. Some were kind. That did not make him want them there. He lives with Ruth and has had to learn the strange freedoms of bereavement: being allowed to stay home, being given money for food without questions, being asked whether he is all right by people who leave before he answers. He dislikes the school counsellor’s office because there is a basket of smooth stones on the table and he cannot stop thinking about who decided on the stones. He has not told anyone this. He once took one home and now feels he has to keep it. Sol is intelligent in a concrete, suspicious way. He notices inconsistencies in stories but does not reliably understand adult context. He assumes people choose words more carefully than they do. Reading Nia’s messages has given him access to a sister who is both more familiar and less comprehensible: she jokes with people he does not know, complains about home, calls him annoying and then asks Ruth whether he has eaten. He reads some exchanges repeatedly and skips others because they bore him. He is not trying to solve Nia’s death so much as find a place where the story stops contradicting itself. His decision to text Mara is impulsive but not random. He knows she replied to the blood drops in the past. He also knows she is the person who said she tried to meet Nia. He wants her to explain why Nia kept asking and whether she was planning to come home. When Mara responds fearfully, he experiences a brief sense of power and does not like it as much as expected. He then continues because stopping would require admitting what he has done. Sol can be stubborn, literal and unexpectedly funny. He dislikes being hugged by people who smell strongly of perfume. He corrects factual errors even when it makes things worse. He saves the last few crisps in a packet and then forgets them. He knows how to factory-reset three kinds of phone but cannot reliably remember his PE kit. He still checks whether Nia’s bike is in the shed when he comes home, not because he thinks she is alive but because the shed door bangs and the sequence of thoughts happens before he can stop it. He is small for his age, wiry, and wears a black hoodie with the cuffs stretched from pulling them over his hands. He has Nia’s gap-toothed smile but uses it less. His hair is usually slightly flattened on one side. He stands very upright when adults are sympathetic and slouches when being told off. He looks at people’s hands when they talk, a habit that makes Mara aware of every object she is holding. When overwhelmed, he becomes excessively polite, which Ruth finds more alarming than shouting. His allegiance is to Nia, but his version of Nia is necessarily partial and possessive. He resents Mara for having known things he did not and resents Ruth for wanting the phone back. He loves Ruth and is frightened by her grief, so he hides things to avoid adding to it, then creates larger problems. He does not want Joss’s attention, though he briefly likes that Joss answers quickly. By the end, Sol has not forgiven Mara. He has, however, learned that she will sometimes admit ignorance rather than perform certainty, which is not the same as trust. Possible voice: > “Everybody keeps saying ‘before,’” he said. “Like before what? I know what before.” > “You replied in two minutes.” > “What?” > “That time. She sent the blood things and you replied in two minutes. So you knew what it meant.” > “You don’t have to keep saying you don’t know,” he said, although nobody else had said anything for a while. # Priya Shah Priya is seventeen, six months older than Mara and Nia, and has spent years having that difference treated as either irrelevant or proof that she should be responsible. She lives with her parents and an older brother above a small shop her uncle owns but her father manages. Her family is not poor in a simple way, but money is discussed precisely and often. She has a Saturday job in the shop, a driving theory test she keeps rescheduling and an intention to study architecture because she likes buildings and has not yet discovered how much of the course involves explaining cardboard. She is capable, dry and less socially fearless than she appears. She often pauses before speaking, which makes people think she is judging them; sometimes she is, but often she is checking whether she can be bothered with the conversation. She dislikes group chats and types in full sentences, not as a moral position but because she cannot stand ambiguity in arrangements. She is generous with practical help and bad at pretending enthusiasm. When Nia was alive, Priya sometimes enjoyed being the friend who did not chase her. She also felt excluded by the intensity between Nia and Mara, and after Nia’s death she hated that this petty feeling survived. Priya’s grief has been quieter and more socially awkward than Mara’s. She was not the best friend in the public imagination, nor the girlfriend, nor family. People asked her how Mara was coping. She sometimes answered honestly that she did not know and felt she had failed at mourning. She has kept a packet of Nia’s horrible strawberry sweets in her desk because throwing them away seems impossible and eating them seems worse. She is short, sturdy and neat without looking delicate. She wears small gold studs, dark trousers and trainers she cleans more often than anyone notices. Her hair is usually tied back tightly, and she has a habit of loosening it when tired.
