# Daniel Mercer Daniel is thirty-eight, a technical writer for a company that makes laboratory equipment. His job is to turn engineers’ corrections into instructions that cannot be misunderstood. He is good at it. He likes version histories, numbered steps, and the small satisfaction of removing an ambiguous pronoun. He has never been particularly interested in the supernatural; before Mara became ill, his strongest irrational habit was refusing to board a plane until he had checked that his passport was in his bag three times. He grew up in Coventry with Clare and their mother, a district nurse who treated emotional crises as things that became manageable once everyone had eaten. Their father left when Daniel was eleven, though he remained intermittently present through birthdays and badly timed telephone calls. Daniel learned to be useful before he learned to be forthcoming. As a teenager, he was the boy who knew how to restart the boiler and who sat silently beside friends after disastrous breakups, hoping presence would compensate for not knowing what to say. He met Mara nine years ago at a friend’s ill-attended book launch. He had gone because he felt sorry for the author; she had gone because there was free wine. He liked that she could be funny without performing happiness. Their early relationship was not effortless, but it was easy to return to after arguments. They married six years ago. Daniel wanted children in a way he found difficult to articulate without sounding as though he were reciting someone else’s reasons. After the miscarriage, at twenty-one weeks, he threw himself into practicalities: cancelling orders, phoning relatives, putting the pram in the loft. He also said, while Mara was still in hospital, “At least now we know,” meaning something about her body and future pregnancies. He stopped because she looked at him. He has never been able to remember exactly what he meant, only that it was not what she needed to hear. Daniel’s central flaw is not coldness but **the belief that attention entitles him to understanding**. If he watches carefully enough, records enough, asks the right question, he thinks the truth should become available. This makes him tender in some situations and unbearable in others. He remembers medication schedules but misses the point of a complaint. He apologises thoroughly, sometimes so thoroughly that the injured person ends up reassuring him. He can be resentful of the people he helps and then disgusted by his own resentment. His idiosyncrasies are small and persistent. He tears the corners off shopping receipts and lines them up while thinking. He cannot fall asleep if there is a cup in the sink, though he can leave one beside the bed for three nights. He dislikes being barefoot on kitchen tiles. He reads the final page of instruction manuals first. When frightened, he becomes more polite. He says “sorry” to furniture when he bumps into it, a habit Mara used to imitate. Physically, Daniel is tall and narrow through the shoulders, with dark hair that has begun receding in an uneven way he pretends not to notice. He has a pale scar across one eyebrow from falling off a bicycle as a child. His hands are usually dry from washing them too often. Before the insomnia, he carried himself loosely; now he holds his neck stiffly, as if turning it too quickly might reveal something behind him. He speaks quietly and rarely fills silences immediately. When he does smile, it tends to arrive after the joke, once he has decided it is safe. His allegiance is to Mara, but not cleanly above his allegiance to his own idea of who she is. He wants her well, wants to be forgiven, wants to stop being afraid, and wants someone else to take responsibility for a night. These motives coexist without cancelling one another. He loves Clare but experiences her competence as an accusation. He dislikes Mara’s consultant before meeting him, simply because the man has access to a professional language Daniel cannot control. **Voice experiments:** > “I wasn’t checking on her. Checking implies you stop once you know.” > “There’s a correct amount of concern. I’ve never been able to find it. You either get called cold or you end up counting someone’s breaths with your hand hovering over their mouth.” > “I said her name before I turned the light on. I don’t know why. Whatever was in the room already knew who I meant.” # Mara Mercer Mara is thirty-six and, until recently, worked as a restorative bookbinder for a small firm attached to a university library. The work suited her patience and her tolerance for repetitive tasks. She could spend an afternoon repairing the spine of a book no one would borrow again and feel that the afternoon had been properly used. She is knowledgeable about paper, adhesives, and the damage done by well-meaning people. She hates the phrase “good as new”; most repairs, she says, should be allowed to show if you know where to look. She grew up in Norwich, the only child of parents who ran a failing seaside guesthouse despite living nowhere near the sea. Her father was charming in public and sullen at home; her mother survived by making jokes at exactly the wrong moment. Mara inherited the timing but not always the cruelty. She left home at eighteen and has kept affection for her parents at a manageable distance. She sends birthday cards on time and rarely answers telephone calls from her father without first making tea. Mara is observant in a less systematic way than Daniel. She notices when someone has changed their shampoo, when a shop assistant wants to cry, when Daniel has bought a different brand of butter and is hoping she will not mention it. She dislikes direct questions when she feels vulnerable. Instead, she answers adjacent questions, sometimes for days. This can make her seem evasive even when she is trying very hard to be honest. She is funny, stubborn, and occasionally vain about strange things: her excellent handwriting, her ability to open jars, the fact that she has never lost a library book. She bites the inside of her cheek when concentrating. She keeps pencils that are too short to use comfortably. She sings while cleaning but stops if anyone enters the room. She has a habit of pressing her thumb hard against the centre of her palm when she is trying not to cry. Before her illness, she was physically assured without being especially athletic. She is short, compact, and strong through the hands and forearms from years of binding work. She has thick brown hair usually twisted into a knot and secured with whatever is nearby—a pencil, once a clean paintbrush. Her face is expressive around the mouth; when she disapproves, one corner tightens before the rest of her expression changes. She has grey-green eyes that become bloodshot easily, which used to make people think she had been crying when she had only been awake too long. Now she moves cautiously, often pausing after standing as though waiting for information from her body. She becomes irritated when Daniel anticipates the pause. At times she hunches protectively around her ribs. At other times she sits unnaturally still, not with serenity but with the vacant stillness of someone who has forgotten what to do next. Her fear is not always dramatic. Sometimes it appears as annoyance: at a question repeated, at a light switched on, at being helped into a cardigan she did not ask for. Mara’s deepest motive is **to remain a person whose account of herself counts**. She wants Daniel’s love but not his custody. She is frightened that he can tolerate her grief only when it is quiet and that he prefers being needed to being known. She also feels guilt for the relief she sometimes experiences when he leaves the room. Her allegiance to their marriage is real but strained; she has imagined leaving, not because she stopped loving him, but because she wanted one room in which nobody was monitoring her recovery. The miscarriage did not instantly transform their marriage. There were better weeks afterwards. They went away for two nights and laughed in a terrible restaurant. She returned to work. Daniel made her laugh by pretending to conduct an orchestra of kettle noises. This makes the present worse: neither of them can point to a single day when everything ended. Mara’s relationship with Clare is warmer than Daniel assumes. They exchange photographs of ugly ceramics and occasionally complain about him with an accuracy that leaves both women faintly guilty. Mara trusts Clare’s practical kindness but fears becoming another family problem Clare has to organise. **Voice experiments:** > “You keep asking if I’m back. I didn’t know I’d been anywhere.” > “Don’t make that face. The one where you’re being patient. I’d rather you were just annoyed.” > “Sometimes I wake up and you’re looking at me like I’m a door you can’t get open.” > “No, I said I was tired. Those are different words. You can check your notebook.” # Clare Mercer Clare is forty-one, Daniel’s older sister, and a primary-school deputy head. She is used to entering rooms in which several people are insisting on incompatible versions of events. This has made her calm, but not infinitely patient. She has a tendency to decide which practical action is necessary and then treat disagreement as a delay. Usually she is right. Occasionally she is merely fast. Their mother relied on Clare too heavily when they were children. Clare cooked some dinners, attended school meetings, and learned to interpret adult silences. She resented Daniel for being allowed to withdraw, while also protecting his right to do so. As adults, they love each other with a mixture of ease and old irritation. She can make him laugh more quickly than almost anyone, but she can also reduce him to a defensive eleven-year-old by saying his name in a particular tone. Clare is divorced and has no children. She was married for seven years to a man she still likes in small doses. She does not regard the divorce as a tragedy and dislikes people treating childlessness as an explanatory wound. She has two close friends, a chaotic garden, and a godson whose birthday she remembers without reminders. She runs badly but regularly. She reads crime novels and skips descriptions of meals. Her idiosyncrasies include carrying tissues she never seems to use, clicking her tongue once before delivering bad news, and putting on her coat before she has decided to leave. She drinks tea while it is too hot and then complains about burning her tongue. She swears more freely away from work, though rarely in front of Mara unless she is very tired. Clare is broad-shouldered and of average height, with Daniel’s dark hair cut into a practical, slightly uneven bob. She dresses in bright colours partly because she likes them and partly because children can find her easily in a crowd. She stands with her weight evenly planted and looks directly at people when they speak. Unlike Daniel, she touches objects without seeming to interrogate them: picks up a mug, moves a chair, folds a towel. Her physical competence can make the Mercer house feel less airless, which is one reason Daniel finds her visits both relieving and intolerable. Her primary motive is to prevent Daniel and Mara from turning fear into a private system no one else can enter. She does not need to decide whether the haunting is real before acting. She sees dehydration, injury, sleep deprivation, coercive habits, and two people who are no longer safe authorities on themselves. Her loyalty is to both of them, though Daniel initially experiences this as betrayal. She is not secretly certain of a rational explanation; she is simply unwilling to let uncertainty paralyse her. Clare’s flaw is that she can mistake intervention for care and leave too little room for humiliation. She does not fully understand how frightening it is for Daniel to surrender the watch. She also underestimates Mara’s attachment to the house and to the parts of her marriage that remain private. **Voice experiments:** > “I’m not saying you imagined it. I’m saying you’ve had four hours’ sleep and you’ve locked us in.” > “Don’t make me choose which one of you sounds sane. It’s a horrible question and neither of you would like the marking criteria.” > “Mara, do you want me to stay? Not Daniel’s answer. Yours.” > “You were always like this. You’d let the house burn down if you thought asking for the hose would make a scene.” # The Presence in the Night The presence is not treated as a character with a recoverable biography, even in private planning. It has no confirmed name, childhood, mission, or coherent grievance. Giving it those things would make it too easy for Daniel—and the reader—to organise. What can be said is that it appears in connection with **attention, repetition, and displaced speech**. It uses phrases from the wrong moments. It sometimes seems to know Daniel’s thoughts, but this may be because he has become predictable. It watches him with apparent fascination, yet its interest is not consistently hostile. It may want something as simple as a response; it may not want anything in a human sense at all. Its behaviour should not establish reliable rules. Daniel’s watching may feed it, but deleting the recordings does not defeat it. It may be using Mara’s memories, or Mara may be using its stillness to protect herself. The story does not decide. If it has a physical signature, it is not monstrous transformation but **misalignment**: attention arriving before movement, familiarity appearing in the wrong context, a voice carrying no effort. It should never become witty enough to dominate a scene. It does not taunt like a conventional villain. When it speaks at length, something has already gone wrong with the writing. Its nearest thing to a voice is ventriloquism with imperfect timing: > “You looked so peaceful before.” > “Not that one. That was for later.” > “Are you awake?” The last question matters because it is also something Mara might reasonably ask her husband. The horror lies in Daniel no longer being able to tell the difference.

I caught her staring at me again. She thought I’d been sleeping. Her face was close enough that I could see the red veins in the whites of her eyes. They were wet, brimming without spilling, and fixed on mine. I counted because counting gave me somewhere to put my attention. Eleven. Twelve. Thirteen. She did not blink. My arm had gone numb beneath me. I was lying on my side with one hand trapped under the pillow, my knees drawn up, my mouth slightly open. I had arranged myself carefully. People look different when they sleep. I had thought about that while getting into bed, and then hated myself for thinking it. At twenty-three, I breathed in through my nose. Mara’s eyes moved, not away but down, following some small change in my face. “Dan,” she said. I held the breath. The room smelled faintly of dust and the lavender spray she used on the curtains, though neither of us liked lavender. It had been a gift from Clare. The digital clock on Mara’s side was turned towards the wall, but its light made a green line under the bedside table. Somewhere below us, the fridge stopped humming. Mara waited. “Why are you holding your breath?” she asked. I opened my eyes properly. There was no way to make the movement look natural. “I wasn’t.” She continued looking at me. Then she blinked, once, and her eyes spilled over. She wiped her cheek with the heel of her hand. “You were awake,” she said. “Just now.” “Before.” “I don’t know.” Her mouth tightened at one corner. It was such an ordinary expression, so exactly hers, that I reached for her. She shifted back before my hand crossed the space between us. “I’m sorry,” I said. “For what?” I didn’t answer. She turned onto her other side and pulled the duvet over her shoulder. Within a few minutes her breathing lengthened. Or she allowed it to. I stayed where I was until my neck began to ache. Her hair had come loose from its knot and lay across the pillow, one strand touching the sheet between us. I wanted to lift it away. Instead I watched the rise of her shoulder and tried to remember whether she had been facing me when I got into bed. At half past three I got up and went to the bathroom. There was a cup beside the bed, half full of water gone warm. I drank it before leaving because I knew I would think about it otherwise. My face in the bathroom mirror looked unfinished. There was a red crease along my cheek and dried salt at the corner of my mouth. I ran the tap so Mara would hear something ordinary if she was awake. When I came out, I checked the hallway before going back in. She had not moved. In the morning she was sitting at the kitchen table with her cardigan buttoned wrongly. The top button was through the second hole, pulling the fabric sideways. She had made tea for both of us. Mine had too much milk, the way she used to make it when she was teasing me. “You’re up early,” I said. “So are you.” “I didn’t sleep much.” She looked into her tea. “No.” I put two pieces of bread in the toaster. The spring had broken months ago, so you had to hold the lever down until it caught. I stood with my thumb on it, waiting. “Were you awake last night?” I asked. “You know I was.” “Before you spoke.” Her fingers stopped around the cup. “I don’t know,” she said. “You were sitting up.” “Was I?” “Looking at me.” She gave a small laugh. There was no humour in it, but it wasn’t cruel either. “That sounds awful.” “It’s not the first time.” “I know. You’ve told me.” The toast came up. I had forgotten to watch it, and one piece was dark at the edges. I put both on a plate and set the plate between us. Mara picked at a loose thread on her cuff. “You watch me too.” “When you’re ill.” “When I’m asleep.” I looked at her. “You do,” she said. “You put your hand near my face.” “To see if you’re breathing.” “I know why.” She pulled the thread until the cuff gathered. “I didn’t say you didn’t have a reason.” The kettle clicked off behind me, though I couldn’t remember switching it on. Mara glanced at it, then at me. “I’m going back to bed,” she said. “You haven’t eaten.” “Neither have you.” She stood carefully, one hand on the table. I moved to help and she gave me a look that stopped me where I was. At the kitchen door she paused. “Don’t move the blanket again,” she said. “What?” But she had already started up the stairs. I ate the burnt toast standing over the sink. It tasted of nothing except the charred edge. Afterward I washed her cup and mine, dried them, and put them away. There was still a mark on the draining board where a third cup had been. My phone was on the worktop, face down. I had left it charging in the bedroom. The screen was warm. When I unlocked it, the video application was open. There were twelve recordings in the night folder, each labelled with the date and a time. I had made eleven. The last file was already playing. For a second I saw only the dark shape of the duvet and a strip of wall. The microphone picked up the rustle of fabric, then my own breathing, slow and deliberately even. The time in the corner read 03:17. Mara’s voice came through the small speaker, close to the phone. “Why are you holding your breath?” On the screen, my eyes opened. I stopped the video. The kitchen was very quiet. Upstairs, a floorboard creaked beneath the bed. The file showed forty-three seconds remaining.

I also bought a small packet of screws, though I had nothing immediate to screw. The receipt lay on the passenger seat. I tore off one corner before starting the car. Mara was asleep on the sofa when I returned. The television was playing an old panel show with the volume low. I stood in the doorway longer than I meant to. Her mouth was open. The watchfulness left her face. I went into the kitchen and put the milk away. When I came back, she was awake and laughing. A man on the television had dropped a tray of glasses. He knew before he picked it up.” They replayed it. The man glanced down at the tray, made a tiny adjustment, and then lifted it. The glasses slid off together. “He did,” I said. “He absolutely did.” I laughed. It came out louder than hers, an ugly bark after weeks of speaking quietly. Mara laughed again, and for several seconds neither of us could stop. My eyes watered. I had to put the screws on the floor before I dropped them. “God,” she said, wiping her cheek. “That’s pathetic.” “It’s not that funny.” “No.” We looked at each other and started again. STRENGTHS: The chapter's greatest achievement is its management of tone. The supernatural dread is kept almost entirely submerged beneath the mundane — burned soup, a pharmacy visit, a missed work call — yet the chapter never loses its undertow of wrongness. This is exactly what the plan called for, and the execution is precise. The detail of Daniel giving his own date of birth instead of Mara's at the pharmacy is a small, perfect touch: it suggests his identity is beginning to blur, his sense of self eroding under the weight of caregiving, without the story ever announcing this. The laughter scene is the chapter's centerpiece and its most accomplished passage. The plan called for Daniel to "knowingly accept a moment of comfort from something he does not trust," and this is delivered with real subtlety. The laughter is genuine — the man who knew he'd drop the tray is a genuinely funny observation — and then the moment curdles not through anything overtly supernatural but through Mara's watching. "I liked hearing it" is an unsettling line precisely because it could be tender or predatory, and the chapter refuses to decide. The shift from shared laughter to her watching him is handled with restraint: "Her laughter faded naturally, her shoulders settling." No dramatic cut. Just the slow withdrawal of warmth. Daniel's voice is consistent and well-realized. The detail about restoring the deleted recording "telling myself this was not indecision but good practice" is excellent characterization — his self-justifying rationalism rendered in a single sentence. The observation about "carefully" in the centrifuge manual ("Either removing the rotor required a specific precaution or it did not. Carefully meant nothing except that something might go wrong") functions as thematic resonance without being heavy-handed. It mirrors his situation without the story underlining it. The dialogue is notably strong. "You keep saying that before I know what's happened" is a perfect Mara line — it captures her sharpness, her exhaustion with Daniel's preemptive guilt, and the slight wrongness of their dynamic. "He absolutely did" during the laughter scene feels genuinely warm and natural. The final exchange — "You should sleep" with her eyes already open — lands with quiet menace. The chapter also handles the supernatural element (the blanket, the spare room) with appropriate restraint. The disagreement about who moved the blanket is not resolved; it simply sits there, unresolved, as these things do. WEAKNESSES: The chapter is not without minor issues. The pharmacy scene, while grounded and realistic, runs slightly long for what it contributes. The woman with the childproof cap is a nice character beat (Daniel's compulsive helpfulness, his social awkwardness) but the scene could be trimmed without loss. The screws he buys "though I had nothing immediate to screw" is a slightly odd detail — it works as a portrait of distracted anxiety-shopping, but it's the one moment where the accumulation of mundane details feels slightly arbitrary rather than purposeful. The line "She looked younger asleep. People said that, but with Mara it was true" is the chapter's one moment of mild cliché — the acknowledgment that it's a cliché doesn't fully redeem it. The ending is effective but perhaps slightly too neat in its callback to Chapter 1's watching motif. "Her eyes were open" followed by "You should sleep" is good, but it's doing exactly what the plan prescribed, and one can feel the plan's hand here more than elsewhere in the chapter. OVERALL: This is sophisticated, disciplined literary horror writing. The chapter follows its plan faithfully while feeling organic rather than mechanical. The characters are consistent with their profiles — Daniel's compulsive management, Mara's sharpness and vulnerability, the way their dynamic is both loving and coercive. The prose is direct and sensory without being showy. The supernatural is present but not overdone. The emotional register is genuinely affecting. I did not set an alarm. I did not bring the phone upstairs or write the time in the notebook. I went to bed with the intention of staying awake, which was different from deciding to watch her. Mara lay facing the wall. Her breathing remained shallow for a long time. I listened to the pipes knocking in the bathroom wall and tried to recall whether they had always done that. At some point the central heating clicked off and the room became colder. I must have slept. When I opened my eyes, the bed beside me was empty. There was no shock in it. My body seemed to understand before I did. I sat up with my heart already beating hard and my hand pressed against the sheet where she had been. It was cool. The bedroom door stood open. Beyond it, the landing was dark except for the weak blue light beneath the bathroom door. We did not have a light there. I thought of the extractor fan, the streetlamp, the standby light on something we had forgotten we owned. “Mara?” A board creaked in the hall. I found her standing outside the spare room. She was wearing the white nightdress with the torn hem, the one she had meant to repair for more than a year. Her back was to me. Both arms hung at her sides. She was speaking too quietly for me to hear the words. I stopped a few feet away. The carpet prickled through my socks. “Mara.” She continued. There were pauses in it, small spaces left after certain phrases. At first I thought she was listening. Then she said, “No, it’s all right,” and I knew the voice. Not the tone, but the shape of the sentence. It was mine. It was what I said on the telephone when someone apologised for calling too late. She said something else. This time it might have been her own voice. I touched her shoulder. She turned so quickly that I stepped back. Her face was wet from the nose down. She put a hand to her chin and looked at her fingers. “Have I been crying?” she asked. “I don’t know.” “You don’t know?” “I just woke up.” She looked past me towards the bedroom. “Why are we out here?” “You were talking.” “To who?” “I couldn’t hear.” Her eyes moved to the spare-room door. It was closed. She reached for the handle, and I caught her wrist before I knew I was going to. “Don’t,” I said. She stared at my hand. I let go. “Don’t what?” “I don’t know.” She gave a tired, disbelieving laugh. “That’s helpful.” We stood there. The blue light under the bathroom door went out. Mara wrapped her arms around herself. “I want to go back to bed.” “All right.” “You don’t have to announce it.” “I wasn’t—” “Just come, Dan.” I followed her. She got into bed and pulled the duvet up, leaving me standing beside it like someone who had arrived too late for a conversation. “I’m frightened,” she said. The words were so plain that I could not answer immediately. “I know.” “No, I am. Not you.” I sat on the edge of the mattress. “Of what?” She looked at the ceiling. Her mouth opened, then closed. “Of waking up with you there,” she said. I waited. She turned her head towards me. “That’s not fair,” she said. “I know.” “It’s all right.” “No, it’s all right,” she repeated, in my voice. I stood up. Mara’s expression emptied. For a second I thought she had not heard herself. Then she whispered, “Oh.” I went to the window. There was nothing outside except next door’s car and the hedge shining with rain. My reflection stood between them, thin and transparent. “After the hospital,” she said behind me, “you said something.” I did not turn. “You were sitting by the window. You had that paper cup. You kept bending the rim.” “Mara, don’t.” “You said, ‘At least now we know.’” My throat tightened. “I was trying to—” “Then later you said something else.” “I didn’t.” “You did.” I faced her. She was sitting up now, both hands flat on the duvet. “What did I say?” She looked almost relieved that I had asked. Then her face changed, not into anything monstrous, but into uncertainty. “I don’t remember.” “You just said—” “I know what I said.” Her voice rose. “I don’t remember why I was thinking about it.” I came back to the bed but did not sit. “Was it about the baby?” She flinched. I had not said *the baby* aloud in months. We said *the pregnancy*, *what happened*, *before*. Sometimes Daniel, in my own head, I called it nothing at all. Mara looked down at her hands. “You said you wished it had been you.” “That isn’t cruel.” “No.” “You said that wasn’t cruel.” “I didn’t say you were cruel.” We had lost the order of things. I could feel it happening and could not stop it. Every answer seemed to belong to a question asked a moment earlier or later. She lay down again. I remained beside the bed until she said, “Please stop standing there.” I got in. For a long time neither of us spoke. The rain started against the window, sparse and hard. I thought of the phone downstairs, the notebook in the kitchen drawer, the recordings with their neat times. I thought about going to get them. Instead I stayed still and hated the relief of having decided nothing. Mara turned towards me. Her face was close, but her eyes were closed. I thought she was asleep until her hand came up and touched my cheek. Her thumb moved once beneath my eye, following the bone. “You looked so peaceful before,” she said. “When?” Her thumb stopped. I waited. The room smelled of rain and the faint medicinal sweetness of the cream she used on her hands. “Before you were tired,” she said. It was a reasonable answer. It was almost kind. She put her arm across my chest. After a moment I held her. Her body fitted against mine with a familiarity that made my eyes burn. I pressed my face into her hair and breathed in. She was warm. She was there. I knew I should ask what she meant. I knew there were questions I had not asked, times I had not written down, things I should have heard in the hallway. Instead I tightened my arm around her. Mara sighed. For several minutes, perhaps longer, I let myself believe that this was what she needed from me. Not the watching. Not the notebook. Just this. Then her hand moved against my back, slowly, as if learning the shape of it. I kept holding her.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 3)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a genuinely accomplished piece of horror writing that earns its effects through restraint and precision rather than spectacle. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. NUANCED CHARACTERS: Daniel is rendered with considerable psychological complexity. His impulse to grab Mara's wrist before he knows why, his inability to stop standing beside the bed, his relief at "having decided nothing" — these are the actions of a man whose controlling tendencies and genuine love are inseparable. The line "I knew I should ask what she meant. I knew there were questions I had not asked" captures his self-awareness without excusing him. Mara is harder to assess since she's partly absent, but her "That's not helpful" and "You don't have to announce it" feel like authentic flashes of her pre-illness personality. The chapter successfully maintains the ambiguity between Mara-as-ill-person and Mara-as-vessel. DIALOGUE: The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. The exchange about "At least now we know" is devastating precisely because it's fragmented and confused — neither character can hold the thread. "No, it's all right" repeated in Daniel's voice is chilling without being theatrical. The dialogue avoids the common horror-writing failure of having characters speak too clearly about what's happening. The confusion about who said what, and when, mirrors the reader's own disorientation. "That's not fair. I know." is a perfect small moment of Mara's self-awareness. PLOT AND PLAN ADHERENCE: The chapter follows its plan closely. The private sentence Daniel said after the miscarriage is deployed — though the plan specified "something cruel and frightened" and the chapter gives us "you said you wished it had been you," which is actually tender rather than cruel. This is a slight deviation from the plan's description of "something cruel and frightened that he has never repeated aloud." The plan also mentions Mara appearing "genuinely horrified and asks whether he told someone" — this doesn't quite happen; instead she seems confused about why she was thinking of it. The tenderness at the end, Daniel accepting comfort from something he doesn't trust, is executed beautifully. "You looked so peaceful before" lands as planned. HORROR MECHANICS: The horror is handled with admirable economy. The blue light that goes out, the voice that uses Daniel's sentence shapes, the hand "learning the shape" of his back at the end — these are precise and unsettling without being overwrought. The chapter avoids the catalogue of stock body horror the plan warned against. The most frightening moment — "No, it's all right," she repeated, in my voice — is followed immediately by Mara's own horror at herself ("Oh"), which is more disturbing than if she'd been oblivious. PROSE QUALITY: The prose is direct and sensory as intended. "The carpet prickled through my socks" is exactly the kind of grounded detail the plan called for. "Her body fitted against mine with a familiarity that made my eyes burn" is earned sentiment. There are occasional moments where the prose reaches slightly — "thin and transparent" for the reflection is a touch obvious — but nothing that constitutes purple prose. The repetitive quality shaped by insomnia is present without becoming tedious. WEAKNESSES: The chapter's main weakness is that the "cruel sentence" from the plan becomes something more ambiguous and arguably tender ("I wished it had been you"), which slightly undercuts the planned dynamic of Daniel being confronted with his own cruelty. The plan specified something that would make him feel exposed and guilty; what we get is more ambiguous. Additionally, the conversation loses its thread in a way that's intentional but occasionally makes it hard to follow who is responding to what — this is a feature, not a bug, but it risks losing readers. The ending, while effective, is perhaps slightly too neat in its comfort — the plan called for Daniel to "hate how much he needs it," and while that's present, the final image of the hand "learning the shape" of his back is almost too poetic, slightly more literary than the insomnia-prose register the plan specified. OVERALL: This is high-quality literary horror writing. It successfully executes a difficult tonal balance, maintains character consistency, and delivers genuine unease through restraint. The dialogue is particularly strong. Minor deviations from the plan and one slightly too-polished final image prevent it from being a masterpiece, but it's well above average. Clare arrived at eleven with a paper bag of food and her coat already buttoned, though she had driven for nearly two hours. “You look awful,” she said. “So people keep telling me.” “Perhaps there’s a consensus.” She kissed my cheek and went past me into the house. I had asked her not to come. Then, at six that morning, I had sent her a message saying *perhaps today would be good after all*. She had replied with a thumbs-up, which irritated me more than a question would have. Mara was in the kitchen. She had dressed in jeans and a green jumper, and her hair was washed. For a moment I saw her as Clare must: thin, tired, but unmistakably present. “There she is,” Clare said. Mara smiled. “There who is?” “No idea. I was hoping you’d tell me.” They hugged. Mara’s arms went round Clare properly, and her face tightened against Clare’s shoulder. Clare looked at me over it. I turned away and unpacked the bag: bread, tomatoes, a cooked chicken, three oranges, and the salted chocolate Mara liked. Clare had remembered. I had bought screws. We ate at the kitchen table. Clare talked about a child at school who had hidden the class hamster’s bedding in the head teacher’s handbag. She made it funny without making the child sound stupid. Mara laughed once and asked what the hamster was called. “Brian,” Clare said. “Of course he was.” It went so nearly well that I began to watch for the point at which it would stop. I hated myself for that too. Clare noticed the notebook when I took it from the drawer to find a pen. It was a black softback with an elastic band around it. She did not ask to see it. She only looked at the cover and then at the dark bruises beneath my eyes. “What’s that?” “Work.” “At lunch?” “I was making a list.” Mara buttered a piece of bread. “He writes down the nights.” Clare set her cup down. “Not every night,” I said. “No,” Mara said. “Just when there’s something to write.” “What sort of thing?” Clare asked. “Times. Sleep. Whether she’s been up.” “Whether I’ve been looking at him,” Mara said. Clare clicked her tongue once. “Right.” “It helps with the doctor,” I said. “Does the doctor know?” “Not yet.” Mara looked down at her plate. “There’s a lot he’s saving up.” I felt the heat rise in my face. “You asked me to keep track.” “I asked you to tell me if I got up in the night.” “That’s what I’m doing.” “No,” she said, not angrily. “It isn’t all you’re doing.” Clare stood and took her plate to the sink. She ran the tap, though the plate was nearly clean. “Have either of you slept?” “No,” I said. “Some,” Mara said at the same time. Clare looked from one of us to the other. “I’m going to make an appointment.” “We have one,” I said. “When?” I could not remember. Mara said, “Tuesday,” and I knew immediately that she was right. While Clare was in the hall telephoning the surgery, I went to lock the back door. The key was already turned. I checked it again with my hand. Clare came back and saw me. “Why is the front door locked?” she asked. “At night it is.” “It’s half past twelve.” “Mara went outside once.” “I went to the bins,” Mara said. “In your nightdress.” “It was dark.” Clare put on her coat. She did not seem aware of doing it. “I’m not saying you imagined any of this,” she said to me. “I’m saying you’ve had four hours’ sleep and you’ve locked us in.” “I can unlock it.” “That isn’t my point.” “What is your point?” She looked at Mara, and something in her face softened. “I don’t know yet.” Mara asked if we could have tea. Clare went to fill the kettle. I remained by the back door, feeling foolish and wanting someone to acknowledge that I had unlocked it. A little later I found Clare in the sitting room, looking at the dead plant on the windowsill. Mara was upstairs in the bathroom. “She’s ill,” I said. “Yes.” “You didn’t see her last night.” “No.” “She was standing in the hall talking.” Clare turned. “People sleepwalk.” “She said things.” “What things?” I could not repeat them. That was the worst part: in daylight, every sentence had become either explainable or private. Clare touched my arm. “You need help too.” “I am helping.” “I know you think those are the same thing.” I pulled away. The bathroom door opened upstairs. When Mara came down, she stopped on the bottom step. Clare was beside me, still holding her coat although she had taken it off again. Mara looked at me, then at her. “Don’t leave me alone with him,” she said. The words were quiet. Clare did not move. Mara’s hand tightened on the banister. Her face crumpled with immediate, terrible embarrassment. “I’m sorry,” she said. “I didn’t mean—” “It’s all right,” Clare said. “No, it isn’t. I don’t know why I said that.” I went towards her. She stepped back onto the stairs. “Mara.” “Please don’t.” Clare stayed for another three hours. She did not make a scene or announce that she was staying. She simply took off her coat, made tea, and sat with Mara while I called the surgery to confirm Tuesday’s appointment. Nobody discussed the sentence again. Before she left, Clare arranged to collect us on Tuesday morning. She hugged Mara for a long time. At the door she told me to sleep in the spare room. “She doesn’t want that,” I said. “Did you ask her?” I closed the door without answering. The house seemed larger after Clare had gone. Mara went to bed early. I washed the dishes, wiped the table, and put the oranges in a bowl. Then I looked for the notebook. It was not in the drawer. It was not beside my computer or under the papers on the worktop. I found it finally beneath Mara’s side of the mattress. The elastic band was missing. Several pages had been torn out, leaving narrow strips along the spine. I sat on the floor and turned through what remained. My handwriting filled most of it: times, durations, small observations. *Awake 2:14. Standing 2:19. Spoke?* Near the back were entries I did not remember writing. *00:41 — asleep.* *01:06 — asleep.* *02:33 — asleep.* They continued down the page. The writing looked like mine except that the letters leaned the other way. At the bottom, beneath *04:12 — asleep*, someone had written: *His face changes.*

Clare arrived early on Tuesday and waited in the car. She said the house made her want to tidy things, and she did not trust herself not to start. Mara sat in the back. I sat beside Clare, though I had wanted to sit with Mara. It seemed important, once we were moving, that I had not. The surgery was in a low brick building opposite a closed post office. Inside, the chairs were fixed together in rows and the floor had recently been cleaned. A child was pushing a toy pram into the same table leg over and over. Each time it stuck, she reversed it exactly six inches and tried again. Mara watched her with an expression I could not read. Dr Shah was younger than I expected. He had a small stain on his cuff and a way of looking at the screen only after he had finished looking at whoever was speaking. I disliked him less for that. He asked Mara how she had been sleeping. “Not well,” she said. “Are you waking during the night?” “Yes.” “Do you remember getting out of bed?” “Sometimes.” “She doesn’t,” I said. “Not usually.” He turned to me. “You’ve been keeping notes?” “Some.” Mara looked at her hands. I told him about the staring. I tried to make it sound clinical: episodes of unresponsiveness, possible parasomnia, speech without apparent awareness. He asked how long the episodes lasted. I said I did not always know. He asked whether Mara had ever been injured. I said no, then remembered her wrist and looked at it. The skin showed nothing in the fluorescent light. “What about the recordings?” he asked. “They were for the nights.” “Has she consented to those?” Clare shifted in her chair. Mara said, “I asked him to stop.” Dr Shah nodded. He did not look shocked. That was worse than if he had. He examined her briefly, tested her grip and reflexes, and asked her to follow his finger with her eyes. She did everything he asked. When he shone a light into her eyes, she began to cry. “Sorry,” she said. “That’s all right.” “It’s just bright.” “I know.” He spoke about blood tests, dehydration, referral, the possibility of admission if things became worse. He used the word *confusion* several times. Once he said *neurological*, and once *psychiatric*, giving each word equal care. There was no moment when he looked at me and understood. At the end he asked whether Mara felt safe at home. The child outside began crying. The pram had finally gone under the table. Mara looked at me. I tried not to give her any expression she would have to interpret. “Yes,” she said. Then: “Sometimes.” Dr Shah waited. “I don’t feel well,” she said. “That’s different.” He nodded again. In the car, Clare talked about the tests and said she would come to the next appointment. I answered when necessary. Mara was silent until we stopped outside the house. “I want to walk,” she said. “It’s raining,” Clare told her. “I know.” “I’ll come with you,” I said. “No.” Clare turned off the engine. For a few seconds none of us moved. Mara got out. She walked to the end of our road and stood beneath the horse chestnut tree with her hood down. Clare watched her in the mirror. “Give her five minutes,” she said. “She’s sick.” “Yes.” “She could fall.” “Yes.” I opened the door. Clare caught my sleeve, then let go before I could pull away. Mara was coming back by then. Rain darkened the shoulders of her coat. She got into the rear seat again and said, “Drive round once.” “What?” Clare asked. “Please.” We drove around the block. It took less than two minutes. Nothing changed except that the same houses appeared in a different order. When we stopped, Mara said, “Sometimes I wake up sitting.” Clare looked at her in the mirror. “My neck hurts,” Mara continued. “Here.” She touched the muscle behind her ear. “From looking towards him.” I turned round. “I don’t know how long I’ve been awake,” she said. “It’s like there’s a bit missing before the hurting.” “Why didn’t you tell the doctor?” I asked. “You were talking.” Clare said nothing. Mara’s eyes filled, but she pressed her thumb into her palm and did not cry. “Stop recording me.” “I have.” “The phone was upstairs last night.” “It was charging.” “Stop recording me.” “All right.” “Say you promise.” “I promise.” She looked at my coat. My phone was in the inside pocket. I had my hand closed around it, though I could not remember putting it there. Clare drove us home. She offered to stay, and Mara said she wanted to sleep. I expected Clare to argue, but she only wrote down the blood-test appointment and made me promise to call her that evening. Inside, Mara took off her wet coat and hung it over the banister. Water gathered beneath it on the floor. “Are you angry?” she asked. “No.” “You look angry.” “I’m tired.” “So am I.” We stood in the hall. I wanted to hold her, but the promise about the phone seemed to have made touching another thing I needed permission for. She went upstairs. That evening I deleted six recordings. I stopped before the folder was empty because deleting them felt, absurdly, like destroying evidence of her illness rather than simply letting her go unwatched. I put the phone in a kitchen drawer. Nothing happened that night. Mara slept on her side with her back to me. I lay awake until the birds started. No footsteps. No voice in the hall. No face above mine. At some point I slept. I woke with a start and reached for her. She was there, breathing quietly. The clock showed 04:51. I had been asleep for eleven minutes. The certainty came before the fear: something had happened, and I had missed it.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably controlled piece of writing that demonstrates genuine literary craft. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. The chapter follows the plan closely: the doctor's appointment, Mara's revelation about waking sitting up with her neck hurting, Daniel's broken promise about the phone, the deletion of recordings, and the agonizing quiet night that ends with Daniel convinced he has missed something. The plan is executed with fidelity and intelligence. Character work is strong throughout. Daniel's voice is consistent with his profile: the compulsive note-taking, the way he interrupts with clinical language ("episodes of unresponsiveness, possible parasomnia"), the phone in his pocket with his hand closed around it even as he promises to stop recording. This is not told to us; it is shown through the physical detail of his hand finding the phone without his conscious direction. The moment where he looks at Mara's wrist and "the skin showed nothing in the fluorescent light" is quietly devastating—he was going to lie, then checked, and the truth happened to align with the lie. That ambiguity is handled with real sophistication. Mara is rendered with equal care. Her request to "drive round once" is strange and human and unexplained, and the chapter wisely does not explain it. Her pressing her thumb into her palm not to cry is drawn directly from the character profile and lands naturally rather than feeling like a checklist item. Her "Sometimes" in response to whether she feels safe is one of the best moments in the chapter—it does exactly what the plan calls for: a response that could belong to a sick woman or to something using her. Clare's brief presence is efficient. She catches Daniel's sleeve and lets go before he can pull away—a small gesture that captures her character's tendency to intervene and then recalibrate. Her dialogue is minimal but precise: "Yes" repeated twice when Daniel says Mara could fall is not agreement but a refusal to be manipulated into preventing Mara's autonomy. The dialogue throughout is excellent. It is spare, loaded, and never expository. "You were talking" as Mara's explanation for why she didn't tell the doctor is a perfect line—accusatory, sad, and entirely plausible. The exchange about the phone ("It was charging." / "Stop recording me." / "All right." / "Say you promise." / "I promise.") escalates through repetition in a way that feels true to how these conversations actually go. The prose is direct and sensory without being showy. "Water gathered beneath it on the floor" after Mara hangs her wet coat is the kind of detail that earns its place. The child with the toy pram is a well-chosen image—repetitive, futile, slightly mechanical—that resonates with the chapter's themes without being heavy-handed. The fluorescent light making Mara's wrist show nothing is a good example of the supernatural and the mundane remaining genuinely ambiguous. The ending is excellent. Eleven minutes of sleep, the certainty arriving before the fear, the conviction that something happened and was missed—this is the chapter's promised payoff, and it delivers. The absence of incident being "almost worse" is exactly what the plan called for, and the execution earns that claim. If there are weaknesses, they are minor. The chapter is perhaps slightly less surprising than the best chapters of this kind of fiction—the doctor's appointment proceeds more or less as one would expect, and the emotional beats, while well-executed, follow a predictable arc of tension and release. The child with the pram is a good image but not a startling one. The chapter does not quite achieve the uncanny quality of the best moments in the plan (the face remaining turned while the body moves away, for instance), but that image is reserved for Chapter 6, so this is appropriate restraint rather than a failure. The prose avoids purple passages and forced metaphor almost entirely. There is no straining for effect. The writing trusts its material. Overall, this is a high-quality chapter: disciplined, emotionally intelligent, faithful to its plan and characters, with dialogue that consistently earns its place and a prose style that serves the story rather than performing for the reader. Mara was not in bed when I woke again. The sheet on her side was pulled tight beneath the mattress, and her slippers were still by the door. I found her in the spare room. She was sitting on the floor with her back against the chest of drawers. The baby blanket lay open across her knees. We had kept it folded for so long that I had forgotten its size. It was cream-coloured, with a narrow green border and one uneven square near the middle. Mara had knitted that part badly and refused to let me pretend otherwise. Threads had been pulled from the border. She was laying them on the carpet in rows, each about the length of her little finger. Some were straight. Others had curled back into themselves. There were perhaps thirty. “What are you doing?” I asked. She did not look up. “They don’t lie flat.” “Mara.” “If you wet them, they might.” I crouched a few feet away. The room smelled of old paper and the cedar blocks we kept in the drawers. The pram was above us in the loft. I had put it there myself, driving my knee into the ceiling hatch as I pushed it through. “Where did you get the blanket?” “It was here.” “You asked me not to move it.” “Did I?” “Yesterday.” She considered this, then picked at another loop in the border. “Don’t,” I said. Her hand stopped. I expected anger. Instead she looked around the room as if she had only just noticed where she was. The desk. The narrow bed made up for guests. The chair with my old coat over it. “This isn’t how it was,” she said. “What?” “The window was on that side.” “It’s always been there.” She looked at the window. “Not always.” I sat back on my heels. There was a pain behind my eyes from sleeping badly, or from the little sleep I had managed. “Do you know where you are?” Mara’s mouth tightened. “Don’t do that.” “Do what?” “Make your voice soft.” “I’m asking if you know where you are.” “Our house.” “Which room?” She looked at me then. Her eyes were bloodshot, the lids swollen. “The one you don’t like.” I stood too quickly and had to put a hand on the desk. “We’re going back to bed,” I said. “I’m tired of bed.” “You need to rest.” “I was resting.” “You were pulling it apart.” She looked down at the blanket. For the first time, she seemed to see the rows of thread. One hand opened over them, not quite touching. “Did I do this?” she asked. “Yes.” “All of it?” “I don’t know.” She began gathering the threads. They clung to her fingers and the wool on her knees. “I can put them back.” “You can’t.” Her head came up. “I mean we can fix it,” I said. “You can. You know how.” “I know how to mend books.” “It’s the same sort of thing.” “No, it isn’t.” She tried to stand. The blanket slid from her lap, and the threads scattered. I reached under her arms to help. She resisted, not strongly, but enough that I tightened my grip. “Let go.” “You’ll fall.” “Let go.” “I’ve got you.” “That isn’t what I said.” I pulled her upright. She turned towards the door, and for one instant her face remained turned towards me. There was no crack, no dramatic movement. Her shoulders went with my hands. Her body followed. Her eyes stayed fixed on mine over a neck that could not have held that angle. Then she cried out, and everything came back into line. I released her so suddenly that she struck the drawers. “My wrist,” she said. “I’m sorry.” “You’re hurting me.” “I’ve let go.” “You’re still—” She stopped and looked at my hands. They were at my sides. I wanted to tell her what I had seen. I wanted her to confirm it, to say she had felt it too. Instead she held her wrist against her chest and moved away from me. “Mara, your neck.” “What about it?” “Did it hurt?” “Everything hurts.” “Just now.” She backed towards the landing. “Don’t come near me.” “I won’t.” “You say that while you’re walking.” I stopped. She went into our bedroom and shut the door. A moment later I heard the lock. We had never used it. I did not know it worked. I sat on the spare-room bed. The blanket lay at my feet, its green border unravelled. I picked up one of the threads and rolled it between my fingers until it disappeared into the grain of my skin. Downstairs, I made tea and left it outside the bedroom door. Then I took the phone from the kitchen drawer. There were six recordings left. I deleted them one by one. The confirmation box appeared each time, and each time I pressed it with my thumb. I deleted the restored file from the first morning. I deleted the notes with their dates and durations. I emptied the deleted folder until there was nothing in it except a photograph of a dishwasher error code and a document called *rotor revisions*. It did not feel like defeat. It did not feel like goodness either. Mostly I felt the peculiar lightness of having made an irreversible decision while no one was watching. Mara did not come out. The tea remained where it was. At four I went to check whether it had gone cold. My phone vibrated in my pocket. There was no message. The video application had opened by itself, or I had opened it without noticing. The screen showed one file in the deleted folder. Its name was tomorrow’s date. The thumbnail was black. The duration was eleven minutes. I pressed play. A circle turned in the centre of the screen, then stopped. *This item cannot be opened.* I tried again. Upstairs, the bedroom lock clicked. I put the phone face down on the hall table. When Mara opened the door, she looked at it before she looked at me. Her wrist had begun to bruise where my fingers had been. “I thought you deleted them,” she said. “I did.” She nodded, as though I had confirmed something she had known for a long time. Behind her, the duvet was folded back on both sides of the bed.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a strong piece of horror writing that demonstrates considerable craft and restraint. Let me examine it across the relevant dimensions. **Nuanced Characters** Daniel is rendered with genuine complexity here. His impulse to help Mara stand is immediately complicated by his grip tightening when she resists—he cannot distinguish care from control, and the prose doesn't editorialize about this. His decision to delete the recordings is handled with admirable ambiguity: "It did not feel like defeat. It did not feel like goodness either." This is exactly the kind of self-aware but not self-congratulatory interiority the character profile demands. Mara's fear of him after the incident—"Don't come near me" / "You say that while you're walking"—is devastating and precise. She is frightened of the right things for possibly the wrong reasons, or the right reasons. The chapter maintains this productive uncertainty. **The Central Horror Image** The plan called for the central physical image: "Mara's face remains turned towards him when the rest of her has moved away." The execution here is deliberately understated: "Her eyes stayed fixed on mine over a neck that could not have held that angle." The brevity is correct. The chapter doesn't linger or repeat the image; it passes through it and moves on to the bruised wrist, which is the more lasting horror. This is sophisticated pacing. **Dialogue** The dialogue is largely excellent. "Don't do that." / "Do what?" / "Make your voice soft." This is character-specific, revealing, and economical. "You say that while you're walking" is a particularly sharp line—it captures Mara's frightened precision and Daniel's unconscious encroachment simultaneously. The exchange about the window ("Not always") is appropriately unsettling without being theatrical. The only slightly weaker moment is "Everything hurts" / "Just now"—this is functional but slightly generic compared to the surrounding dialogue. **The File with Tomorrow's Date** This is the chapter's most inventive supernatural detail. A file dated tomorrow that cannot be opened is genuinely unnerving because it operates on a different logic than conventional horror—it's not a threat, it's a bureaucratic impossibility. The thumbnail being black and the duration being eleven minutes are exactly the right specific details. This last detail is excellent—it's practical, physical, and carries enormous emotional weight without announcing itself. The insomnia-shaped repetition ("I deleted them one by one") works. **Potential Weaknesses** The thread-counting ("There were perhaps thirty") is a nice touch but the threads-as-metaphor for unraveling is perhaps the most conventional element in the chapter—it's not forced, but it's the least surprising image. The chapter ending with the duvet "folded back on both sides of the bed" is strong but slightly telegraphed as a final image—it's doing obvious symbolic work (invitation? expectation? normalcy?) that the rest of the chapter earns through indirection. The line "rolled it between my fingers until it disappeared into the grain of my skin" is the one moment where the prose reaches for something poetic that doesn't quite land—threads don't disappear into skin grain in any meaningful physical sense, and it feels like a reach. **Faithfulness to Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely: the spare room, the blanket, the thread-pulling, the impossible neck turn, Daniel hurting Mara's wrist, the deletion of recordings, and the file with tomorrow's date. All major beats are present and executed with care. The plan's note that "she is more afraid of him than of anything else" is fully realized. **Overall Assessment** This is accomplished literary horror. It avoids stock moves, maintains character consistency, and finds its horror in domestic and relational detail rather than spectacle. The writing is controlled without being cold. Its weaknesses are minor: one slightly reaching metaphor, one slightly conventional central image (the threads), and an ending image that does slightly more symbolic work than the chapter's best moments. Mara watched me do it. “You can bring it,” she said. “No.” “It doesn’t matter.” “It does to you.” She considered that, holding her bruised wrist against her body. “I don’t know.” We went into the bedroom together. I unlocked the window a few inches because the room was stuffy, then closed it again when the rain blew in. Mara sat on the edge of the bed. Neither of us suggested the spare room. There was no plan beyond staying awake. I had imagined I would say certain things, but now that she was there they seemed like entries in another notebook. Observation. Explanation. A request for her to behave in a way I could recognise. “I’m sorry about your wrist,” I said. She looked at the bruise. “I know.” “I thought you were going to fall.” “I know that too.” It was not forgiveness. I was grateful she did not pretend it was. I sat in the chair by the window. After a while she said, “You can sit here.” “Are you sure?” “No.” I stayed where I was. Outside, a car passed without its lights on. I watched its shape move between the hedge and the lamp post. When I looked back, Mara had lain down with her head on my pillow. “Do you remember the restaurant?” she asked. “Which one?” “The one with the violin.” There had been no violin. A man at the next table had played music from his telephone until the waiter asked him to stop. It had been a violin concerto. We had laughed because the waiter called it *ambient noise*. “Yes,” I said. “You stole the pepper.” “I did not.” “You put it in your coat.” I remembered then. The pepper grinder had been tiny, made for one person, and I had knocked it into my sleeve. I had pretended all evening that it was intentional. “You told me to,” I said. Mara smiled faintly. “You were very obedient.” “I thought it was a good bit.” “It was.” We were quiet. Her eyes closed. “Afterwards,” she said, “I thought we might be all right.” “We were.” “For a bit.” “Yes.” She opened her eyes. “You hate that, don’t you?” “What?” “When things aren’t one thing or the other.” I looked at my hands. There was a small strip of receipt still caught beneath my thumbnail. “I hate not knowing what to do.” “That isn’t what I said.” “No.” The lamp went off. Neither of us moved. The room was not completely dark; rain held a little of the streetlight against the curtains. Mara said, “Did you do that?” “No.” “I didn’t.” “I know.” “Don’t say you know when you don’t.” I stood. The lamp switch was still in the on position. I turned it off and on. Nothing happened. “Leave it,” Mara said. I sat on the bed. She was crying without any change in her breathing. Tears went sideways into my pillow. I wanted to wipe them away and did not. “Sometimes there’s a delay,” she said. “Before what?” “Before I understand you.” She pressed her fingers to her temple. “You’ll say something, and I know the words. I know I know them. Then they arrive.” “Like you can’t hear?” “Like I hear them later.” I thought of her pauses, her answers coming just after I had decided she would not give one. “Is it happening now?” I asked. She looked towards the window. “You tell me.” “Mara.” “No. It isn’t.” I took a breath. “After the hospital, what I said—” “Don’t.” “I need to.” “No, you need to be finished with it.” That stopped me. She turned her face towards mine. “You want to tell me what you meant. Then I can say it was all right.” “It wasn’t all right.” “I know.” “I was trying to make it smaller.” “It wasn’t small.” “No.” “Not to me.” I nodded. My throat hurt. “I know.” She waited, and I understood that I had said it again as a way of ending the conversation. “I don’t,” I said. “Not properly.” Her expression loosened. It was such a slight change that I might have invented it. “I wanted you to stop being in hospital,” I said. “I wanted the forms done. I wanted to take you home. I kept thinking if I could get everything put away, we could start before it got any worse.” “It was already worse.” “Yes.” “There wasn’t a before I could go back to.” “I know.” This time she let it stand. Rain ticked against the glass. Mara reached for my hand. Her fingers were cold, and I thought, with sudden, humiliating happiness, *she wants me here*. “Do you still wish it had been you?” she asked. I had not said that in the bedroom. I had said it in the hospital corridor, to Clare, while Mara was asleep. Clare had told me not to be stupid. I looked at Mara. Her face was open, tired, waiting. “No,” I said. She withdrew her hand. “I don’t know,” I said quickly. “I don’t know what I wished.” “Yes, you do.” “I wished none of it had happened.” “That isn’t the same thing.” “No.” The room seemed to contract around us. I could hear my own pulse in my ears. Mara’s eyes moved to a point just behind me. “He’s going to ask if I’m still in here.” I turned. There was only the chair and my coat hanging over its back. “Who?” She blinked. “What?” “You said *he*.” “Did I?” I caught her shoulders, then immediately let go. The bruise on her wrist seemed to darken in the grey light. “I’m sorry,” I said. “I’m sorry. I won’t touch you.” She began to cry properly then. Not silently, not in the careful way she had before. Her face folded, and she made a small, furious sound. “I don’t know what you want,” she said. “I want you.” “Which bit?” I could not answer. She looked at me for a long time. Then something in her face settled, and she was so entirely Mara that the question became obscene. Not her smile exactly, not her voice, but the impatient tenderness with which she had once watched me try to parallel park outside our first flat. “Come here,” she said. I went. She put her arms around me. I held her and said I was sorry into her hair, without listing what for. I said it for the hospital and the notebook, for the wrist and the phone, for every time I had mistaken her stillness for peace. I said it because it was true, and because I could not think of anything else that was. Her hand rested between my shoulder blades. “Close your eyes,” she whispered. “I can’t.” “Just for a minute.” “No.” “Dan.” I shook my head against her. She waited. Her fingers moved once, slowly, down my back. I closed my eyes. When I opened them, the curtains were pale with morning. Mara lay beside me, asleep and breathing normally. My arm burned beneath the sleeve. Four thin scratches ran from my elbow to my wrist. On the hall table, downstairs, the phone began to vibrate.

The phone stopped before I reached it. There was no missed call. The screen showed the date, the time, and a low-battery warning. I stood in the hall with my sleeve pulled back, looking at the four scratches on my arm. They were shallow. Two had already stopped bleeding. Upstairs, Mara was still asleep. I made coffee and forgot to drink it. At eight I called Clare. “How is she?” she asked. “Asleep.” “And you?” I looked towards the stairs. “I don’t know.” Clare was quiet for a moment. “I’ll come over.” I expected to argue. Instead I said, “All right.” Mara woke while Clare was in the kitchen making tea. She came downstairs in her dressing gown and stopped when she saw her. “What day is it?” she asked. “Wednesday,” Clare said. Mara looked at me. “Did we go to the doctor?” “Yesterday.” She nodded slowly. Her gaze settled on the spare-room door. “Did something happen in there?” “You don’t remember?” “No.” I could have told her everything then. I could have described the blanket, the threads, her face turned towards me. Instead I said, “You were upset.” She touched her wrist. The bruise had come up in four faint marks. “Did you do that?” “Yes.” Clare put down the teapot. Mara considered my answer. “I thought so.” There was no triumph in it, no accusation. She only sounded tired. The blood tests showed dehydration and low iron. Nothing else came back quickly enough to satisfy me. Dr Shah arranged further appointments and spoke about a bed on a ward if Mara became more confused. Clare suggested Mara stay with her for a few nights, nearer the hospital and away from the house. “Just while we get you assessed,” she said. Mara sat at the kitchen table, turning a teaspoon over and over. “Do you want that?” I asked. She looked surprised by the question. “Yes.” I packed her bag. I put in two jumpers, her nightdress, the cream for her hands, and three pairs of socks. I forgot her toothbrush and had to go back upstairs. Clare found Mara’s medication and wrote the appointments on a card in large letters. Nobody mentioned an exorcism. Nobody said the word *possession*. It would have made the morning ridiculous, and I resented that most of all: how easily everything became arrangements. At the car, Mara touched my wrist. Not the injured one. The one she had hurt. Her thumb rested briefly on the bone. “I’ll call,” she said. “All right.” “Answer when I do.” “I will.” She got into the back seat. Before Clare closed the door, Mara looked at the house. There was no fear in her face that I could identify. She might only have been checking whether we had locked up. I stood on the pavement until the car turned the corner. The first day, I washed the sheets. I did it because there was blood on my pillowcase, though I could not find any after the wash and began to think I had imagined it. I cleaned the bathroom. I threw away the burned saucepan. The blackened layer had lifted in one piece during the night, leaving the metal bright and pitted underneath. I left the blanket in the spare room. It lay across the chair, still unfolded. The threads were gone. I searched the carpet on my hands and knees and found only one, caught beneath the leg of the desk. I put it on the windowsill. By evening I could not see it there. Mara called on Thursday. She sounded better, or at least more awake. Clare had bought her a ridiculous pair of slippers with ears. Mara described them without laughing. “Are you sleeping?” she asked. “Some.” “Don’t say some.” “Four hours.” “That’s not enough.” “No.” She was quiet. In the background Clare told someone to put a knife in the sink, not on the draining board. “I keep waking up sitting,” Mara said. I gripped the phone. “But it’s different,” she added. “There’s a light outside Clare’s room. I think it wakes me.” “Does your neck hurt?” “No.” “Good.” Neither of us seemed to know what to do with that. On Friday she did not call. Clare sent a message saying they had been at the hospital most of the day and Mara was exhausted. I read it several times, looking for the sentence she had chosen not to include. I slept on the sofa that night. The bedroom door remained open. By Saturday the house had stopped feeling expectant. This should have been a relief. Instead I found myself listening for the fridge to stop, for the pipes to knock, for the small shift in silence that used to mean Mara was awake. Nothing carried meaning for long. A floorboard creaked because it was cold. The bathroom light came on because I had switched it. I went back to work for two hours. The centrifuge manual was still open on my computer. Someone had added a comment beside *Remove the rotor using both hands*: *What if rotor is stuck?* I wrote, *Do not attempt removal*. Then I deleted it and sat with my hands on the keyboard. That night I went to bed early. I took no phone, no notebook. I left the hall light off. The sheets smelled of detergent. Without Mara, the bed was too wide, and I kept one hand on her side to stop myself rolling into the middle. I thought about the first nights after the hospital, when she had slept with her back against mine and I had been grateful for any part of her that would touch me. I woke in darkness. Something was breathing beside me. It was a slow, uneven sound, with a small catch at the end of each breath. My breath. The one I made when I was pretending to be asleep. I lay still. The sound came from Mara’s side of the bed. There was no weight in the mattress, no warmth against my arm. I could have reached out. I could have switched on the lamp. Instead I kept my eyes closed and listened to the breath continue, patiently, without getting any closer. After a while it stopped. Then Mara spoke from the darkness beside me. “Are you awake?” I did not answer. My mouth was dry. My heart was beating hard enough to move the sheet, and I tried to breathe slowly, evenly, as though none of it could give me away.

The grief subplot (the lost pregnancy, the hospital, "At least now we know") is woven in organically and gives the horror emotional weight. The possession horror becomes a metaphor for grief's alienating effects on a relationship, and the story earns this reading without being schematic about it. The notebook entries written in mirror-image handwriting, the video file dated tomorrow, the threads disappearing—these are well-deployed uncanny details that accumulate without becoming a checklist. WEAKNESSES: The pacing in the middle chapters (3-5) occasionally becomes repetitive. The pattern of: Dan observes something wrong, Mara says something ambiguous, they fail to communicate, someone apologizes—repeats enough times that momentum slackens. Chapter 4 (Clare's visit) is the weakest chapter; Clare functions primarily as an expository device and her character is thin compared to the two leads. The world-building is minimal, which is appropriate for the claustrophobic domestic setting, but the story occasionally feels hermetically sealed in a way that limits its resonance. We know almost nothing about Dan's work beyond the centrifuge manual (which is used cleverly as a mirror for his controlling tendencies), and the lavender spray/Clare's gift detail is introduced and then abandoned. Some of the uncanny details feel slightly underexplored. The video file dated tomorrow is a genuinely disturbing image, but it's introduced and then essentially dropped—the file can't be opened, and it's never returned to. This could be intentional (the horror of the unknowable) but it reads slightly like an abandoned thread. The "He's going to ask if I'm still in here" line in Chapter 7 is the story's most explicit supernatural moment besides the neck turn, and it's handled well, but the story's ending—while structurally elegant—doesn't quite resolve the question of what is actually happening. This is a deliberate choice, but some readers will find it unsatisfying rather than haunting. The Clare chapter introduces "Don't leave me alone with him" which is a strong moment, but its aftermath is handled too quickly. The story moves past it without fully exploiting its implications for Dan's reliability as a narrator. The piece is faithful to the prompt and genuinely inventive in its approach to possession horror—treating it as domestic, ambiguous, and grief-inflected rather than spectacular. The final chapter's return to the opening image (Dan pretending to sleep, something watching) is structurally satisfying. Overall this is a high-quality piece of literary horror with genuine emotional intelligence, strong dialogue, and controlled prose. Its weaknesses are primarily structural (some repetition, one underdeveloped character, a few dropped threads) rather than fundamental.
