I did not go to the dairy door. This was partly pride and partly because I could not find it. Blackwood had been built by people who considered a straight path an insult to the imagination, and its offices had grown round the original house like fungi. There were three yards where one expected two, a brewhouse where the laundry had been in my time, and a new wall whose only apparent purpose was to make the old wall feel wanted. By Thursday I had also talked myself out of going at all. Julian Thorne had spoken from pity, or shock, or the sort of nervous benevolence that makes a man offer his purse to a beggar and then write to the newspapers about the increase in mendicancy. If I returned, he would have recovered himself. There might be a constable behind the dairy door. There might be Mrs. Gant with a Bible and a policeman, which was worse. At half past twelve I pawned my good shawl for ninepence. At one I was beneath the library window. The rain had gone, leaving a washed, pitiless sky. In daylight the east front of Blackwood was less romantic and more informative. I could see where the mortar had perished, where a lead pipe ran down from a cistern, and where the ivy had been cut back from the study windows but not from the library. Ivy is an accommodating plant if one respects its limitations. It will hold a hand. It will not hold a fool. I had brought a length of clothesline, which I looped round my waist, and a pair of my landlady's son's boots, which were too large and therefore better than my own. I had stuffed the toes with paper. The pipe took my weight. The ivy complained but held. I reached the ledge with only one bad moment, when a piece of mortar came away under my boot and went rattling down the wall. I waited for a window to open below. None did. The library sash was shut. I tapped on the glass. Nothing happened. I tapped again, harder, and considered the several ways in which I had been stupid. The most recent seemed the finest. Then the curtain moved. Julian Thorne drew it back and stared at me through the glass. He was fully dressed this time, in a dark coat, and held a small bundle wrapped in brown paper. For a man expecting a visitor, he looked remarkably appalled to see one. He opened the window. "I said the dairy door." "I said Thursday. We were both a little vague about the middle." "You might have been seen." "I might still be." He stepped back at once. I climbed in without sitting in anything, which I counted as an improvement. The library by day was a tired, handsome room. The carpet had faded in long squares where the sun reached it. There were books on the shelves in orderly rows and books on every table in less orderly ones. A microscope stood by the window with a saucer over its lens to keep off dust. Beside it was a chipped blue cup. Julian held out the parcel. Inside was my mother's locket. I had prepared myself to be cool about receiving it. I had not prepared for the small weight of it in my palm, or for the way the little catch still resisted before opening. My mother's hair was there, brown and fine, coiled under glass. I shut it. "Thank you," I said. He nodded, looking relieved and then, oddly, less so. "There was no difficulty?" "Mrs. Gant believes it was sent to be valued." "Was it?" "No." I looked at him. His ears began to colour. "An untruth?" I asked. "A premature account of my intentions." That was so exactly the sort of thing I had expected him to say that I nearly laughed. I put the locket into my bodice, where it lay cold against my skin. "What do I owe you?" "Nothing." "Then I'll go." "Yes." He did not move aside. "That is—yes, of course." I reached the window before he spoke again. "Was it true?" "Was what true?" "What you said. About its being worth sixpence to anyone but you." "More or less." "And you risked your neck for it." I put one hand on the sash. "You risked Mrs. Gant for it. We must all have our amusements." He frowned, not at the joke but at some thought behind it. On the table beside him lay a journal with a green cover. He turned it round with one finger, aligning it with the edge of the table. "I wished to ask you something," he said. "A matter of natural history." "Then you want a naturalist." "There is a plant. *Parietaria officinalis*. Pellitory-of-the-wall. It grows on old masonry." "It grows on the side of the Pike Street privy." He blinked. "You know it?" "I know the privy." "Ah." "The plant has little green flowers and leaves like a nettle that has lost its temper." "Yes," he said, with sudden animation. "Yes, precisely. The flowers are generally described as insignificant, which seems to me a failure of observation rather than a property of the plant." I looked at him for a moment. "You brought me here to discuss weeds?" "No. I brought you here to return your locket. You came through the window. The weed is a subsequent development." He took a sheet of paper from beneath the journal. On it was a careful drawing of a stem and leaf, with measurements written in the margin. "I should like a fresh specimen," he said. "The root especially. My books are not in agreement." "Dig one up." "The plant does not grow here." "Then go to Pike Street." His animation went out so quietly that I felt I had watched a candle pinched between fingers. "No," he said. "I cannot." There were a dozen answers to that. You have two legs was the one that came first. Then I saw his hand tighten on the edge of the paper and remembered church again: Julian Thorne walking behind his father, stopping once while the others went on, his face set against the effort of breathing. I looked instead at the drawing. "What is it worth?" He raised his head. "The specimen," I said. "With the root. And no soil knocked off, I suppose, since you gentlemen like everything made difficult." "A shilling." "Two." "One and six." "Two, and you pay for the journal if you want that too." His gaze dropped to the green cover. "You read *The Annals and Magazine of Natural History*?" "No. But Mr. Pell at the bookshop reads his till, and I can read a price ticket." For the first time, he smiled. It was not a practised expression. It altered his face so much that I looked away. "Two shillings," he said. "For the plant. The journal is not required." I should have taken the bargain and left. Instead I said, "What number?" He told me. It was an old number, from the spring, and contained an article on British mosses he had not been able to obtain. His father, he explained, had lately taken an interest in his correspondence. "An interest," I repeated. "He opens it." The clock on the mantel ticked. Beyond the window, a gardener wheeled a barrow across the east lawn. I thought of my room over the chandler's, where the plaster fell into my bed when the people upstairs walked about. I thought of ninepence for my shawl, and of Mrs. Gant's face when she told me I would never again be trusted in a respectable house. "Two shillings for the plant," I said. "Four for the journal, if Pell has it. I don't carry anything stolen into this house." Julian's expression changed. "I did not suppose—" "You did. It doesn't matter. Those are my terms." He opened a drawer and took out a small purse. His hands were ink-stained at the fingers. He counted two shillings onto the table, then added sixpence. "For your boots," he said. I looked down at the paper-stuffed toes. "My boots are not for sale." "No. I meant—" He stopped, hearing how it sounded. "Yes. Of course. Forgive me." I swept up the two shillings and left the sixpence. "Next Thursday," I said. "If the window's locked, I won't wait." This time he did not suggest the dairy door. He only stood beside the microscope with his rejected sixpence in his hand and watched me climb out. At the bottom, I found my first glove in the laurels. It had been lying there for four days, soaked through and half eaten by something. I put it on anyway. A person can become accustomed to almost anything, I thought, if it is damp enough.

"Two, and you pay for the journal") is particularly well-handled, establishing their dynamic through action rather than description. The gardener with the barrow is a nice grounding detail but could be used more actively. By November I had opinions about ivy. The common sort on Blackwood's east front was *Hedera helix*, Julian informed me, as if a Latin name made it more trustworthy. The leaves were five-lobed on the young growth and oval near the flowers. This interested him. What interested me was that the old stems near the library were as thick as my wrist, while the pretty new growth by the study came away in handfuls. "One must distinguish," I told him, "between a plant and a ladder." He was examining a piece of pellitory root through his microscope and did not look up. "One must also distinguish between a root and a quantity of Pike Street." "You said not to knock the soil off." "I did not ask you to bring the wall." There was a small brick in the specimen tin. I maintained that it had been attached when I found it. Our arrangements had settled into something that was not quite regular enough to be called a routine. I came on Thursdays when Lord Thorne dined out, and once on a Monday when he did not. I brought Julian two numbers of his journal, a paper of pins, three snails in a tobacco box, and a pamphlet on sewage that Mr. Pell had been so glad to be rid of that he charged me only for the string. Julian paid me in coins laid neatly on the corner of the table. I never took them until he had inspected what I brought. This was not delicacy. It was bookkeeping. I learned to come after the house had quieted and before the kitchen cat began its courtship beneath the east windows. I learned that the third slate above the morning room was loose, that the lead pipe gave a hollow note if struck, and that Mrs. Gant walked past the library door at twenty minutes to eleven with a step like a measured rebuke. I kept my good stockings in my pocket and changed into them on the ledge, leaving the wet pair outside. There is no use in learning an art if one refuses to be particular about it. Julian never asked how I came. He had stopped suggesting doors, but he still looked at the window whenever the wind moved the ivy. That night he had left a towel on the chair. I used it without comment. He pretended not to notice, which was his way of being polite, and turned the pellitory leaf beneath the lens. "The root hairs are visible," he said. "I'm glad somebody's are." He looked then. "Your hair is wet." "That is generally what rain does." "There is a fire." "There generally is." He pushed the small heater nearer my chair with his foot. It was an awkward movement, made without looking at me, and for some reason it silenced me more completely than kindness spoken aloud would have done. I sat with my hands near the warmth. My fingers had gone white at the tips. Julian returned to his microscope. After a moment he said, "You have brought the wrong journal." I looked at the green cover on my lap. "Mr. Pell said it was the April number." "It is April of last year." "He said April." "Yes," Julian said. "I see that he would." The disappointment was slight and quickly hidden. That made it worse. If he had complained, I could have told him what a day's searching cost me, and how Pell kept his old stock in a cellar where the damp had fused the pages into bricks. Instead he laid the journal aside and drew his sheet of notes towards him. "I'll take it back," I said. "There is no need." "I said I would get it." "And you have been exceedingly—" He stopped. "It is not important." That was a lie so badly made that even he seemed to hear it. His ears coloured. I opened the journal. The article he wanted was listed on the cover: *On the Fructification of Certain British Mosses*. Beneath it, someone had drawn a small, obscene addition to the word *British*. Mr. Pell's cellar had other amusements, evidently. "What is fructification?" He explained. I understood perhaps half, but the half I understood was interesting: that a thing could be common, underfoot, and still not properly known. He showed me a capsule through the microscope. It looked like a tiny lantern on a stalk. "And you write about these?" "Sometimes." "For money?" "No." "For fame?" "No." "Then why?" He considered the question seriously. "Because when I began, there was a confusion in the descriptions. Two species had been treated as one. It seemed worth putting right." "And did anyone thank you?" "A man in Aberdeen wrote to say I was mistaken." "Were you?" "Not entirely." I laughed. He looked startled, then smiled down at his notes. On the following Thursday I brought him the correct April number. Pell had not had it. I had found it in a box at a stall by the cattle market, under a sermon and a cookbook missing its first twelve pages. It cost three shillings, which was more than Julian had agreed to pay, and a morning I could ill spare. He knew. I saw him know, and wished I had lied about it. "Thank you," he said. "Four shillings." "Clara—" "Four. You can give a lecture on the difference if you like." He gave me four shillings. I took them, because pride that refuses agreed wages is only another sort of vanity. For a while we read, or he read and I turned pages when he asked. The fire settled. My wet skirt steamed faintly. I had nearly fallen asleep when he said, "You pronounce it *Parietaria*." "I what?" "The plant. You said *Parry-terrier* on your first visit." "I did not." "You did." "Well, it grows by a privy. It cannot be particular." "It is *Parry-eh-taria*." I repeated it incorrectly on purpose. He corrected me again. I threw the towel at him. It struck the microscope, which rocked. He caught it with both hands, and for one instant we were both frozen in mutual horror. Then he began to laugh. It was not the little suppressed sound from our first meeting. He laughed until he had to take off his spectacles, and I laughed because he looked so unlike himself doing it. The noise seemed too large for the cautious room. A floorboard creaked in the passage. We stopped. Julian rose too quickly and knocked his knee against the table. I blew out the candle nearest me; he turned down the lamp. Darkness came in except for the red square of the fire. The steps were not Mrs. Gant's. They were lighter, hesitant. A housemaid, perhaps, or someone who had forgotten where she was going. They paused outside the library. I stood behind the curtain with Julian's towel still in my hand. He was beside me, close enough that I could feel the warmth of his arm through his shirt. Neither of us moved. His shoulder rose and fell once, and I heard the small roughness in his breathing. The handle did not turn. After a time the steps went on. We remained in the dark. "That," Julian whispered at last, "was probably nothing." "Most things are, until they aren't." He did not answer. I became aware that my hand was against his waistcoat, though I could not remember putting it there. I removed it. He lit the lamp again. The room returned: books, microscope, faded carpet, two people standing much nearer than was required. "I should go," I said. "Yes." Neither of us looked at the window. At the ledge I put on my wet stockings and immediately regretted every improvement I had ever made to my method. Julian held the sash. "Next Thursday?" he asked. "If your father dines out." "He does." I had one foot in the ivy when he spoke again. "The towel was not an errand." I looked up. "No," I said. "I had gathered that." Then I went down, because there are remarks after which a sensible woman does not remain on a windowsill. At the bottom I discovered that I had taken his pen wiper instead of my gloves. It was a sorry piece of green cloth, ink-black at one end. I kept it.

Miss Hawthorne came to Blackwood on a Tuesday, and by Thursday half the county knew that she had brought six trunks, a French maid, and a father who owned enough of Manchester to make the rest of it nervous. I heard this at the butter market, where news was sold more cheaply than butter and kept about as well. The woman beside me said Miss Hawthorne had a fortune of eighty thousand pounds. The man at the egg stall said it was a hundred and twenty, and that Lord Thorne meant to have the west roof repaired before Christmas. Neither seemed to think Julian's opinion material to the transaction. I told myself I was glad. An heiress in the house meant more coming and going, which was inconvenient. It also meant Julian would no longer require weeds fetched from privies or old journals rescued from cattle-market stalls. He could send a servant to London for anything he wanted. He could go to London himself, perhaps, and stand in a bookshop like an ordinary man with two legs and money. I spent the afternoon mending a hotel tablecloth and thinking of reasons not to go to Blackwood. At ten o'clock I put on my climbing boots. The library was cold when I got in. Julian had let the fire burn low, and the lamp stood on his desk rather than by the hearth. He was not reading. A sheet of paper lay before him with three lines written on it and a great deal of ink scratched out beneath. He looked round when my boot knocked the sill. "You came," he said. "You sound disappointed." "No. Surprised." "That is often disappointment with better manners." I set a parcel on the table. It contained a tin of gentian root he had asked for and two dried fungi that had looked more impressive when I found them. The journey had reduced one to crumbs. He did not open it. "Your payment is there," he said, nodding towards the coins. "Don't you want to inspect the damage first?" "Not particularly." I took off my wet gloves and laid them over the back of the chair. He watched without appearing to see them. "Well?" I said. "Well what?" "Am I to congratulate you?" His face changed so slightly that another person might not have noticed. I had become, to my own annoyance, another person who did. "On what?" "The roof, principally. I hear it is to be repaired." He looked at the dead fire. "My father has spoken to Mr. Hawthorne." "That was economical of him. The whole county has spoken to Mr. Hawthorne." "Nothing is settled." "But you are to marry her." Julian picked up his pen, found it dry, and put it down again. "It is considered a suitable arrangement." "By whom?" "By everyone concerned." "Then you must be no one." His head came up. For a moment I thought I had angered him. Instead he looked tired. "She is perfectly unobjectionable." "What a foundation for happiness." "You know nothing about it." "No," I said. "I have never had eighty thousand pounds. My objections are cheaper." He rose and went to the window. I had to move aside to avoid being walked through. He stood with his back to me, one hand on the curtain. "The estate is in debt," he said. "Not the sort of debt my father discusses at dinner, but the sort that determines whether farms are sold and men are turned off. There are mortgages. The home farm has lost money for three years. My mother's jointure is charged on land that no longer—" He stopped. "You do not need the details." "No. I expect they are very refining." "Clara." It was the first time he had said my name as a rebuke. I liked it less than I expected. He turned. "You speak as though I had a choice between this and some other life I have merely neglected to select." "Haven't you?" "No." "Then what are all these books for? Decoration?" "Some people find knowledge preferable to ignorance, even when it does not immediately increase their income." "And some people find a spine useful, even when it doesn't." The words were out before I could make them kinder. I would not have made them kinder. Julian went white. That gave me a small, vicious satisfaction, followed at once by shame. "A spine," he repeated. "You let him open your letters. You let him decide what you may read and where you may walk and whom you may marry. You sit here making notes on things no one else can see, and call it a life because the bars have books on them." "You think this is a cage I enjoy?" "I think you have polished the lock." He took off his spectacles. Without them his face looked younger and more exposed. "You have no conception of duty." "I had a duty to Mrs. Gant, apparently. It consisted of holding my tongue while she made a child of fourteen scrub a floor twice for missing a spot." "This is not comparable." "No. You have a fire." His hand closed round the spectacles. "Yes," he said quietly. "I have a fire. I have a house, and food, and a father whose conduct I find intolerable. These advantages ought, I suppose, to make my difficulties contemptible." "I didn't say—" "You have made your opinion of my difficulties sufficiently plain. But permit me to observe that your freedom appears to consist chiefly of being answerable to no one because no one cares whether you live or die." The room became very still. Outside, a small piece of ivy tapped the glass. I thought of my mother's locket under my dress. I thought of the ninepence for my shawl, and the tablecloth, and how I had walked two miles that morning because the carrier's cart cost a penny. "That is true," I said. "It is not the improvement you seem to think." He closed his eyes. "Clara, I—" I picked up my gloves. "You needn't pay me for the gentian. It was growing where anyone could get it." "Please don't go like this." "How would you like me to go? Obediently?" That struck him too. I saw it, and was glad, and hated myself for being glad. I put one leg over the sill. The coins remained on the table. "Take your money," he said. "No." "You earned it." "Then consider it a donation to the estate." His mouth tightened. "You are being unjust." "Yes," I said. "It is one of my few luxuries." The descent was dry and easy. That seemed an additional insult. My hands knew where to go; my boots found every hold. At the bottom I looked up and saw Julian still at the window, a narrow figure against the weak lamp. He did not call after me. I walked across the park instead of keeping to the shrubbery. If a keeper saw me, let him. Let Lord Thorne come out with his gun and his mortgages and his suitable arrangements. I was so angry that for nearly half a mile I walked without feeling the cold. Then the anger began to wear thin, and beneath it was something much less useful. He was to marry a woman he found perfectly unobjectionable. He would live at Blackwood with the roof mended and his letters unopened, perhaps, as a wedding present. There would be children with delicate lungs and large fortunes. He would grow older at the desk by the window. On wet nights he would hear the ivy and think of nothing at all. I stopped by the ha-ha and pressed the heel of my hand against my eyes. "Fool," I said aloud. It was not clear which of us I meant. At my lodging, the landlady had left a bill under my door. Four shillings for the week, and sixpence for the boots her son had missed at last. I sat on the bed and counted what remained after the market stall, the journal, and my mother's locket redeemed from the pawnbroker's—an extravagance I had not mentioned to Julian. There was not enough. For the first time I understood that I had not been going to Blackwood for the money. This was inconvenient knowledge. Like most of Julian's specimens, it had been there all along, small and common and waiting for someone to look properly.

CHARACTERIZATION: Both characters are rendered with considerable nuance and remain consistent with their profiles. I stayed away for nine days. This was not a decision. A decision would have required me to admit there was something to decide. I had work, or said I had. There were sheets from the Crown to mend, a christening cap to alter for a woman who paid in soup, and a pair of curtains whose former owner had kept a cat with strong views. On Saturday I walked to Pell's bookshop, remembered I had no reason to go in, and bought a pennyworth of barley sugar from the woman next door instead. I made it last until Tuesday. On Thursday evening my landlady's son came home with a tale that Blackwood was to have a dinner party, that the Hawthornes were stopping another fortnight, and that Mr. Julian had been taken poorly after riding with Miss Hawthorne. "Riding?" I said. "That's what my aunt's girl heard. Fell off, perhaps." "Julian Thorne would not fall off a horse. He would apologise to it." The boy looked at me strangely. I returned to my sheet. At ten I was beneath the library window with no parcel, no errand, and no intention of going in. The sash was latched. I had never known it latched against me. Once, when Julian had been called to his father, it had been shut but not fastened. Now the little brass catch sat squarely behind the glass. I tapped once. Nothing. The sensible thing was to descend. I had my hand on the ivy when the curtain moved. Julian drew it back. For a second we looked at one another through the window. He was in his dressing gown, with a scarf wrapped badly round his throat, and his hair stood up at one side. He opened the catch and pushed up the sash. "You shouldn't be here," he said. "Nor should you. Go back to bed." "I am not in bed." "That explains the dressing gown." He coughed. It was a dry, hard sound that seemed to hurt him. I climbed in and shut the window before he could object. The room smelt of medicine and cold ash. There was a bowl on the table with a cloth over it, and an untouched glass of milk. His papers had been stacked with unusual neatness, as though someone else had tidied them. "Are you ill?" I asked. "A cold." "Did you fall off a horse?" "No." "Did Miss Hawthorne?" "No." He looked bewildered. "Why should she?" "Because the whole neighbourhood appears determined that one of you must." He sat down in the chair by the dead fire. I put my hand to the coals, found no heat, and began laying fresh wood. "You need not do that." "You need not sit in an icehouse." "I did not know you were coming." "No." He watched me use the bellows. His silence had a different quality from before. It was not offended, only exhausted. When the kindling caught, I stood. "Well," I said. "You are alive. The neighbourhood exaggerates." "Clara." I went to the table and began folding the cloth over the bowl. There was nothing useful in it, but it gave my hands an occupation. "I am sorry," he said. The cloth slipped. I folded it again. "For which part?" "For saying no one cared whether you lived or died." "Oh." "It was untrue, and I knew it was untrue when I said it. I wished to injure you." "You succeeded." "Yes." He looked at his hands. "I have been thinking that I might have managed it with more elegance." I gave a short laugh before I could stop myself. He glanced up, and then away. "You were right," he said. "Not about everything. About the lock." The fire made a small ticking noise. "I don't want to be right." "No. That would be inconvenient for both of us." I sat opposite him. There was a foot of hearthrug between our knees. He told me then, not all at once and not very well, about the dinner party. Miss Hawthorne had been seated beside him. She had spoken twice: once about the weather and once to ask whether he preferred town or country. He had answered country, and then spent ten minutes trying to think of something else to say. His father had afterwards called him an ungrateful blockhead, though not in those words and not until Mr. Hawthorne had gone. "She isn't unkind," Julian said. "I never said she was." "No. You did not." "Is she pretty?" He considered this with such genuine difficulty that I almost forgave him everything. "I believe so. She has very straight hair." "A compelling recommendation." "She asked whether I read for pleasure." "What did you say?" "That I did. She said she preferred a person who read to one who talked incessantly." "She sounds sensible." "Yes." We looked at one another. "I think," Julian said, "that she and I might manage very well, if neither of us required anything from the other." The fire had begun to draw. A little flame ran along the bark and vanished. "And do you?" I asked. "Require anything?" He did not answer quickly. That was one of the things I had come to like in him: he did not always seize the first available sentence. "My father requires an heir," he said. "Mr. Hawthorne requires a connection. The estate requires money. I have been trying for some years to determine what I require, but it has seemed an impertinent question." "And now?" "Now it seems the only one." He began to cough again. I gave him the milk; he made a face and drank it. When he could speak, he said, "I am afraid of him. That is the whole of it. I can give you reasons about the farms and the debts, and they are true, but underneath them is that I am twenty-seven years old and when he comes into a room I am still waiting to be told I have disappointed him." There was no answer that would not have diminished it. So I gave him none. After a while I said, "My freedom is not what you called it either." He looked at me. "I sleep with a chair under the door handle. Not because anyone has tried it, but because they might. I owe six weeks' rent. I steal things, Julian. Not only from people who can spare them." "I know." "You don't know all of it." "No," he said. "I did not mean that I did." I took the barley sugar from my pocket. It had broken in two. I offered him half; he shook his head, and I put it back. "I hate being poor," I said. "Not the cold. Not even being hungry. I hate how much of the day it takes. People think poverty is having nothing. It is having to think about everything." His face changed, but not with pity. That was why I could bear it. "I am sorry," he said. "You didn't cause it." "No. But I have benefited from a great many arrangements I did not cause." "That sounds like one of your papers." "It does, rather." We smiled faintly. Then he reached across the space between us and took my hand. His fingers were cold. Mine were not much better. There was nothing expert in it; he caught my little finger first and had to adjust his hold. I could have withdrawn. I did not. "I missed your visits," he said. "I was busy." "Yes." "You needn't believe me." "I was trying to be polite." "Don't. It doesn't suit you." His thumb moved once over my knuckles. I looked at our hands because looking at his face had become too difficult. "I cannot promise you anything," he said. "I haven't asked you to." "No. But you might, and I should like to be honest before you did." I raised my eyes. He was frightened again, but he did not let go. "Don't make a sacrifice of yourself on my account," I said. "I haven't the room for it." "I will endeavour not to." We sat until the fire burned down and the milk left a skin in the glass. We spoke of small things: Pell's dishonest cellar, the snail that had escaped into his desk, whether Miss Hawthorne's straight hair was naturally so. Near dawn I fell asleep in the chair and woke with my head against his shoulder. Neither of us mentioned it. When I left, he latched the window behind me, then opened it again. "For air," he said. The sky was turning grey over the park. "Of course," I said, and went home by the long way, because for once the ground did not seem quite steady beneath me.

For three weeks I was happy in a manner I distrusted. Nothing had been settled. Julian still coughed when the wind was east, Lord Thorne still intended to repair his fortunes with his son, and I still mended hotel linen in a room where the plaster came down at night. Yet on Thursday there would be a fire, and Julian would have left the window unlatched, and for several hours I would not have to explain why I had come. Once he gave me a book to keep. It was a small flora with plain covers, not valuable enough to make accepting it an argument. He had marked three plants in pencil. "So that you may correct me," he said. "I correct you without a book." "Yes, but inaccurately." Another time I fell asleep while he was reading aloud about glaciers. He did not wake me until the clock struck three. I accused him of letting me miss the safest hour for leaving; he said I had been snoring. I said I did not snore. He replied that he had not wished to introduce further distressing information into our acquaintance. That was the nearest we came to speaking of the future. On the last Thursday in November, I found the park full of lamps. Not full of them, exactly. There were four: one at the stables, one moving beside the home wood, and two on the terrace. Four lights at Blackwood after midnight were more remarkable than forty would have been in town. I stayed behind the wall until the moving lamp went towards the kennels. A dog barked, was cursed, and stopped. The library window was dark. I climbed because I had come too far to think sensibly. The ivy was wet, and my hands were cold before I began. Halfway up, a man's voice spoke on the other side of the morning-room wall. I flattened myself against the stone and waited while he passed beneath me. "—in his room now," he said. Another man answered too softly to hear. "His lordship means it this time. No more of your—" A door shut. I remained on the wall until my arms shook. Then I went up. The sash would not move. I put my penknife between the frames and felt for the catch, though I knew it was not the catch resisting me. Something had been fastened across the inside. A light appeared under the door. I dropped to the ledge below the window just as the library door opened. My boot struck the pipe; it gave its hollow note. "What's that?" a woman said inside. I stopped breathing. "The wind," a man replied. Mrs. Gant said, "There is no wind." There was, a little, but not enough to argue with her. Their steps crossed the room. I hung beneath the sill with my fingers in a joint of mortar and thought, very clearly, that Julian had better be dying. The curtain drew aside an inch. "Well?" Mrs. Gant said. "Nothing." "His lordship will have the ivy cut tomorrow. All of it. I have said for years that it harboured vermin." The curtain fell. Their steps went away. A key turned in the door from the outside. I got down without knowing how. At the bottom my knees gave way, and I sat in the laurels until the dog began barking again. The kitchen yard was lit. I ought to have gone home. Instead I went round by the wall where, in my time, the under-housemaid had sometimes stood to speak to the groom. There was no groom now. There was Alice Pimm, who had been fourteen when Mrs. Gant made her scrub the flags twice, and who was seventeen and too thin. She came out with a pail and saw me before I could speak. The pail hit the stones. "Miss Vane," she whispered. "Don't scream." "I wasn't going to." "You looked as though you might." She picked up the pail. Water had gone over her shoes. "You mustn't be here. There's a man from the constable's been, and Mr. Warren's got a gun." "For whom?" Alice looked towards the house. "For anyone breaking in, he says." "What has happened?" She told me in pieces. Lord Thorne had found a journal in Julian's desk, not one of the natural-history ones but a stationer's wrapper with Pike Street written on it in my hand. That was the beginning, or the beginning Alice knew. There had been questions about money. A footman remembered mud in the library. Mrs. Gant had found my wet stocking behind a curtain, where I must have dropped it weeks before, and had recognised the mending. Of course she had. She had taught me to mend. "Mr. Julian said there was nothing stolen," Alice whispered. "His lordship said that wasn't the point. Miss Hawthorne's father was there. They were in the study until ever so late." "Where is Julian?" "In the blue room. Mr. Warren's outside." "And Miss Hawthorne?" Alice stared. "Gone back to the west wing, I suppose." It had not occurred to me until then that she was still in the house. I had a sudden, useless picture of her sitting upright in bed with her straight hair braided, listening to men decide what sort of life she could afford. Alice caught my sleeve. "You mustn't try to see him." "I wasn't going to." This was such an obvious lie that she let go. "He said you'd say that," she said. I went still. Alice put her hand into her apron and brought out a folded scrap of paper. "He made me promise not to give it you unless you came. He said you wouldn't come, and then I was to burn it." "Then he has had one sensible thought." But I took it. The paper had been torn from a letter. Julian's writing was smaller than usual and blotted where his pen had failed. *He knows your name. There is to be a warrant if you are found here again. I have agreed to everything. Do not attempt to see me. The money enclosed is not a payment. Please take it and go somewhere he cannot reach.* There was no money enclosed. Alice saw me look. "His lordship took it," she said. "Mr. Julian had it in an envelope first." I read the message again. *I have agreed to everything.* "What has he agreed?" Alice's face crumpled. "The settlement was signed tonight. They're to be married before Christmas, and Mr. Julian's to go to Italy after. For his health." Italy. He had once told me he should like to see the mosses of the Apennines. His father had found a way to make even that a sentence. "When?" "The banns—no, it's a licence, I think. Cook says a licence. Miss Hawthorne's father doesn't like waiting." A door opened at the far side of the yard. Alice pushed me behind the water butt. It was not large enough to conceal a cat, but the man who came out only wanted to empty a bottle and go in again. We stood pressed against the wall, smelling beer and wet stone. "You have to go," she whispered. "Yes." "Miss Vane—he did it so they wouldn't take you." I looked at her. She was crying without making a sound, because servants learn that early. "No," I said. "He did it so he wouldn't have to watch them try." She flinched. I was sorry at once, but sorrow had become a slow organ in me. The anger got there first. I gave her Julian's note. "Burn it." "You said—" "I know what I said." She held it against her apron. "Will you come back?" "No." That, at least, I intended. I crossed the home field at a run, keeping low until I reached the lane. Twice I thought I heard someone behind me. Once it was a sheep. The other time I did not look round. At my lodging there was a paper nailed to the front door. Not for me; the landlord was behind with his taxes, and the notice concerned the house. I stood reading it by the light of the area lamp because my own name had made any official printing alarming. My landlady was waiting in the passage. "A man came," she said. "Asking about a young woman who did needlework. He knew about the boots." I went upstairs and packed. There was not much: two shirts, the flora, my mother's locket, a needle case, Julian's green pen wiper, and three shillings and fourpence. I left the christening cap half altered, which troubled me more than it should have done. At dawn I took the carrier's cart as far as Millbridge and walked the rest of the way to a lodging whose landlady did not ask for a reference. I told her my name was Carter. For two days I did not go out except to buy bread. On the third I read Julian's note in my memory until the words lost their shape. *I have agreed to everything.* He had written it as if agreement were a medicine he had taken for my good. Bitter, perhaps, but administered with clean hands. He had decided what danger I could bear. He had decided what life he could bear. He had put us both away in drawers and called it protection. On the fourth day I bought a map. There were twelve miles between Millbridge and Blackwood by the road. By the fields it was nearer ten. The blue room was on the south front, above the old drawing room. I remembered its balcony, and the ornamental pear tree below it, which had been pruned so hard every year that its branches were like knuckles. A sensible woman would have gone to Liverpool. I had never claimed to be sensible. I had only claimed, on several occasions, to know what I was doing. This time I did not.

The pear tree would not take my weight. I knew this before I left Millbridge, and remembered it afresh when I saw how little of it remained. Blackwood's gardeners had been at the ivy. It lay in heaps along the east front, dark leaves already limp, with pale wounds on the stone where the old stems had been torn away. The library route was gone. On the south front a balcony projected above the drawing room, and beside it a soil pipe descended into a bed of laurustinus. Between pipe and balcony there was a space of perhaps four feet. Perhaps is a word that gets people killed. I waited until after two. The house was not quiet; houses expecting weddings never are. A lamp burned in the servants' hall, and twice someone crossed an upper passage. Rain came in gusts, hard enough to drum on my cap and then stop, leaving me conspicuous in the silence. The pipe held. The laurustinus did not, but it broke my first slip and made enough noise to bring a dog round the corner. It was the old liver-and-white spaniel, not the keeper's bitch. He knew me, or thought he did. I had fed him once from the stillroom window in my scullery days. He stood beneath me with his head on one side while I hung from the pipe and whispered his name. He sat down. "Good," I said. "We have both risen in the world." The balcony balustrade was iron. I caught the lowest curl with my fingers, got a knee over, and lay on the wet boards until my arms stopped trembling. The blue room's window was above and to the left. There was no convenient ledge, only the stone architrave of the drawing-room window below and a hornbeam branch that had been trained against the wall. I used the branch. It bent, sprang back, and slapped me across the mouth. For the next minute I was occupied in not falling and not swearing. When I reached the window, my lip was bleeding and one sleeve had torn loose at the shoulder. The glass reflected the park: black trees, a pale seam of sky, and a woman who looked as if she had been pulled through a hedge by someone with a grudge. I tapped. The curtain opened so quickly that I nearly let go. Julian stood on the other side. He was dressed, though his collar was unfastened, and there was a portmanteau on the bed behind him. For a moment he only stared. Then he lifted the sash. "No," he said. "Yes." "Clara, you cannot—" "Then come and help me before I fall and make your argument for you." He caught my wrists. His first pull was too timid; his second brought me against the frame hard enough to knock the breath out of me. I got one knee inside, then the other, and slid to the floor. He shut the window. "You must go," he whispered. I sat where I was. "You have developed a monotony of conversation." "There is a man outside the door." "Then don't shout." "I am not shouting." "You are whispering in capital letters." He went to the door and listened. I used the time to stand. My legs were not entirely in agreement. Julian came back. "My father means to send me to Bath tomorrow. The licence is being obtained. He has a man watching the road." "Then it is fortunate I didn't use it." "He will kill you if he finds you here." "Your father is unlikely to kill me. He will have me transported, which takes longer and inconveniences more people." He flinched. "You think this is amusing?" "No." The word came out harder than I intended. He saw my face then, properly: the cut lip, the rain, the torn sleeve. Something in his expression gave way. "You are hurt." "Not materially." "That is what you said before." "It was true before." He reached towards my mouth and stopped before touching it. I caught his hand and held it between us. "You agreed to everything," I said. He looked down. "Yes." "You sent me money you didn't have and instructions I was to obey, and then you packed your bag." "I thought if I complied, he would leave you alone." "And did you ask him?" Julian was silent. "Did you make that a condition? Did you get it in writing? Did you do anything except decide what was best and call the deciding courage?" "It was not courage." "No. It was not." He pulled his hand away. For an instant I thought I had lost him, that he would retreat behind one of his careful sentences and come out only when it was safe. Instead he said, "What would you have had me do?" "Tell me." "He was going to have you arrested." "Tell me." "And then what? You would have come, as you have come now. You would have stood in a room with my father and informed him he had no moral authority over you. He knows that. It would not stop him." "So you saved me the trouble." "Yes." "And yourself the sight." His face tightened. I went on because I had climbed a wall to say it and could not stop at the window. "You have made me a fugitive and yourself a prisoner. That is not sacrifice. It is only a tidier sort of surrender." He turned away and walked to the bed. The portmanteau was open. Inside were shirts, two books, and a leather case I recognised as his microscope. "I do not know how to defy him," he said. The sentence was so quiet that the anger went out of me. Not all of it. I kept some. I expected to need it. "No," I said. "You have had no practice." He sat on the edge of the bed. "When I was twelve, I ran away." I waited. "I got as far as the lodge. I had a bag of apples and a volume of Virgil. It began to rain, and I remembered I had not brought a coat. My father found me sitting under the gate arch. He did not strike me. He said, 'You see, Julian, even your rebellions require supervision.'" Julian gave a small, terrible smile. "I have remembered that for fifteen years. Every time I think of doing something he has forbidden, I hear it. And I think: he will be right. I shall get as far as the gate and discover I have forgotten the essential thing." "Then we shall make a list." He looked at me. "A list," he repeated. "Coat. Money. Dry stockings. Bread, if there is any. Not Virgil." The smile changed. It became almost human. "There is no money," he said. "My father has taken my keys. Mr. Hawthorne is paying my debts in advance, I believe, which gives the whole arrangement an admirably commercial air." "How much is in your purse?" "Seven shillings." "I have three and fourpence." "We are rich." "We are ruined. It is more concise." He looked towards the door. Someone coughed in the passage. Julian stood so quickly that the portmanteau fell shut. "I don't want to marry her," he said. "I know." "No. You know I am unhappy. That is not the same thing." He pressed the heel of his hand against his forehead. "I do not want to marry her. I do not want to go to Italy because my father has ordered it. I do not want to discover, at fifty, that I have been considerate to everyone except myself and have called it duty." His breath caught. He waited until he could speak evenly. "I don't want to do this anymore." There was no triumph in it. He looked ill. "All right," I said. "All right?" "That is the beginning. We can find you a more impressive declaration later." He gave a breath that might have been a laugh. Then he went to the washstand and picked up his coat. "What are you doing?" "Putting on my coat." "Not yet. What do you actually need?" He looked round the room. It was painful to watch: books on the table, drawers half open, a life arranged in objects and none of them portable. "The microscope," he said. "No." "It is my mother's." I looked at the leather case. "Can you carry it in one hand?" "Yes." "Then that. One book. Paper and a pen. Money. Warm clothes. Nothing because it is valuable." He chose the flora he had given me, saw it was not there, and looked confused. "I have it," I said. He nodded, and for a moment neither of us could speak. He packed quickly after that. Badly, but quickly. I rolled stockings round the microscope and took out two of the three waistcoats he had included. He did not argue. At the bottom of a drawer he found five sovereigns in a old purse and stood staring at them. "Your essential thing," I said. "It appears so." A key turned in the corridor. We both froze. The lock did not open; the key was withdrawn, and a man's voice muttered to another about the draught. Julian looked at the door, then at the window. "We cannot get past Warren," he said. "No." "My father will be in the study until four. He has been writing to Mr. Hawthorne's solicitor." "Then we won't call on him." Julian understood. His eyes went to the balcony, the wet glass, the distance down. "No," he said. "Yes." "Clara, I have never—" "I know." "I am not strong enough." "Then you will have to be stubborn instead." He gave me a look of such pure alarm that, if there had been time, I might have laughed. I tied my clothesline to the balcony support below the window. It was too short. Julian watched me measure it against the drop. "That will not reach." "No." "What do we do at the end?" "Get down." He shut his eyes briefly. "Not through the front door," he said. I looked at him. "If I go out through the front door, Warren will stop me. If I go into my father's study, I shall—I do not know what I shall do. But I have been in that study all my life." He picked up the microscope case. "We had better go out your way." It was the first sensible thing he had said all night.

Model Output:
The art of leaving a manor by its upper windows is much like the art of entering, except that one has a companion, a microscope, and no longer any reason to be quiet about tearing one's clothes. I went first. The clothesline reached the drawing-room architrave with a foot to spare, provided one did not mind trusting a stone ornament shaped like a bunch of grapes. I minded very much. I also minded Julian leaning out above me and whispering, "Be careful," as if I had intended to be careless. "Go back until I call," I said. He withdrew his head. It reappeared almost at once. "What?" "Nothing." "Then nothing can wait." He disappeared again. I got onto the architrave, then down to the balcony. The pear tree bent under my boot but held long enough for me to reach the laurustinus. From there it was a drop into wet leaves and a mouthful of soil. When I looked up, Julian was sitting on the window ledge with his legs inside. "Come out backwards," I called softly. "I am considering the alternatives." "There aren't any." He came out backwards. His coat caught on the sash. His spectacles slipped. He had tied the microscope case to his belt with a scarf, and it swung against the stone with a sound that made us both stop. Somewhere inside, a dog barked. "Leave it," I whispered. "It is my mother's." "Then tell it to stop knocking." He unfastened the scarf and lowered the case to me on the clothesline. This took time. His hands were shaking, and the knot he had chosen was one of those that become more determined the more one pulls them. At last the case came down. I put it behind the laurustinus. Julian descended six feet and stopped. "I cannot find the next hold." "Left foot. There is a stone lip." "There is not." "There is. You are standing beside it." "My spectacles are wet." "Then take them off." "I shall not be able to see." "You cannot see now." He took them off, folded them, and put them in his coat. This left him clinging to the rope with one hand while he performed an operation requiring two. I watched with my heart in my mouth and my temper rising to keep it company. "Julian." "Yes?" "Put your foot where I tell you and stop improving the plan." He put his foot where I told him. The rope gave a little. Not much. A strand parted against the iron above with a small, dry noise. He heard it. "Clara?" "Come down." He came down. Not gracefully, and not by the route I had chosen, but quickly. The last eight feet were more a matter of arrival than descent. He struck the balcony, missed the pear tree, and landed in the laurustinus beside me. For a moment we lay there. "Are you hurt?" I asked. "No." "Materially?" He turned his head. Without his spectacles his eyes looked defenceless. "I believe," he said, "that I have swallowed a leaf." The spaniel came round the corner. I swore and pulled Julian up. The dog trotted over, sniffed Julian's hand, and sat on his foot. "Your influence is remarkable," I said. "He knows me." "He knows everyone. That is why he is a bad watchdog." We left him beside the balcony. He did not bark. I have thought since that he deserved some memorial, though a spaniel is unlikely to value one. We did not go through the gates. Warren's lamp moved near the lodge, and beyond it the road to Bath lay white in the darkness. We crossed the home field instead, climbed two fences, and went through a copse where every branch found Julian's face. He carried the microscope. I carried the bag, which contained, in the end, one book, three shirts, five pairs of stockings, paper, pens, a loaf Alice had left by the stillroom window—I chose not to examine how she knew—and no coat brush. At the boundary wall Julian stopped. He was breathing badly. Not the little cough I knew, but a deep, tearing effort that frightened me. "We rest," I said. "We have only just—" "We rest." He sat on the wall. I stood in front of him so that he could not see Blackwood unless he leaned sideways. He leaned sideways. The house was mostly dark. One lamp burned in what I thought was his father's study. "He will say I have run away because I was afraid," Julian said. "You have." "Yes." "You can be afraid somewhere else." He considered this, still breathing hard. "That is not an especially noble account of it." "No. I expect you'll improve it when you write your memoirs." He smiled faintly. Then he looked at me. "You need not come further." I had been waiting for this. Not because I believed he wanted me gone, but because he was the sort of man who would think politeness required at the edge of a catastrophe. "Where is further?" "Millbridge. After that, I don't know." "Neither do I." "You have done enough." "That is for me to decide." "Yes." He looked down at his wet hands. "Yes, it is." We walked on. By morning we had reached the high road beyond Millbridge and taken a lift on a cart carrying hurdles. The carter asked no questions because Julian gave him a shilling and then fell asleep against the hurdles with his mouth open. I kept the microscope on my knees. It was heavier than it looked and had a corner that pressed painfully into my thigh. We got down at a town neither of us knew. Julian's boots were split. His coat was stained green at the shoulder, and he had lost his scarf. I had lost my cap and most of the skin from two knuckles. Between us we had six pounds odd, a book of British plants, and no references worth showing to anyone. At an inn we asked for one room. Julian began, "My sister and I—" at the same moment that I said, "My husband and I—" The landlady looked from one of us to the other. "Which?" she said. "We have not decided," Julian told her. His ears went scarlet. I kicked his ankle. She gave us a room because it was empty and we paid in advance. Upstairs, Julian set the microscope on the washstand and looked round at the bed, the single chair, and the cracked basin. "I have made a mess of this," he said. "Yes." "You might occasionally disagree." "Not when you are right." He sat on the chair because I took the bed. There was only one blanket; after an argument conducted chiefly by moving it from one place to another, we lay down side by side in our clothes with our coats over us. He was shivering. I took his hand under the blanket. His fingers closed round mine with none of the hesitation of that night by the fire. "What happens now?" he asked. "Sleep." "After sleep?" "Work, I expect." "Yes." "For both of us." "Yes." He was silent so long that I thought he had fallen asleep. Then he said, "I can identify mosses." "An accomplishment no boarding house can do without." "I can also read Greek." "Better. We shall advertise in the window." He laughed once, tiredly. "And you?" "I can mend, climb, steal, and tell when a man is lying about having read a book." "That last may be valuable." "It has been so far." Outside, carts began to pass. A woman called the price of something below the window. The ordinary morning went on without asking what we had left or what we intended. Julian's shoes stood by the door, ruined beyond repair. He saw me looking at them. "I appear to have forgotten the essential thing again," he said. "No," I told him. "We can buy shoes." After a moment he nodded. We did not live happily ever after. We lived, which took more doing. But that morning there was bread when we woke, and Julian divided it unevenly and pretended he had not. I gave him back the larger piece. He gave it to me again. In the end we left it on the plate and went out to find work, each pretending not to be hungry. One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows. It is a useful art, though limited in its applications. Leaving is harder. There are more things to carry, and one must decide which are worth the weight.
