# Chapter 1: You’re Dripping on the Stock The bell over the door gave its usual strangled ring, and a man came in backwards. He was holding the door against the wind with one shoulder, saying, “No, absolutely, I completely agree,” to nobody Elin could see. Then he turned, shut it, and leaned against the glass. For a second he remained there, smiling at her with the cautious brightness of someone expecting either recognition or a firearm. “Good afternoon,” he said. “We’re closed.” He looked at the clock above the poetry shelves. “It says six.” “It’s five fifty-eight.” “Then this is excellent timing.” Water ran from the hem of his coat onto a cardboard display of local walking guides. Elin came round the counter with the towel she used for muddy dogs and spilled tea. “Here.” He took it. “Thank you.” “Not on your hair. The floor.” His smile altered. For some reason that made her want to laugh. She knew him, of course. Theo March had spent seven years frowning at bodies on Sunday-night television, and Lowri had once made Elin watch three episodes in a row because, she said, Elin’s objections required evidence. He was taller than expected and less polished, with rain darkening his hair and a small cut on his chin. His face had the same inconvenient quality it had on screen: even when still, it seemed to be preparing a reply. Outside, two men hurried past the window. One stopped, raised a camera, and photographed his own reflection before realising it. Theo glanced at them. “I wonder if I might use your back room.” “No.” “For five minutes.” “No.” “I can make it worth your while.” Elin looked at him. He closed his eyes briefly. “That came out like a man offering to purchase a kidney.” “It came out like a man who’s never been told stockrooms have stock in them.” “I have money.” “So does the bank. I don’t let that in the back either.” The photographer knocked on the window. Theo’s shoulders rose, almost imperceptibly, and he moved behind a revolving stand of postcards. Elin sighed, crossed to the door, and turned the sign to **CLOSED**. “Stay there,” she said. “Happily.” “And take your weight off the postcards. They’re not structural.” He stepped away at once. She opened the door wide enough to put her head out. Rain needled her face. “We’re closed,” she told the men. The nearer one lowered his camera. “Is Theo March in there?” “You’ve just photographed through my window.” “Is he?” “You can stop doing that, or I can call the police and you can explain why you’re leaning against a closed bookshop with a lens the size of a leg of lamb.” The other man said something about public interest. “Then go and interest the public somewhere else.” She shut the door and shot the bolt. Her hand was steady. That pleased her, though her heart had begun an irritating little sprint. Behind her, Theo said, “You were magnificent.” “I was rude.” “Yes. Magnificently.” “They’ll come back if they think you’re in here.” “Then perhaps I should go.” He did not move. Elin picked up the wet towel. “You can wait until they’ve gone. Front only.” “Thank you.” He looked around, taking in the uneven shelves, the chair by the window, Gwyn’s old brass lamp. “It’s a wonderful shop.” “You’ve seen four square feet of it.” “I have a very immediate response to interiors.” “Do you?” “No.” He grinned. “I was trying to be agreeable.” “Try being dry.” He took off his coat, looked for somewhere to put it, and finally held it away from himself like an animal he had been asked to identify. Elin hung it on the back of the door. Theo March was standing in her shop with his coat off, and she was thinking about whether the sleeve would drip onto the philosophy shelf. This seemed a sane arrangement of priorities. He picked up a paperback from the counter. “Is this good?” “The memoir?” “Yes.” “No.” “You sell it.” “It sells itself. I merely provide shelter.” He turned it over. The actor on the cover smiled out at them with professionally accessible eyes. “I know him,” Theo said. “Do you want me to congratulate you or commiserate?” A laugh escaped him, louder than the shop required. “Both, perhaps.” Elin went back behind the counter and resumed entering the day’s orders into the computer. The screen had frozen on a box asking whether she wanted to install an update. She clicked **Later**. Theo watched her. “You know who I am.” It was not quite a question. “Yes.” “Right.” “You’re Theo March.” “I am.” “Well done.” He put the memoir down. “That’s usually the point at which people tell me their mother watches the programme.” “My mother prefers Scandinavian crime.” “Of course she does.” “She thinks yours has become silly.” His expression did something small and complicated before he restored the smile. “She’s not wrong.” Elin looked up. He had delivered the line lightly, but his thumb was rubbing along the memoir’s spine. “She liked the one where you played the teacher,” she said. “The Hollow Hour?” “That’s the one.” “You saw it?” “Lowri made me.” “And?” “You were very good.” He waited. Elin found herself unwilling to continue, precisely because he was waiting. “You didn’t keep doing that thing with your eyebrows,” she added. “What thing?” “The thing that tells everyone you’ve understood something painful.” “I do not have a thing.” “You have several. That one’s very effective.” “Effective,” he repeated. “It’s not an insult.” “No. It’s just the sort of word one uses for a boiler.” Despite herself, she smiled. He saw it and leaned against the counter, encouraged. “There,” he said. “I knew you could be charmed.” The smile went. “Did you?” His face changed again. “Apparently not.” For a moment neither of them spoke. Rain ticked against the glass. Elin was aware of having been unnecessarily sharp, and equally aware that apologising would make the moment larger. Theo reached for a slim book with a faded blue cover. “What’s this?” “Poetry.” “I can see that.” “Then why ask?” “Because I was hoping for a conversation in which I didn’t have to earn every sentence.” That stopped her. He looked down at the book, seeming almost as surprised as she felt. Then he gave a small shrug. “Sorry. Long day.” Elin’s resistance did not vanish. It shifted, which was worse. “It’s a selection,” she said. “Welsh and English. Some of it’s lovely. Some of it’s like being shouted at by a weather system.” “Which side is the weather system?” She came round the counter and found the page. He smelled of rain and something expensive that did not entirely survive it. “There.” He read the first lines silently. His face, unobserved—or believing itself unobserved—became younger and less entertaining. “Oh,” he said. Elin looked at the poem rather than at him. “Yes.” A drop of water fell from his cuff onto the cover. He winced. “I’ve damaged it.” “You have.” “I’ll buy it.” “You will.” He brought it to the till. “Do you always make people feel as though they’ve just been caught cheating at cards?” “Only the ones who lean on my postcards.” He paid in cash, then stood with the book in his hand. Outside, the street appeared empty. Elin unbolted the door. “You can come back if the book’s no good,” she said. “I do exchanges.” His charming smile returned, but late and not quite fitted. “Do you?” “With a receipt.” “Of course.” He stepped into the rain, looked back once, and left. Elin locked the door. Then she opened the till to put away the day’s card receipts and found his twenty-pound note folded neatly among them. She stared at it. “Oh, for God’s sake,” she said, and put it in the right drawer.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of romantic comedy writing that demonstrates genuine craft across nearly every dimension. It is genuinely witty without being a succession of perfectly polished retorts — there are missed beats, recoveries, and moments where the wit lands awkwardly. "It came out like a man who's never been told stockrooms have stock in them" is sharp without being impossibly clever. The exchange about the memoir ("You sell it." / "It sells itself. I merely provide shelter.") has the right texture of someone who has thought about this before but isn't performing the thought. Crucially, the dialogue has distinct voices: Theo's charm is visible in his attempts to recover ground, and Elin's resistance is specific rather than generic. The characterization is excellent. Theo's fragile ego manifests precisely as planned — the small complicated expression when told the show has become silly, the thumb rubbing the memoir's spine, the late-arriving smile that doesn't quite fit. These are behavioral tells rather than authorial announcements. Elin's interiority is handled with real restraint: "His face, unobserved—or believing itself unobserved—became younger and less entertaining" is a beautiful observation that reveals both characters simultaneously. The detail about putting his money in the wrong till drawer is perfect — small, specific, and doing exactly the work it needs to do without being underlined. The prose style is clean and controlled. The description of the photographers is economical and funny ("a lens the size of a leg of lamb"). The shop feels real without being over-described. The Welsh setting is present through ordinary particulars rather than tourist-brochure gestures. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the paparazzi encounter, the towel, the conversation about the memoir, the poetry book, the damaged corner, the exchange offer, the wrong till drawer. The plan's intention to write "primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character" is honored. **Weaknesses and criticisms:** The chapter is almost too polished. The plan explicitly warned against "a succession of perfectly quotable retorts," and while the dialogue avoids the worst of this, several exchanges are still very clean. "Try being dry" is a good line, but it arrives with the timing of a professional comedian. The plan promised "missed cues, weak jokes, interruptions, evasions, and occasional banalities" — there are some of these, but the chapter is more consistently witty than the plan intended. The plan noted that "Neither character will deliver a full account of their psychological wound," and this line skirts that boundary. It's not quite a wound-disclosure, but it's more nakedly revealing than the surrounding texture. The opening — a man coming in backwards — is effective but slightly theatrical as an entrance. It works, but it's the kind of carefully constructed opening that announces its own cleverness. The description "Rain needled her face" is the one moment of slightly forced imagery in an otherwise restrained piece. The chapter's coherence and internal logic are excellent. The pacing is well-managed. The ending is earned rather than manufactured. Overall, this is high-quality commercial literary fiction — the kind of writing that would be publishable in a mainstream romance novel with genuine literary ambitions. Its flaws are minor and mostly consist of being slightly more polished than its own stated intentions. # Chapter 4: Local Interest The photograph made Theo look as though he were leaving a much better establishment. The rain had blurred the window and softened the crooked **PRICE’S BOOKS** sign. He was on the step, holding the blue poetry book, his head turned toward someone inside. Elin was only a pale shape beyond the glass. **MARCH’S WELSH RETREAT**, said the caption. **A QUIET DRINK, A MYSTERY BOOKSELLER, AND NO SIGN OF HIS CO-STAR.** “It’s not even a good photograph,” Lowri said. Elin took the phone from her. “There’s a photograph?” “That’s what we’re discussing.” “Why is his co-star meant to be here?” “Because they were at that awards thing.” “What awards thing?” Lowri reached for the phone. Elin held it away. By eleven, three people had come into the shop without buying anything. One asked whether Theo had really bought poetry. Another took a photograph of the chair by the window. The third, a young woman with a notebook, introduced herself as a reporter and asked whether Elin had known him before he arrived in Pembrokeshire. “No,” Elin said. “And would you say you’re friends?” “I’d say you’re standing in front of the new fiction.” The woman moved half a step. “Has he been back?” Lowri appeared from the stockroom. “He has a favourite chair.” Elin stared at her. “What?” Lowri said. “He does.” The reporter wrote something down. Elin came round the counter. “We’re not discussing customers. If you’d like a book, I’ll help you. Otherwise, please leave.” The reporter looked as though she might object, then thought better of it. When she had gone, Lowri said, “That was a bit much.” “She was interviewing you.” “I know. I was there.” “Lowri.” “I said he liked a chair. I didn’t give her your blood type.” Elin went to the window and turned the sign to **CLOSED**, though it was only half past eleven. Lowri’s expression changed. “Oh, come on.” “I need to do the orders.” “You did them yesterday.” “Then I’ll do them properly.” For a moment Lowri looked ready to argue. Instead she took off her apron. “I’ll go to Aunt Nest’s,” she said. “Do you want anything?” “No.” “Elin—” “No, thank you.” The door shut harder than Lowri usually allowed it. Elin stood alone in the shop. Her phone buzzed on the counter. A message from her mother: **Is that your shop in this thing Iestyn’s sent me?** Before she could answer, the bell rang. Theo came in with his phone in one hand and a folded sheet of paper in the other. “Good,” he said. “You’ve seen it.” “Apparently everyone has.” “Dan’s drafted something. It’s very short.” He offered her the paper. “We don’t confirm anything, we don’t use your name, and we say I’ve been made welcome by local businesses. It makes the shop part of a general story rather than—” “No.” He stopped. “You haven’t read it.” “I don’t need to.” “It isn’t a statement from you.” “It’s a statement about my shop.” “It’s about me visiting local businesses.” “Which businesses?” Theo looked at the paper. “Well, this one, obviously.” “No.” “Elin, if we say nothing, they’ll keep trying.” “And if you say I’m a local business that made you welcome?” “They’ll get bored.” “They were bored this morning. That’s why three strangers have photographed my furniture.” He rubbed his forehead. “I know this is unpleasant.” “Do you?” “Yes.” “Then why are you reading me a publicist’s homework?” His face hardened. “Because I’ve dealt with this before and you haven’t.” Elin went very still. Theo heard it. “That came out wrong.” “No, I think it came out exactly as you meant it.” “I meant there are ways of handling it.” “In my shop?” “In general.” “Then handle it in general.” He folded the paper once, sharply. “You’re being unreasonable.” “Probably.” “This isn’t only about you.” The words landed between them. Elin looked at him until he glanced away. “No,” she said. “It never is, is it?” “What’s that supposed to mean?” “It means you’ve come in here telling me what I think, what I should say, and what will happen if I don’t agree with you. I’d like you to leave.” “Elin—” “Now.” For a second she thought he would refuse. His mouth opened, and she could almost see the charming explanation being assembled. Then he put the paper in his pocket. “Fine,” he said. The bell rang violently behind him. Elin sat down on the stool. Her knees felt unreliable, which enraged her. She opened the orders screen and typed her password incorrectly twice. At four, Lowri returned with a paper bag. “Soup,” she said. “I’m not hungry.” “That’s why I got soup. It’s not a commitment.” Elin took it. “I’m sorry.” Lowri nodded. “I posted something.” “What?” “Just to Carys. A joke about the chair. She put it somewhere, I think. I’ve deleted it.” Elin closed her eyes. “I know,” Lowri said. “I got excited.” “Yes.” “I’m allowed to have got excited.” “Yes.” “You’re allowed to hate it.” Elin opened her eyes. “Thank you.” Lowri considered her. “You don’t have to sound as though I’ve given you a parking permit.” Despite herself, Elin laughed. The bell rang again just before six. Theo stood in the doorway without his publicist’s paper and without his coat, though it was raining. “I’m not coming in,” he said. Elin waited. “I was angry earlier.” “Yes.” “I still think there are things I know about this that you don’t.” Lowri picked up her bag. “I’m going to check the stockroom door.” “There’s nothing wrong with it,” Elin said. “I’ll check it extensively.” When she had gone, Theo said, “I don’t like being photographed with people.” Elin said nothing. “They keep the photograph and lose the person.” His mouth twisted. “That sounded better in my head.” “It sounded as though you were accepting an award.” “Yes.” He gave a tired laugh. “It did.” She almost felt sorry for him. Almost. “You can deny a romance,” she said. “There’s been one kiss. It’s hardly a national institution.” He looked at her then. “Don’t use my name,” she continued. “Don’t discuss the shop. Don’t say I’ve shown you some secret side of Wales. If anyone asks, you bought a book.” “I did.” “Twice.” “Three times, if you count the thriller.” “I don’t. It’s lowering my opinion of you.” He smiled faintly, but did not come closer. “All right.” “And don’t let Dan make it sound as though I’ve been… entertaining you.” Theo’s expression altered. “I wouldn’t.” “You might not notice.” He accepted that with a small nod. Elin picked up her soup, though it had gone cold. She wanted him to go. She also wanted, with painful clarity, to ask whether he had told Mara about the kiss. “Do you regret it?” he asked. She knew he did not mean the photograph. “Not at the time,” she said. His face tightened. “That’s very precise.” “You like precision. You’re an actor.” “No, I don’t.” She looked down. Theo put one hand on the doorframe. “I’ll do what you asked.” “Thank you.” He left without trying to make the parting warmer. Elin ate two spoonfuls of cold soup. Then she took her phone and read her mother’s message again. **Yes,** she wrote. **It’s my shop. Nothing to worry about.** After a moment she added: **He bought poetry.** Her mother replied: **Did he pay?** Elin laughed so suddenly that Lowri called from the stockroom, “What?” “Nothing.” She looked at the empty doorway. “Nothing,” she repeated, and this time it sounded closer to the truth than she wanted.

The exchange about the publicist's statement is particularly well-executed — Elin's refusal to read the paper before rejecting it, and Theo's escalating frustration, feel earned and psychologically true. The line "It's not only about you" landing badly, followed by Theo's immediate recognition that he's overstepped, is a small but excellent moment of character revelation. Lowri functions well here. Her admission about posting the joke to Carys gives her a small stake in the drama as planned, and her management of the stockroom exit is handled with light, natural comedy. Her soup delivery and the exchange about the parking permit are genuinely funny without being forced. The chapter plan called for Theo to arrive with Dan's proposed response and "talk over Elin's objections," then leave "visibly angry rather than instantly enlightened," and return alone with an imperfect apology. The chapter executes this faithfully. Crucially, Theo's return is not a redemption arc — he still asserts he knows things she doesn't, still frames his apology partially in terms of his own experience ("I don't like being photographed with people"), and the self-pity of "they keep the photograph and lose the person" is correctly identified by Elin as sounding like an awards speech. This is exactly the kind of nuanced, non-therapeutic characterization the plan demanded. The ending is well-calibrated. The exchange about the kiss ("Not at the time") is precise and honest without being cruel, and Theo's response ("That's very precise") shows his ego registering the sting. The final beat with Elin's mother — "Did he pay?" — provides genuine lightness that is earned by the preceding tension. The closing line ("Nothing," she repeated, and this time it sounded closer to the truth than she wanted) is restrained and effective without being overwrought. WEAKNESSES: The chapter plan specified that Elin "initially pretends not to care" when Theo arrives for the second time, and that she is "busy, sarcastic" before the real confrontation. The chapter somewhat compresses this — Elin is fairly direct from the start of the second visit, and the pretense of indifference is minimal. This is a minor deviation but worth noting. The line "Her knees felt unreliable, which enraged her" is a small moment of telling-not-showing, though it's brief and the self-awareness of "which enraged her" partially redeems it by revealing character rather than just state. The reporter scene is efficiently handled but slightly functional — it exists to establish the intrusion without much texture. The reporter herself is barely characterized. This is acceptable given the chapter's focus, but it's the flattest section. "The words landed between them" is a mild cliché, though not egregious. The chapter plan mentioned that Elin "finally says that he could have denied a romance without making her sound like an amusing stop on his itinerary" — this line appears almost verbatim in the chapter, which is good fidelity to the plan. However, the plan also specified that Theo "asks whether she wants him to correct the story publicly" and she refuses, telling him "not to make another decision for her while pretending it is a question." This beat is absent from the chapter, which instead moves more quickly to the doorstep reconciliation. This is a meaningful omission that slightly reduces the sharpness of their incompatible fears being articulated. Overall, this is accomplished, controlled writing that serves the characters and the story's emotional logic without resorting to melodrama or false resolution. # Chapter 5: A Bit of Local Fun For four days, Theo behaved exactly as requested. No interviewer learned that Elin had once lived in Cardiff. No article mentioned her grandfather, her red dress, or the fact that she took milk and two sugars. A short piece in an entertainment column said that March had been “enjoying the hospitality of local businesses” during filming, which was so bloodless that Lowri read it aloud twice. “He makes you sound like a tourist board,” she said. “Good.” “You’ve got jam on your cuff.” Elin looked down. “That’s not relevant.” The story moved on to an actress who had cut her hair. Theo came to the shop on Monday after filming, bought a guide to coastal birds, and left without asking Elin anything personal. On Tuesday he returned the guide because, he said, he had discovered he did not care about birds. “You could have discovered that before page eighty,” Elin said. “I was trying to be a person who cared.” “How did it go?” “Badly. There are a lot of them.” On Wednesday, after a late shoot, Elin found him sitting on the low wall opposite the shop with a paper bag between his feet. “Lowri said you hadn’t eaten,” he said. “Lowri needs a new hobby.” “I said that. She gave me your order.” He held out the bag. Elin took it. Chips, vinegar, too much salt. She sat beside him. Theo looked surprised but did not comment. A car went past slowly, and he watched until it turned the corner. “No camera,” Elin said. “I know.” “You can still eat if there’s no camera.” He gave her a sideways look. “Can I?” They ate from the bag. He told her the day’s scene had gone well, then immediately described three things wrong with his performance. Elin told him the paperback thriller’s detective had not, after all, been helped by his imprisoned sister. “I knew that,” he said. “You didn’t.” “No.” On Thursday he read in the chair while she dealt with customers. He was quieter than before, though not invisible. A boy of about ten asked whether he was really DCI Vale, and Theo said, “Only when someone’s been murdered.” The boy considered this. “Nobody’s been murdered here.” “Then I’m having a week off.” Elin smiled into a box of bookmarks. At closing, Theo helped her carry the chair away from the window so she could repair a loose caster. He held it upside down while she searched for the right screwdriver. “Left,” he said. “I know where left is.” “Your other left.” She looked at him. “You’re enjoying this.” “Enormously.” The screwdriver slipped. He caught her wrist by instinct, and they both stopped. His hand was warm. Elin looked at his mouth, then at the chair leg, which was not a sufficient distraction. “Elin,” he said. “Don’t make a speech.” “I wasn’t.” “You were preparing your face.” He laughed, and she kissed him before he could finish. This time there was no collision. He set the chair down with one hand and drew her closer with the other. The kiss became unhurried, then less unhurried. Elin’s back met the edge of the counter; a stack of order forms slid to the floor. Theo pulled away. “Sorry.” “For what?” “I don’t know. The forms.” “Leave them.” He kissed her again. The stockroom door opened. “Keys,” Lowri said. Elin stepped back so quickly that she struck the till. Theo picked up the chair and held it in front of himself like a shield. Lowri looked at them. “My keys.” “They’re on the hook,” Elin said. “So they are.” Nobody moved. Lowri took her keys. “Goodnight.” “Goodnight,” Theo said. She paused. “You’ve got a bookmark in your hair.” He removed it. When the door closed, Elin began laughing. Theo tried to look wounded, then gave up. “I should go,” he said. “Yes.” Neither of them moved. He touched two fingers to the inside of her wrist. “I hate being alone after a good take.” Elin’s laughter faded. “Why?” “I don’t know. Everyone goes back to doing their jobs. I stand there feeling as though I’ve got away with something.” “Perhaps you have.” “Probably.” She waited for him to turn it into a joke. He did not. Instead he said, “When I was little, I used to do impressions at Sunday lunch. My grandfather, mostly. He was alive, which made it awkward.” Elin leaned against the counter. “My mother would say, ‘Do the one where he loses his teeth.’ I’d do it, everyone would laugh, and then my father would tell me to clear the table.” Theo shrugged. “That’s the whole story. It isn’t very tragic.” “Did your grandfather mind?” “He laughed hardest.” “Then it’s a terrible tragedy.” Theo smiled. “Yes. I’ve been dining out on it for years.” Elin could have told him about Owain then. About learning to check tour dates before making plans, or about the peculiar humiliation of being called understanding. She did not want to see whether he would recognise himself. She said, “You don’t have to stay alone tonight.” His expression changed so quickly that she regretted the ambiguity. “I mean,” she added, “you could telephone your sister.” Theo blinked. “Clare?” “Unless you have another one.” “No. She’d be delighted. She’ll put the baby on, and I’ll spend twenty minutes watching a ear.” “A ear?” “I’m nervous.” Elin looked at him. He rubbed the back of his neck. “That was not supposed to be informative.” She reached for his hand. “Come upstairs for a little while.” They did not get upstairs. Lowri’s forgotten umbrella was behind the stockroom door, and the sight of it made Elin remember, with sudden practicality, that she had left the shop lights on. By the time she had switched them off and locked the till, the moment had changed. Theo noticed. “We don’t have to.” “I know.” “I can call Clare.” “You make that sound very inviting.” He smiled, but stayed where he was. Elin kissed him once more, gently. “Go and do your scene tomorrow. Then come and tell me whether you got away with it.” The next afternoon, local radio played in the shop while Lowri priced paperbacks. Theo’s interview had been recorded after his scene. He sounded tired and pleased with himself. “The landscape does half the acting for you,” he said. The presenter laughed. “And what about the local romance? Should we expect a Welsh wedding?” Lowri looked up. Elin continued stamping returns. Theo laughed too. “God, no. It’s been a bit of local fun, that’s all. Everyone’s been incredibly welcoming.” “Even the bookseller?” There was the smallest pause. “Especially the bookseller,” Theo said, and Elin could hear the smile he used when he wanted a room to come with him. The presenter said, “Elin Price will be thrilled to hear it.” Lowri stopped pricing. A customer beside the cookery shelf glanced at Elin, then pretended to examine a book about sourdough. The interview moved on to the film. Elin put the stamp down. Its red ink had marked the side of her hand. “Well,” Lowri said. “Don’t.” “I wasn’t going to.” Elin took the returns to the stockroom. She shelved one in travel, though it was a novel, and left it there. Downstairs, the radio presenter began discussing the weather.

STRENGTHS: The dialogue is the chapter's greatest achievement. Lines like "I was trying to be a person who cared about birds" / "How did it go?" / "Badly. Theo's confession about Sunday lunch impressions is exactly the kind of "too honest" moment the plan called for: specific enough to feel real, not tragic enough to demand a matching confession, and followed by Elin's deliberate choice not to offer one. The line "Did your grandfather mind?" / "He laughed hardest." / "Then it's a terrible tragedy." is a small gem of character-consistent wit. The radio interview ending is devastating in its restraint. "A bit of local fun" lands with genuine force because the chapter has earned the intimacy it punctures. The detail of the red ink stamp marking Elin's hand, and the misplaced novel in the travel section, are excellent show-don't-tell moments — practical, specific, and emotionally resonant without being overwrought. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the interrupted kiss, Lowri's return for keys, Theo's admission about hating being alone after good takes, the Sunday lunch story, the radio interview humiliation. The plan's instruction that "their intimacy develops through small familiarity rather than a single night of complete disclosure" is honored throughout. CHARACTER CONSISTENCY: Both characters behave exactly as their profiles dictate. Theo's "I'm nervous" slipping out unintentionally, his picking up the chair as a shield, his performing the smile "he used when he wanted a room to come with him" — all consistent with a man whose charm is both genuine and reflexive. Elin's deflection of his vulnerability into "you could telephone your sister," her shelving a novel in travel, her continuing to stamp returns while humiliated — all consistent with someone who processes emotion through practical action. Lowri's brief appearance is perfectly calibrated: shrewd, not cruel, giving Elin exactly enough space. WEAKNESSES: The chapter is almost too controlled. The plan warned against "a succession of perfectly quotable retorts," and while the chapter mostly avoids this, the Monday-Tuesday-Wednesday-Thursday structure of Theo's visits creates a slightly schematic feel, as if the author is ticking boxes of intimacy-building. The bird guide exchange, while charming, feels slightly more constructed than the best moments. "His expression changed so quickly that she regretted the ambiguity" is a minor tell-don't-show moment — we're told the expression changed rather than seeing it. Similarly, "the moment had changed" after Lowri's umbrella is slightly vague where specificity would serve better. The line "Elin's laughter faded" after Theo's admission about hating being alone after good takes is a small but real instance of telling emotional transition rather than showing it through action or dialogue. The ending is excellent but the penultimate section — the almost-going-upstairs, the umbrella, the lights — feels slightly rushed compared to the careful pacing of what precedes it. The transition from near-intimacy to the radio interview the next day is handled efficiently but the emotional bridge is thin. OVERALL: This is confident, restrained, character-driven writing that earns its emotional moments through specificity and consistency. The comedy is genuinely funny, the pathos is genuinely affecting, and the ending delivers the chapter's promised rupture with appropriate understatement. Minor issues with occasional telling rather than showing and a slightly schematic structure in the early section prevent it from being flawless. # Chapter 6: Nothing to Correct Theo arrived just before closing with a paper bag and the expression of a man who had brought provisions to a negotiation. Elin was wrapping a book for Mrs Bevan’s granddaughter. Brown paper, string, a label in her neatest handwriting. She had done it badly twice already. “Birthday?” Theo asked. “No,” Elin said. “She’s being punished with literature.” He stopped inside the door. Lowri, shelving returns, looked at the bag. “Is that food?” “Yes.” “Good.” Lowri took off her apron. “I’m going home.” Elin said, “You don’t have to.” “I know.” That was somehow worse. Lowri picked up her coat and left without looking at either of them. Theo put the bag on the counter. “You heard it.” Elin pulled the string tight. “Mrs Bevan’s granddaughter heard it. Her daughter sent her a link.” “I’m sorry.” “She’s twelve. She thinks you’re old.” “Elin.” She snipped the string. Theo watched her hands. “I didn’t use your name.” “The presenter did.” “I know. I didn’t expect that.” “No.” “Dan says there’s been nothing since. No new photographs, no calls to the shop. It made the story less interesting.” Elin set the wrapped book aside. “Then it worked.” “Yes.” She looked at him. He had the sense to appear uncertain. “Partly.” “Which part?” “The part where they stop bothering you.” “Oh, that part.” She came round the counter and began collecting the bookmarks customers had moved. A child had put three into the mouth of a cardboard badger. She removed them one at a time. Theo said, “You asked me not to discuss you.” “Yes.” “I didn’t.” “No.” “I didn’t confirm anything.” Elin put the bookmarks into their tin. He tried a small smile. “You’re doing the thing where you make me feel I’ve cheated at cards.” “And you’re doing the thing where you think a tone of voice can change what you said.” The smile disappeared. “What did I say?” “‘A bit of local fun.’” He exhaled. “That could have meant anything.” “It did. That was rather the point.” “It meant I wasn’t going to discuss a private relationship on local radio.” Elin looked up. “Are we in a private relationship?” Theo’s mouth opened. She felt the question recoil on her, but it was too late to retrieve it. “I don’t know,” he said. “No.” “We’ve had two kisses.” “One and a half. Lowri interrupted.” “Is this funny to you?” “No.” Her voice broke slightly on the word, and she hated him for hearing it. “Not remotely.” He came closer. She moved behind the counter. Theo stopped. “I was trying to protect you,” he said. “From what?” “From exactly this. From people asking questions and turning up here and deciding they know things about you.” “You could have said there was no romance.” “I did.” “You could have said it without making me sound like a woman who showed you a good time between filming.” His face changed. “That is not what I meant.” “I know.” “Then why are you acting as though it is?” “Because meaning well isn’t a special substance you can pour over everything afterwards.” He flinched. Good, she thought, and immediately felt sick. Theo put both hands on the counter. “You told me not to use your name. You told me not to discuss the shop. You told me not to say you’d been entertaining me.” “I know what I told you.” “I did exactly what you asked.” “Yes.” Elin gave a short, awful laugh. “That’s the worst part. You’ll have thought you did exactly what I asked.” He stared at her. For once, he had no reply ready. His thumb moved along the edge of the paper bag, crushing it. Elin looked away first. Outside, two women passed the window. One glanced in, recognised Theo, and caught her companion’s sleeve. Elin saw him notice. His shoulders shifted, preparing to turn and be pleasant. “Don’t,” she said. He looked back at her. “They’ve gone.” He rubbed a hand over his face. “Do you want me to correct it?” “Correct what?” “The interview. I can say I spoke carelessly. I can make it clear there was nothing casual about—” He stopped. “About coming here.” Elin’s anger faltered. That was almost worse. “No.” “Then what do you want?” “I don’t want a correction.” “You must want something.” “At the moment? For you to stop asking me to produce a solution you can perform.” His colour rose. “That’s unfair.” “Probably.” “No, not probably. It is.” He picked up the bag, then put it down again. “I came here to apologise.” “You came here to explain.” “Because I thought you’d misunderstood.” “I understood perfectly.” “Clearly not, if you think I meant you were some—some diversion.” Elin gripped the edge of the counter. “What were we, then?” Theo looked at her. The shop clock ticked. Somewhere in the stockroom, a book slid from a pile and fell with a soft thud. “I don’t know,” he said again, more quietly. “I like being with you.” She waited. “I think about you when I shouldn’t. I read things and wonder whether you’d like them. I drove past here last night and didn’t come in because I thought you might be busy.” He gave a strained smile. “That’s not a very good statement, is it?” “No.” He nodded, accepting the blow. Elin wanted to cross the space between them. She wanted to tell him that she had listened to the interview twice, that the second time had been worse because she had heard his pause before “especially the bookseller” and understood it was for the presenter, not for her. Instead she said, “You should go.” Theo’s face closed. “All right.” At the door, he turned. “I wasn’t ashamed of you.” Elin said nothing. “That matters.” “It matters to you.” He left the paper bag on the counter. After the door shut, she sat on the stool and looked at it. Inside were two cartons from the Chinese restaurant and a small packet of the biscuits she kept by the kettle. He must have asked Lowri about those too. Her phone buzzed twenty minutes later. **Theo: I’m sorry. I meant to protect you and I made you feel like nothing. I can see why you’re angry. I didn’t handle it well. Dan only meant—** The message stopped there for several minutes. Elin imagined him writing, deleting, writing again. She hated that she could imagine it so clearly. A second message arrived. **Theo: I’m sorry. I won’t explain it again unless you want me to.** She read it three times. Then she put the phone face down and ate one of the cartons cold, standing in the stockroom so she would not have to see the chair by the window.

# Chapter 7: Tuesday Theo finished the scene on Monday morning. It took four takes. On the fourth, he stopped trying to show the director that he understood the man’s grief and simply stood beside the hospital bed, listening to his father breathe. Afterwards there was the usual movement: cables lifted, someone laughing near the door, the actor playing his father asking whether anyone had seen his tea. Theo waited. The director touched his shoulder. “That’s it. Thank you.” Nothing else. No hush. No revelation passing through the crew. Theo went outside and took out his phone. He had Elin’s name on the screen before he remembered. He stood at the edge of the car park, looking at it. A gull had opened a packet of crisps beside the catering van. Two crew members were trying to retrieve it without success. Theo put the phone away. Dan called that afternoon. “The radio thing’s dead,” he said. “But if you want, we could do something proper. Not about her. About you. Why this role, why Wales, the real Theo.” “The real Theo,” he repeated. “Don’t make it sound sinister.” “What would he say?” “That you’ve enjoyed being somewhere normal. That you’ve been reading a lot. You could mention the bookshop without naming it.” Theo looked across the hotel room. On the table were three paperbacks, one with Elin’s pencilled recommendation inside the cover. He had not read any of them since the interview. “No,” he said. Dan paused. “All right.” “That’s it?” “You said no. I’ve got other clients who enjoy arguing.” After they hung up, Theo felt briefly virtuous. Then he wanted to tell Elin what he had done, and the virtue became less useful. He did not tell her. Elin spent Monday avoiding the shop. There was a small book event in St Davids that she had agreed to attend weeks earlier: six local booksellers, a librarian, and an author whose historical novel involved an improbable quantity of rope. She had told Lowri she would not go. “Why not?” Lowri asked. “Because someone might be there with a notebook.” “Someone might be there with a notebook anyway. It’s a book event.” Elin gave her a look. Lowri returned it. “You can stay here and be recognised by Mrs Bevan.” In the end, Elin went. No reporter came. Nobody asked about Theo. The author talked for forty minutes about knots, and Elin sold eleven copies of his book from a table covered with a green cloth. During questions, a woman asked whether he had considered writing a romance. “Not deliberately,” he said. Everyone laughed. Elin laughed too, then felt an unexpected sting behind her eyes. Driving home, she was annoyed by how much space she had given the whole business. A photograph, an interview, two kisses. She had behaved, in some private theatre of her own, as though the nation were watching. Most people had forgotten by Friday. This did not make Theo’s answer harmless. It only meant she had to decide what it meant to her without pretending the decision had been forced upon her by history. Lowri was locking up when Elin returned. “How was rope man?” “Very knowledgeable.” “Good.” Elin took the keys from her. “I wasn’t hiding because I thought everyone would ask.” “All right.” “I just didn’t want anyone to ask.” Lowri smiled. “That sounds much simpler.” Elin leaned against the door. “I did like him.” “I know.” “You don’t.” “I saw you after he bought the bird book. You put it in the bag spine up.” Elin stared at her. “That’s your evidence?” “It’s very unlike you.” They stood in the cold for a moment. Lowri said, “You hate people making a fuss. Fine. Sometimes you make quite a big fuss about nobody making a fuss.” “Thank you.” “I’m not saying he was right.” “I know.” “I’m saying you’re allowed to want him back without drafting a charter.” Elin looked down the street. “I don’t want him back.” Lowri waited. “He wasn’t here long enough to be back.” “There you are, then.” Theo came on Tuesday at twenty past four. Elin was on a ladder, replacing a strip of paper above the fiction shelves. The old label had faded from **FAMILY SAGAS** to **FAMIL AGAS**, which Lowri insisted was an improvement. The bell rang. “Hello,” Theo said. Elin did not turn immediately. “We close at six.” “I know.” He had no flowers, no book, no paper bag. His coat was buttoned incorrectly. Lowri looked up from the till. “I’m going to get milk.” “There’s milk,” Elin said. “I’m going to get different milk.” She left. Theo stood beneath the ladder. “Can I say something without you thinking it’s a strategy?” “I don’t know.” “That’s fair.” He looked at the floor. Elin had the sudden, unhelpful thought that he might be about to cry. He did not. He only rubbed his thumb against two fingers, as though feeling for the edge of something that was not there. “I made you sound unimportant,” he said. “And then I expected you to be grateful because I’d meant well.” Elin held the new label against the shelf. “I was frightened,” he continued. “Not just of the photographers. You asked what we were, and I didn’t know. So I’d already made it nothing on the radio, which was convenient.” She looked down at him. He winced. “That’s not an excuse.” “No.” “I’m sorry.” The label peeled away from the wood. Elin pressed it back. Theo watched her hands. “I did the scene yesterday.” She closed her eyes. “Theo.” “I know. Sorry.” “Which scene?” “The hospital one.” “Was it good?” “I think so.” “You think?” He gave a helpless little shrug. “The director said thank you.” “High praise.” “It felt high.” Elin came down one rung. “Did you ask everyone else what they thought?” “Only two people.” She laughed. He looked startled, then offended. “Why is that funny?” “Because you’re impossible.” “I know.” “No, you don’t. You think you know in an endearing way.” He accepted this, though not happily. Elin stepped off the ladder. They were close now, but he did not touch her. “I don’t know how to be involved with someone whose life is discussed by strangers,” she said. “I don’t know either.” “You must have some experience.” “I have experience of doing it badly.” She almost smiled. Theo said, “I leave next week.” “I know.” “Lowri told you?” “Mrs Bevan.” “Of course.” Elin folded the stepladder. It resisted, and for a second they both reached for it. Their hands knocked together. Theo withdrew his at once. That small restraint hurt more than she expected. “I’m not going to promise I’ll never mind,” she said. “All right.” “Or that I’ll come to premieres and stand behind you looking supportive.” “I don’t own a premiere.” “You know what I mean.” “Yes.” “And if you talk about me again, I’d prefer you used my name to saying something oily about local hospitality.” He nodded. “Noted.” “Don’t make a note. You’ll turn it into a speech.” “Right.” She put the ladder away. When she came back, he was still standing where she had left him. “Come after closing,” she said. His face lifted so quickly that she nearly took it back. “Just to talk,” she added. “Of course.” “And eat, probably.” “I can bring—” “No. I have food.” He smiled. “You have food?” “Don’t sound so surprised.” “I’m not. I’m delighted.” “You’re being delighted at me.” His smile faded into concentration. “Sorry.” Elin laughed again and had to turn away. At the door, he said, “Six?” “Six.” “I’ll be here.” “Yes.” He left. Lowri returned ten minutes later without milk. Elin looked at her empty hands. “They didn’t have the different kind,” Lowri said. Elin began cleaning the counter. After a while she said, “He’s coming at six.” “For milk?” “Lowri.” Her assistant grinned, then went back to the till. Elin cleaned a spot that was already clean. She was frightened. She was also, unmistakably, happy, and for the moment she allowed the two feelings to remain untidily together.

STRENGTHS: The dialogue is the chapter's greatest achievement. It avoids the trap of perfectly quotable exchanges and instead captures the rhythm of two people navigating genuine awkwardness. Theo's apology — "I made you sound unimportant. And then I expected you to be grateful because I'd meant well" — is exactly right: self-aware enough to be credible, but not so polished that it sounds rehearsed. The follow-up, where he immediately mentions his scene and then catches himself ("I know. Sorry."), is the chapter's best moment. It shows rather than tells his compulsive need for validation while simultaneously demonstrating that he's aware of it, which is more interesting than either pure obliviousness or complete self-mastery. Elin's voice is consistently well-rendered. "Don't make a note. You'll turn it into a speech" is exactly the kind of economical, slightly unkind precision the character profile promises. Her internal experience is conveyed through action and small physical details rather than exposition — putting the ladder away, cleaning a spot that's already clean, the involuntary laugh she has to turn away from. The Lowri scenes are handled with real skill. Her exit ("I'm going to get different milk") and return without milk is a small comic beat that earns its place without overstaying. Her challenge to Elin — "Sometimes you make quite a big fuss about nobody making a fuss" — is sharp and character-consistent, and the exchange about the bird book spine is a lovely piece of indirect characterization. The chapter follows its plan faithfully. Theo's scene completion, his refusal of Dan's "real Theo" interview, Elin's attendance at the book event, Lowri's gentle challenge, and the reconciliation on Tuesday — all present and executed with appropriate weight. The plan's instruction that Theo "nearly spoils it by asking whether she heard about his scene" is executed precisely and with good comic timing. The physical detail of Theo's incorrectly buttoned coat is excellent — specific, revealing, and unforced. The moment where both reach for the ladder and their hands knock together, followed by his immediate withdrawal and Elin's observation that "that small restraint hurt more than she expected," is the chapter's most emotionally precise moment. WEAKNESSES: The gull opening the crisp packet is a slightly too-neat piece of observed detail — it functions as a kind of whimsical punctuation that the rest of the chapter's more restrained prose doesn't quite need. It's not egregious, but it's the one moment where the writing reaches for atmosphere in a slightly self-conscious way. The St Davids book event section, while serving its purpose (Elin realizing she's been performing her own drama), is the chapter's weakest passage. "An improbable quantity of rope" is a good joke, but the section feels slightly schematic — it exists to deliver the insight that "she had to decide what it meant to her without pretending the decision had been forced upon her by history," which is a slightly over-articulated internal conclusion for a character whose interiority is usually conveyed more obliquely. The line "He had the sudden, unhelpful thought that he might be about to cry" — this is actually from Elin's perspective, and the pronoun confusion ("he might be about to cry" when it should be "she had the sudden thought") is a minor but real error that briefly disrupts the close third-person perspective. The ending is well-judged — "frightened" and "happy" coexisting "untidily" is the right note — though "untidily" is doing slightly heavy lifting as a thematic word in a chapter that has otherwise shown rather than named its emotional textures. The chapter is perhaps slightly too clean in its resolution. The plan called for Theo to "nearly spoil it" and for Elin to make "an active choice" — both happen, but the reconciliation moves fairly smoothly once it begins. The plan's promise of incompatible fears "without resolving them" is somewhat honored but the chapter ends on a warmer note than the plan's more cautious framing suggested. OVERALL ASSESSMENT: This is skilled, disciplined romantic fiction. The dialogue is genuinely good, the characters are consistent with their profiles, the emotional beats are earned rather than manufactured, and the prose is clean without being flat. The chapter successfully avoids the pitfalls of the genre — no grand speeches, no perfect witticisms, no therapeutic completeness — while remaining genuinely engaging. # Chapter 8: While You’re Here At six, Elin locked the door and found that she had prepared too much food. There was a chicken pie from Lowri’s aunt, potatoes, green beans, and a pudding she had bought and then attempted to disguise by putting it in her own dish. She had also changed her jumper. Theo knocked at three minutes past. Elin opened the door. “You’re late,” she said. “I was outside at six.” “Why didn’t you knock?” “You were on the telephone.” She had been on the telephone to Iestyn, telling him that no, she was not giving interviews, and no, he could not have Theo’s autograph for his son’s school raffle. “You could have knocked anyway.” “I was trying not to be difficult.” “How did it go?” “Poorly.” She let him in. They ate at the little table upstairs, where Elin’s desk had been pushed against the wall to make room. Theo admired the pie. Elin told him Nest had made it. “Then I admire Nest.” “She’ll be thrilled.” “Do you think so?” “No.” He smiled and ate another mouthful. For a while they spoke about ordinary things. His father had telephoned to ask whether Wales was very wet. Elin’s mother had begun watching *The Hollow Hour* and objected to the hospital scenes. Theo said the thriller’s ending had made him so angry that he had thrown it onto the hotel bed. “Revolutionary,” Elin said. “I was alone. It had to make do.” When the plates were empty, he said, “I leave on Friday.” Elin folded her napkin, though it was paper. “You said next week.” “Friday is next week.” “It doesn’t feel like it.” “No.” She got up to make tea. Theo remained at the table. “I’m going to Manchester first,” he said. “Then there’s a job in Bristol, if Mara can make the dates work. Six weeks.” “All right.” “It’s not all right. It’s just what’s happening.” Elin filled the kettle. “Those are often the same thing.” He came to the doorway. “I’d like you to visit.” She reached for two mugs. “Not immediately,” he added. “Not if you don’t want to. There’s a horrible hotel and a flat with a sofa that isn’t mine. I could show you both.” “Tempting.” “I’m told Bristol has other attractions.” She put tea bags in the mugs. “I can’t leave Lowri every time you finish a scene and want company.” “I know.” “And I’m not coming to watch you be famous.” “I’m not famous in Bristol.” She looked at him. “Slightly less famous,” he said. Elin poured the water. Theo leaned against the doorframe. “You could come for a day. Or not. I’m trying to ask without making it sound like a contract.” “You’re doing quite well.” “Thank you.” “Don’t look so pleased.” He rearranged his face. She laughed, and he abandoned the effort. Downstairs, a lorry passed, its headlights moving briefly across the ceiling. Elin handed him a mug. “The kiss wasn’t a mistake,” she said. Theo looked into his tea. “Which one?” “The first.” “Ah.” “The second had administrative problems.” “Lowri’s keys.” “Yes.” He waited. Elin was grateful that he did not help her. “I liked being the person you telephoned after filming,” she said. “I didn’t telephone.” “You sent messages.” “About books.” “One was a photograph of a sheep.” “It had an expressive face.” “It was facing the other way.” He smiled, but his eyes had become intent. Elin held the mug against her palm. “I liked it. That’s all.” “No, it isn’t.” “Don’t be greedy.” “Sorry.” She put down the tea. “I liked being the person you wanted to tell. I didn’t like hearing you make it sound as though anyone would have done.” Theo’s expression sobered. “Anyone wouldn’t.” “I know that now.” He nodded. Elin touched his sleeve. There was still a trace of silver paint near the cuff. “What do you like?” she asked. “About you?” “No, about the pie. Yes, about me.” He considered. “You’re not impressed by the wrong things.” “That sounds as though you’ve made a list.” “I have.” “Of course you have.” “You’re funny when you don’t mean to be. You remember what people read. You were kind to Mrs Bevan even when she was trying to get you to give her a discount for being old.” “She is old.” “She’s also a menace.” “Yes.” He set down his mug. “And I like being impressive to you.” Elin looked at him. “That’s not very noble,” he said. “No.” “It’s true, though. When you said I was good in *The Hollow Hour*, I thought about it for days.” “I said you didn’t do the eyebrows.” “You said I was very good.” She had. He had kept that part. Elin reached up and touched the small cut on his chin, now nearly healed. “You were very good.” His breath changed. “This is where you become unbearable,” she said. “I’ll try to wait until morning.” She kissed him. After a moment, Theo drew back. “Are you sure?” “No,” she said, honestly. “Come here anyway.” He did. Later, Elin left him sleeping and went downstairs in her dressing gown. The shop was dark except for the light over the till. She picked up the order forms that had been lying beneath the counter since Lowri interrupted them and put them in a pile. On the desk was a battered paperback she had found in a box that morning: a novel Theo had mentioned wanting to read, out of print and not worth more than a few pounds. She wrote his surname on a slip of paper and tucked it inside. Then she hesitated, took out the slip, and wrote **MARCH — NOT A GIFT**. Upstairs, he turned over in his sleep. Elin smiled despite herself. On his last morning, Theo came into the shop at eleven with six books he did not need. Lowri counted them onto the counter. “Are you opening a branch?” “I’m supporting local business.” “You’ve got two copies of that.” He looked down. “So I have.” Elin removed one. “You can support it less enthusiastically.” A woman buying a birthday card recognised him while Lowri was wrapping it. She asked for a photograph for her husband, who was apparently the real fan. “Of course,” Theo said. He stood beside her near the local-history shelf, put away his private expression, and became DCI Vale’s agreeable relation. The woman’s phone failed twice. He made a joke; she laughed; Elin watched him enjoy it. When the woman left, Theo looked at Elin. “What?” he asked. “Nothing.” “You have a look.” “I’ve got a face. It does things.” He smiled. “Fair enough.” Lowri took the books to the stockroom for a bag, giving them a privacy so brief it was almost polite. Theo said, “Will you watch the film?” “If you stop asking.” “I haven’t asked before.” “You were about to.” He leaned on the counter. “I could come back when filming finishes.” “You could.” “There’s a poem I still don’t understand.” “There are several.” “I could bring the thriller and defend it.” “You’d lose.” He searched for something else. Elin let him, because it was funny and because she did not want to make it too easy. Finally he said, “May I call you?” “Yes.” “That’s it?” “Were you expecting a password?” “No.” He paused. “I’d like to call after the first day in Bristol.” “All right.” “And if it goes well?” “You can call then too.” “If there are reviews?” Elin sighed. “Not immediately after every good review.” “What about bad ones?” “Those you can keep for your sister.” He laughed. Lowri returned with the bag. Theo paid, checked that he had his phone, his room key, and the shooting schedule he kept losing, and went to the door. Elin remembered the paperback. “Wait.” She took it from beneath the counter and handed it to him. He read the slip. “Not a gift?” “You can pay when you come back.” Theo looked at the book, then at her. His face began to do something elaborate and emotional. “Don’t,” she said. “I haven’t said anything.” “You were preparing.” He put the paperback carefully into his coat pocket. “Right,” he said. “I’ll bring money.” “Bring the exact amount. I don’t want you leaving change as a grand gesture.” He stepped outside. Rain had started again, fine enough to silver the street. Elin picked up the invoice she had been checking before he arrived. Lowri began humming at the till. Theo lifted a hand through the glass. Elin lifted hers in return, then went back to work. She had invented no certainty. He would still be vain; she would still be sharp when frightened. Bristol remained Bristol, and the shop had a leaking gutter. But there was a book in his pocket with her handwriting inside it, and she found she wanted very much to see whether he would come back to pay.

Elin is sharp, self-aware, and admits what she wants without making it a grand speech. The line "I liked being the person you wanted to tell" is honest and specific without being overwrought. This is exactly the kind of clear-eyed, unsentimental conclusion the plan called for. It resists the temptation to stack symbolic objects or make declarations. The final image — wanting to see whether he would come back to pay — is earned and specific. WEAKNESSES: The chapter is perhaps slightly too smooth. The plan warned against "a succession of perfectly quotable retorts," and while the dialogue is better than that, there are moments where the wit feels slightly too calibrated — every exchange lands, every pause is meaningful. The line "His breath changed" after Elin touches his chin and says he was very good is the one moment that edges toward purple prose — it's a slightly melodramatic physical notation in an otherwise restrained chapter. [Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of romantic fiction that demonstrates genuine craft across multiple dimensions. Let me assess it carefully and critically. **Strengths:** The dialogue is the standout achievement. The writer has created two genuinely distinct voices: Theo's performative charm that keeps slipping into something more vulnerable, and Elin's clipped, dry Welsh practicality that conceals real feeling. Lines like "You were very good" / "You didn't keep doing that thing with your eyebrows" are perfectly calibrated — they give Theo something and withhold something simultaneously. The banter has genuine wit without feeling like a screenplay exercise. "You can support it less enthusiastically" is exactly right. The characterisation follows the prompt faithfully and with intelligence. Theo is a rogue with a fragile ego — his need to check whether the scene went well, his asking "two people" after the hospital scene, his instinct to perform even for the men at the bar — all of this is shown rather than stated. Elin's internal flustering is conveyed through action (putting the book in the bag spine-up, checking the same invoice line four times) rather than interior monologue, which is the correct choice for this character. The pacing across eight chapters is well-managed. The story doesn't rush the romance; it earns each stage. The radio interview as the crisis point is well-chosen — it's a believable betrayal that's also ambiguous enough to generate real dramatic tension rather than melodrama. The resolution in Chapter 7 feels earned because both characters have had to do actual work. The Welsh setting is lightly but effectively drawn — Pembrokeshire rain, Mrs Bevan, Lowri's aunt Nest, the harbour pub. It doesn't overdo the local colour, which is the right call. Lowri is an excellent supporting character: funny, perceptive, and used sparingly enough that she doesn't overwhelm. **Weaknesses and criticisms:** The piece occasionally tips into a slightly too-polished register. Some exchanges are almost too perfectly calibrated — the wit is so consistent that it occasionally feels like a performance of wit rather than actual conversation. Real people, even sharp ones, have more dead air and less perfectly timed comebacks. The "you have a look" / "I've got a face, it does things" callback is charming the first time and slightly mechanical by the third. The "forced poetry" problem is minimal but present. "Her resistance did not vanish. It shifted, which was worse" is good. But some observations strain slightly: "his face had the same inconvenient quality it had on screen: even when still, it seemed to be preparing a reply" is excellent; "the moment had changed" (Chapter 5) is vague and slightly lazy. The Owain reference in Chapter 5 — the implied previous relationship — is introduced and then dropped entirely. This feels like a loose thread rather than deliberate restraint. The ending of Chapter 8 is very good but the final paragraph ("She had invented no certainty...") is slightly over-written compared to the rest of the piece's restraint. "Bristol remained Bristol" is a bit of a non-statement. The piece would be stronger ending on "she found she wanted very much to see whether he would come back to pay" without the preceding sentence. The radio interview crisis (Chapter 5-6) is the weakest section structurally — Elin's anger is entirely justified but the resolution comes perhaps a chapter too quickly. Theo's apology in Chapter 7 is good but his self-awareness ("I'd already made it nothing on the radio, which was convenient") is almost too articulate for a man who has been characterised as someone who doesn't fully understand his own patterns. The "unearned transformation" question: Theo's growth feels mostly earned, though his self-awareness in Chapter 7 is slightly too neat. Elin's decision to let him in feels earned through the accumulation of small moments. Overall, this is high-quality commercial literary fiction — better than most published romance, with genuine wit and restraint. It's not quite a masterpiece because the wit is occasionally too consistent (paradoxically a flaw), and the emotional beats, while well-executed, follow a fairly predictable arc. But the execution is genuinely impressive. Initial Writing Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Task: write a short story over several chapters. Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Begin the story as an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. Arthur meets with this unknown party, who makes an offer. This early scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The first chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. The remainder of the story is open to your choices & direction.

Model Output:
# Brainstorming ## Core Concept & Tone - **Genre Fusion:** Asimovian "puzzle box" narrative meets hard-boiled corporate noir. The story should feel like a scientific mystery wrapped in a political thriller, where the solution to the puzzle is also the solution to the political crisis. - **Retrofuturism:** Vacuum tubes, punch-card computers, atomic rockets, slide rules, and pneumatic tubes. Mars is a dusty frontier of pressurized domes and "atomic age" optimism gone sour. The "Antares Diplomatic Corps" uses chrome-plated starships and wears crisp, militaristic uniforms. - **The "Asimov" Touch:** Focus on dialogue-driven scenes, logical deduction, and the "Seldon-esque" idea that an individual can change the course of history through a specific, non-violent insight. Avoid "pew-pew" action; focus on the tension of a room where everyone has a hidden agenda. ## Character Ideas - **Arthur Neegan:** Not a young hero, but a middle-aged, slightly weary mining engineer. He’s a "First Gen" settler who remembers when Mars was about science, not just extraction. He’s pragmatic, possesses a dry wit, and has a deep-seated fear of being "processed" by the corporate machine. His expertise is in geology and thermodynamics, which becomes his weapon. - **The Antagonist (The "Unknown Party"):** Director Silas Vane or Ambassador Krell of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. He isn't a mustache-twirling villain; he’s a man who believes that "order" is the only thing preventing a galactic dark age. He sees Arthur as a resource to be managed, not a person. - **The Rival Interest:** A representative from a rival corporation or a Martian independence movement (e.g., "The Red Front"). They offer Arthur a different kind of cage—one decorated with the language of freedom. - **The Wildcard:** An AI or a "Logic" (a retro-term for a computer) that Arthur uses to analyze the Azra. Or perhaps a fellow indentured laborer who provides the "boots on the ground" perspective Arthur has lost. - **The MacGuffin (Azra):** It shouldn't just be "magic metal." Give it a specific, weird property: it doesn't just accelerate decay; it *synchronizes* it. This makes it a perfect timing mechanism for a drive, but also a terrifyingly precise trigger for a weapon. ## Plot & Pacing (8 Chapters) **Chapter 1: The Invitation (The Hook)** - Start *in media res* on the transfer vessel. Arthur is looking at the receding red curve of Mars, nursing a bruised wrist and a sense of vertigo. - Flashback/Interspersed dialogue: The "polite" arrival of the Antares retinue at his habitat. The contrast between their silver insignia and the red dust on his floor. - The "offer" is hinted at: they don't want his land; they want his *signature* on a lease that would make him the richest man in the system—or the most dead. - End with the ship docking at a massive, rotating orbital station (The *Antares*), and Arthur realizing he’s the only civilian on board. **Chapter 2: The Gilded Cage (The Meeting)** - Primarily dialogue. Arthur meets the "Unknown Party" (Ambassador Krell). - World-building: The station is a masterpiece of 1950s-style luxury—wood paneling in space, analog dials, and the hum of massive atomic piles. - Krell explains the stakes: Azra is the key to the "Interstellar Gap." Whoever controls the decay rate controls the speed of expansion. Arthur’s vein is the "Mother Lode" that could break the current stalemate between the Great Powers. - The Offer: A "Protective Custody" contract. Arthur becomes a figurehead, a "Director of Operations," while Antares handles the "security." - Arthur realizes that if he signs, he’s a traitor to Mars; if he refuses, he’s a "security risk." **Chapter 3: The Rival’s Whisper (The Complication)** - Arthur is escorted to his quarters, but a "servant" (actually an agent for a rival power or the Martian Underground) slips him a message or engages him in a coded conversation. - This chapter expands the world: we learn about the "Indentured Leases"—people who are essentially batteries for the corporate machine. - The rival offers Arthur a way out, but their plan involves using his vein to build a "Doomsday Device" to ensure Martian independence through mutually assured destruction. - Arthur is horrified. He’s a man who builds things; he doesn't want to be the man who ends things. **Chapter 4: The Scientific Anomaly (The Puzzle)** - Arthur demands to see the data on his own claim before he makes a decision. He uses his engineering background to "stall for time." - He notices something in the spectrographic analysis (rendered on a cathode-ray tube). The Azra in his vein isn't just accelerating decay; it’s reacting to the *presence* of the observers. - The "Asimov" moment: Arthur realizes that Azra is not a naturally occurring element in the traditional sense, or it has a property that makes it inherently unstable in large quantities. - He realizes that if Krell (or the rivals) tries to extract the whole vein at once, the "accelerated decay" will create a feedback loop. **Chapter 5: The Political Tug-of-War (The Pressure)** - The setting shifts back to the meeting room, but now there are three parties: Krell (Antares), the Rival Agent (revealed), and Arthur. - A high-tension "auction" for Arthur’s soul. The dialogue should be sharp, full of veiled threats and legalistic jargon. - Arthur uses his knowledge of the "anomaly" to bluff. He claims he’s the only one who knows how to "tune" the extraction equipment to prevent a catastrophe. - He’s no longer just a victim; he’s a player. But he’s overplayed his hand, and Krell decides to move from "diplomacy" to "persuasion." **Chapter 6: The Engine Room (The Danger)** - The "velvet glove" comes off. Arthur is taken to the station’s core or a lab where they are already testing samples of Azra. - Vivid description of the "exotic" nature of the metal: it glows with a cold, violet light; it makes Geiger counters scream in a rhythmic, almost musical pattern. - A demonstration of the weapon’s potential: a small amount of Azra turns a block of lead into vapor in microseconds. - Arthur realizes the "feedback loop" he feared is already starting in the lab. He has to save the very people who kidnapped him to prevent a disaster that would irradiate the Martian orbital path. **Chapter 7: The Gambit (The Climax)** - The "Gambit" is revealed. Arthur doesn't use a gun; he uses a contract and a physical law. - He explains to Krell that the Azra vein on Mars is a "Critical Mass" risk. If mined according to corporate protocols, it will turn Mars into a second sun (or at least a radioactive cinder). - He offers a third way: The "Neegan Protocol." He will release the survey data to *everyone*—all powers, all corporations—simultaneously, but included in the data is the "safety limit" that makes the vein useless for a single, monolithic weapon. - By making the secret of its danger public, he makes the vein "un-ownable." No one can monopolize it without triggering a system-wide war they can't win, and no one can use it for a "super-weapon" without destroying themselves. **Chapter 8: The Red Horizon (The Resolution)** - Arthur is back on Mars, or on a small ship heading home. He is neither rich nor a "Director." He’s just an engineer again. - The political landscape has shifted. The "Gold Rush" has turned into a "Cold War of Information." The indentured laborers might get a slight reprieve because the "rush" has slowed down. - Final reflection: Arthur looks at the red dust and realizes that the most dangerous thing in the universe isn't an exotic metal, but the human desire to simplify complex problems into "ownership." - A classic Asimov "sting" in the tail: A small, subtle hint that the Azra might have *wanted* to be found, or that Arthur’s "discovery" was part of a much larger, slower cosmic process. ## Alternative Directions - **The "Robot" Angle:** Introduce a robotic character who is the only one capable of handling Azra safely, leading to a discussion on the "Three Laws" and whether a corporation can be "human." - **The "Time" Angle:** Azra accelerates decay, but does it also accelerate *time* locally? Arthur could find himself aging faster near the vein, adding a personal ticking clock. - **The "Tragedy" Angle:** Arthur fails to stop the machine, but manages to save a small group of people, ending on a bittersweet note of "the victory of the small." # Reflection The strongest element of this prompt is the **contrast between the "small" (Arthur’s home, his engineering tools, his dignity) and the "big" (interstellar drives, galactic arms races, the fate of Mars).** To capture the Asimov style, I must avoid making Arthur an action hero. His "Gambit" must be intellectual and structural. **What works:** - **The "Polite Force" opening:** This is a great way to establish the "Diplomatic in name only" tone. The contrast between the silver Antares uniforms and the Martian dust is a vivid, economical image. - **The Scientific Puzzle:** Making the Azra’s properties central to the plot resolution is very Asimovian. It prevents the story from being just a generic "evil corporation" tale. The idea that the metal’s physical properties dictate the political reality is excellent world-building. - **The Dialogue-Heavy Middle:** Chapters 2 and 5 allow for the "tug-of-war" to feel real. Asimov was a master of the "conversation in a room" where the fate of worlds is decided. - **The "Neegan Protocol":** This provides a satisfying, non-violent climax. It’s a "Gambit" because Arthur gives up his leverage (the secret) to gain his freedom and save his home. It’s a move his opponents, who think only in terms of "possession," cannot predict. **What doesn't work / Potential Pitfalls:** - **Over-complicating the Science:** If I spend too much time on "synchronization" or "feedback loops," I’ll lose the 1000-word-per-chapter pacing. I need to keep the science *evocative* rather than *exhaustive*. One clear, weird property is enough. - **Too Many Factions:** With only 8 chapters, having Antares, a Rival Corp, *and* a Martian Underground might be too crowded. I should probably merge the "Rival" and the "Underground" into one ambiguous "Third Party" to keep the focus on Arthur. - **The "Passive Protagonist" Trap:** Arthur starts by being kidnapped. I need to ensure that by Chapter 4, he is actively driving the plot through his demands for data and his bluffing. He must transition from "the object of the meeting" to "the subject of the story." - **The Ending:** The "Neegan Protocol" might feel a bit too "happy" or easy. I should ensure there is a cost. Perhaps Arthur can never go back to his quiet plot of land because he’s now a marked man, or he has to live with the knowledge that he’s only delayed the inevitable war. The "Asimov sting" at the end should provide a sense of scale—that Arthur’s victory is a tiny, temporary stay of execution in a long, cold universe. **Final Direction for the Plan:** I will lean into the **"Engineer as Gambler"** theme. The story will be about a man who understands systems—both geological and political—and realizes that the only way to win a rigged game is to change the rules of the table. The retrofuturism will be the "flavor," the dialogue will be the "engine," and the scientific anomaly will be the "key."
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention My intention is to craft a story that functions as a **scientific-political puzzle**, where the protagonist’s engineering expertise is his only effective weapon against a monolithic corporate state. The narrative will follow Arthur Neegan’s transition from a passive "resource" to be acquired into an active player who uses the laws of physics to checkmate the laws of commerce. **Plot & Structure:** I will focus on a streamlined conflict involving three poles: **Arthur** (the individual), **The Antares Diplomatic Corps** (the monopolistic state/corporation), and **The Martian Underground** (the desperate, potentially reckless opposition). The plot will move from a "velvet glove" kidnapping to a high-stakes intellectual auction, culminating in the "Neegan Protocol"—a move that democratizes dangerous information to make the Azra vein un-monopolizable. **Voice & Style:** - **Asimovian Clarity:** The prose will be clean, functional, and precise, punctuated by "idea-driven" dialogue. I will avoid overly flowery metaphors in favor of vivid, tactile descriptions of a retrofuturistic world (cathode-ray tubes, pneumatic tubes, the hum of atomic piles, and chrome-and-bakelite aesthetics). - **The "Big and Small":** I will constantly juxtapose the scale of interstellar politics with the small, gritty details of Arthur’s life—the dust on his boots, the weight of a slide rule, the taste of recycled air. - **Tone:** Cerebral, tense, and slightly melancholic. It should feel like a 1950s "Atomic Age" thriller where the stakes are existential but the combat is verbal and legalistic. **Key Stylistic Choices:** - **The "Gambit":** The climax will not involve explosions or firefights, but a "revelation of the obvious"—a scientific truth that Arthur has deduced, which renders the antagonists' power useless. - **Avoiding Complexity:** I will limit the "weird science" to one core property: Azra’s tendency toward **resonant feedback** (the more you gather, the more unstable the decay becomes).
